And if we believe blessed Gregory expounding it, in David the adulterer Christ is understood through a mystery, and in innocent Uriah is understood that faithless Jewish people. What wonder therefore if by the unjust king whom we disapprove we understand a just thing which we approve? And indeed in the unjust king, although the will was disordered, yet the power belonging to him was ordered. For there is no power but from God. *And the things which are from God,* the Apostle bearing witness, *are ordered [n: (Rom. XIII)]*. [var: Vulg. Rom. 13:1 *quae autem sunt, a Deo ordinatae sunt*, "the powers that are, are ordained by God"; Migne draws the agent into the relative clause and prints the neuter participle] [1233B] And so fittingly enough the royal power signifies the spirit of virtues, which claims for itself that inward kingdom by its morals; or free will, through which, by cooperating grace, the spirit commands its own affections and passions.



## CHAPTER II. *How the grace of contemplation is to some at one time given, at another withdrawn, and meanwhile, when lost, recovered.*

*In the second year of the reign of Nabuchodonosor, Nabuchodonosor saw a dream, and his spirit was terrified, and his dream fled from him [n: (Dan. II)]*. The first zeal of a manly spirit ought to be that it may have dominion over the affections; the second, that it may command the thoughts; the third, therefore — the spirit, and the soul that is victor over its own vices, [1233C] begins from that time already to have in its own kingdom all spiritual things whatsoever, when, its excesses being now subdued, it prevails to command not only the affections but also the thoughts, so that it may be able to restrain both, the former from unlawful concupiscence and the latter from unfitting wandering. But what is it to see a dream, and to foresee the foretokens of things to come or the mysteries of hidden things, unless to receive divinely the grace of contemplation, and through excess of mind to perceive out of divine revelation the knowledge of the divine judgments? And rightly did this king see the dream in the second year, because every spiritual man, after the taming of concupiscence and the discipline of his knowings, at length at some time prevails and grows accustomed to be at leisure for the zeal of contemplation. [1233D] But it often comes to pass that, while the human spirit is led to contemplate the subtlety, or even the strictness, of the divine judgments, it is shaken to the marrow with a sudden fear out of that very consideration of the divine strictness which it perceives. For while a mind that is untrained, and less instructed in heavenly disciplines, still presumes all things upon its own effort rather than upon divine grace, it easily falls into this fear from the contemplation of the divine severity and the consideration of that equity. For a presumptuous mind, when with wondrous subtlety it beholds how far it is above human virtue to answer to the divine benefits, and how strictly the divine severity, by the right of equity, may and ought to deal with us, is often wont to hurl itself into an immense dread [1234A] (nay, almost even into despair). But while the trembling spirit is confounded with a dread of this sort (to say nothing of how justly, beyond all doubt, and as mercifully as profitably), under this crisis of necessity the grace of contemplation is withdrawn, lest by the excess of its own subtlety it be hurled wholly into the pit of despair. And so the dream as it were flees from him, while he loses that light of contemplation which he was wont to see through excess of mind.

*But the king commanded that the soothsayers, and the magicians, and the sorcerers, and the Chaldeans should be called together, that they might declare to the king his dreams [sic: sommia].* He assuredly bears a kingly spirit who is wont to command his own desires, and to dispose his zeals and his exercises according to the judgment of deliberation. [1234B] And so a kingly spirit of this sort makes all the wise men of Babylon come together into one, and in a manner drives diverse sects into one by scrutiny, when it spends upon the one and only business of heavenly doctrine all that solicitude and searching which it was wont to scatter through varied zeals and exercises. But from wise men of this sort, coming together as it were into one, we seek back as it were our lost dreams, when we busy ourselves to repair, by the manifold and untiring urgency of our zeals, the spectacles of our contemplation that have been withdrawn. *Who, when they had come, set up before the king.* [var: Vulg. Dan. 2:2 *steterunt*, "they stood"; the word Migne prints is transitive and leaves the clause without an object] Behold what is said; behold what manner of assembly is declared to stand before the king. Thou mayest reckon that thou hast not yet a kingly spirit, if thou art not yet able to gather from every side, at thy wish, those most subtle points of thy thoughts, [1234C] and, by the liberty of thy judgment, to fix them unmovably upon the zeal of whatever intention thou wilt. *And the king said to them: I saw a dream, and being confounded in mind I know not what I saw.* We address the assembly of our wise men when in our inmost parts we rebuke the wandering of our searchings, or inflame it to the investigation of sublime things. But let us be zealous, after the likeness of this man, not to neglect the losses of our advances, but rather to stir up our zeals unto their repair.

This surely is to be noted, that above he says that he was terrified, but here that he was confounded in mind. But it is to be known that the human mind, while it is lifted up to contemplate more clearly the steep things of the divine equity, [1234D] is, by the beating back of its own infirmity, at one and the same time confounded from that same source whence it is terrified. For beyond doubt, in the consideration of the divine justice and in the comparison of human weakness, a man shudders at his own infirmity, and equally blushes at it. *And the Chaldeans answered the king in Syriac: O king, live for ever.* Tell the dream to thy servants, and we will declare the interpretation thereof. In the first place it must be considered to whom and in what manner they answered. Namely, to a Chaldean king, in Syriac — which indeed is the same thing, as Jerome has determined upon this same place, as in Chaldee. What then is it to answer the king in his own tongue, unless expressly and manifestly to convey that which it behooves to be known? For when anything is said to a man in [1235A] a foreign and unknown tongue, the noise of the voice indeed comes to the ears, but the sense of it does not enter as far as the spirit. Therefore answer is made as it were in one's own and known tongue, when that which the occasion demands is fittingly made known. But if we have recourse to the interpretation of the name, we are beyond doubt brought back to the same meaning. For Syria is interpreted *sublime.* What then will it be to answer in Syriac, unless to answer sublimely? and what will it be to answer sublimely, unless to answer fittingly and sufficiently? But the spirit knows nothing better, nothing more certain, and nothing more sublime than what it has learned through experience; and perhaps this is the proper and chief, and altogether the most sublime, manner of learning belonging to the human soul, when by our own experience [1235B] we prove something. Do not thy own thoughts or occupations answer thee as properly as openly, and instruct thee unto the truth sublimely enough, when out of their own failure they teach, and as it were through experience declare, how vainly and how rashly anything above the human measure is presumed upon one's own effort? Surely the whole answer of these men seems chiefly to contain this (namely, that) they were altogether unable to do what the king was violently demanding. In wise men of this sort therefore, such as we have showed thee above, this will be, as I judge, their answering: to teach their own impossibility by their own experience. But let us handle the several parts of their answer, and first let us see concerning the first.



## CHAPTER III. *That in all that we do we ought to be zealous for a good intention and to lean upon divine grace.*

[1235C]

*O king,* they say, *live for ever [n: (Dan. II)]*. That we may therefore compare together outward things with inward, bodily with spiritual: would that we had that inward household as well disciplined as we have known this outward one to be disciplined. We have heard what they answer at the first to their king, and perhaps he himself had taught them this very thing; let us also teach our own household (namely, in every endeavour of ours) to answer things most like: O king, live for ever. Yet what will this be, I ask, a wish, or an admonition? A wish, that he may avail for this; or an admonition, that he may spend all zeal upon this very thing? But what is [1235D] the life of that inward prince, and lord of that inward household? What, I say, is the life of that which is chief in the soul (namely, of the human mind), unless a good intention? Whatever a man may do, even if it be good, yet it will be unprofitable unless it be done with a good intention. But then the mind of a man dies even amid good works, when the intention is corrupted. It is the Truth's own attestation: *Because, if thine eye be evil, thy whole body shall be darksome [n: (Matth. VI)]*. What therefore will it be to live for ever, unless to have a good intention in every good work? Would that at every endeavour of ours, at every good beginning, this answer might first meet us; that all our thought might sigh and busy itself for this, that we may live for ever, which indeed will then come to pass, [1236A] if we do nothing but what is good, and nothing without a good intention. For, to say nothing of the rest: oh, how often do we seek the truth itself, not for truth but for vanity, and the truth once found we love, not in truth, but unto vanity; and, what is most wretched, in the words of life we traffic for the gains of death; or at any rate we rightly understand the life of the inner man to be divine grace! For as the body can do nothing without its own life, that is, without the soul, so our inner man can do no good thing without divine grace: *By the grace, of God,* says the apostle, *I am what I am [n: (Cor. XV)]*. And the Truth himself concerning himself: *Without me you can do nothing [n: (Joan. XV)]*. What therefore is it to say, to live for ever, unless unceasingly to cleave to grace? Whatever thou mayest purpose, presume not of thine own effort, but of divine grace. [1236B] Whatever thou accomplishest, ascribe to him, not to thyself this assuredly was to be said to that king, and at that time above all, because he was seeking in a human way that which he had received divinely, and for the other thing that was hoped for was leaning upon human effort rather than upon divine grace. But this is very marvellous (nay, astonishing beyond the human measure), that often, when we say these things silently within ourselves and feel them inwardly, none the less, and at the very same time, we lean upon our own effort, as if we were wholly ignorant of cooperating grace. Often, when we say something subtly to our neighbours concerning the commendation of divine grace, we glory within ourselves over the subtlety of our own speaking. O infinite folly of man, [1236C] and dost thou indeed rightly say that a man can do nothing without grace? But if thou speakest the truth, whence dost thou glory? Let us therefore teach those most subtle searchers-out of hidden things, namely, those thoughts of ours, that in all our zeal, in every business, they busy themselves first and chiefly with this, that they first beget in us this solicitude: that we be zealous to presume of grace all that we propose, and to ascribe to divine grace all that we accomplish; and this belongs to living for ever.

## CHAPTER IV. *How, according to the varied successes of their zeals, some either feebly cast themselves down or emptily exalt themselves.*

*Tell,* says he, *the dream to thy servants, and we will declare the interpretation [1236D] thereof (Dan, II)*. Mark what they say. One thing they demand, and another they promise. They demand of the king the vision, and they promise its interpretation. And yet as vainly as they demand, so falsely do they promise. But there was one thing which they might have said truly, if they had been willing to confess the truth: namely, that they in no wise knew the vision, nor could of themselves have known it at all. They therefore who profess false things, why do they not at least confess true ones? A common modesty; a general shamelessness. It is common modesty to conceal one's own impossibility; it is general shamelessness to presume beyond possibility. *And the king answering said to the Chaldeans: The word has departed from me. Unless you declare to me the dream and the conjecture of it, you shall perish, and your houses shall be made public. But if you shall relate the dream and the conjecture [1237A] of it, you shall receive from me rewards, and gifts, and much honour.* Who, I ask, would not freely rebuke King Nabuchodonosor, that for such a cause he consigns his wise men to destruction, when perhaps he himself does the like, or worse? For what is it to destroy one's own wise men of one's own accord, unless utterly to lay aside the zeals of wisdom, and to be now unwilling to exercise those most subtle points of one's wit any further in the investigation of some doctrine? But what is it to make public the houses of the wise men, and to reduce them to the common use of all? Now by houses we are wont to mean that place of our dwelling to which, after manifold labours and runnings to and fro, we are always accustomed to return for the sake of rest. What therefore is more rightly given to be understood by the house of the wise men [1237B] than those private and secret leisures of their rest, wherein all the studious are wont to be free for the zeals of doctrine? The houses of our wise men therefore are in a manner made public, when those studious leisures of our rest are exposed to every wandering of dissoluteness, and the secret inner chambers of doctrine are prostituted to every care or curiosity. How many do we see, after the glorious marks of their zeals and the great things of their knowledge, when perchance they have been promoted to some step of honour, or perchance have taken up the care of some administration, straightway despise all the discipline of their doctrines, be free for secular affairs only and always, destroy in one day all the cultivators of wisdom, and make public their hidden secrets? [1237C] What would these men do if they received the kingdom of Nabuchodonosor? How many likewise do we see, after much urgency of spiritual exercises, after having at last received the grace of contemplation, when perchance they have been cast down from that state of their sublimity by some temptation or by weariness of whatever kind, and have perceived that they cannot return to that art of their height without some, or perchance without great, labour, straightway lay down or condemn all the effort of spiritual zeals, and expose themselves at every hour to all vagrant and empty runnings to and fro. Thou mayest see them not only not seek again those leisures of their contemplation, but even utterly lay aside all urgency of meditation or of reading. What [1237D] else do these men do than slay their own wise men, who overspread all spiritual understandings within themselves by the varied fluctuation of their own desires? Behold, we have heard concerning the threats; let us see concerning the promises. *But if the dream,* says he, *and the conjecture of it you shall relate, you shall receive rewards and gifts, and much honour from me.* A reward is when we receive that which we have deserved; a gift, when we receive that which we have not yet deserved; but an honour, when we obtain even that for the deserving of which we are less fit. And so a reward is what is rendered to merits; a gift, what is bestowed freely; an honour, what is conferred from dignity alone: rewards, says he, and gifts, and much honour you shall receive from me. Nothing, brethren, is truer: how gladly do we bestow upon our wise men the wages of their merits, [1238A] how thankfully do we confer upon them honour due or gratuitous? And that I may more fully declare what I think thereon: I look for nothing more certain, I fear nothing more, than that every man should busy himself that too much honour, and greater reverence than is fitting, be bestowed upon wise men of this sort, when perchance they have satisfied his desires and have answered his wishes according to his wish. Who would not ascribe more to his own zeals and disciplines than the Truth itself dictates? Who, I ask, would not wish to extend the reputation of his own knowledge and wisdom, not only according to the measure of equity, but even beyond, nay above, what equity owes? And so as often as the spirit gladly presses on in its own zeals, and thence promises itself an enlargement of fame and glory, it speaks in a manner to its own wise men: both rewards, and gifts; [1238B] and much honour you shall receive.



## CHAPTER V. *In how many ways the spirit deceives itself, and not unwillingly hides its own vice from itself.*

The reward being set forth, the king straightway subjoins and says: *Tell me therefore the dream and the interpretation of it [n: (Dan. II)]*. Two things he seeks: the dream, and the interpretation of it. It is one thing to know the secrets of the divine judgments out of divine revelation, and another to have been able to weigh or to penetrate the reason of the same. This belongs to the knowledge of the dream, that to the interpretation of it. How many of the divine judgments do we know, whose reason we penetrate by no discussion of ours. *They answered a second time [1238C] and said: Let the king tell the dream to his servants, and we will declare the interpretation of it.* What is it to answer again, unless to teach their own impossibility more fully and more perfectly by the repeated failure of their own [sic: *conanimis*]? O how hardly is human shamelessness restrained from its own presumption. Behold, after many experiences, still impossible things are demanded, still impossible things are promised. But let us see what follows: *The king answered and said: I know for certain that you buy up the time, knowing that the word has departed from me. If therefore you shall not declare to me the dream, there is one sentence concerning you, that you have framed an interpretation also that is deceitful and full of deception, that you may speak to me until the time pass away. Tell me therefore the dream, that I may know that you speak a true interpretation [1238D] of it also.* Behold, from his urgency the king profited not nothing, who at length at some time detected their duplicity; and do not thou think that thou hast profited but little, when thou shalt be able clearly to detect the duplicity of thine own heart. How many things do we often feign, how many do we dissemble. Our weaknesses we gladly dissemble, and those good things which we are altogether unable to do we feign that we can do or have: and it is very marvellous that the spirit gladly deceives itself, and not unwillingly hides its own vice from itself. Behold, the king detected both vices, of simulation and of dissimulation, in his subjects: that of dissimulation indeed in that he says, I know for certain that you buy up the time. That of simulation, in that after a few words he adds, There is one sentence concerning you, that you have framed a deceitful interpretation [1239A] also. They dissembled their own ignorance, and were willing [cj: *volebant*; read *nolebant*, "were unwilling"] to confess it openly, and in this they were buying up the time, and yet concerning the interpretation of the dream they were promising false things. But the evil of dissimulation in them the king proved by experience, while the evil of simulation he knew from reason, gathering the one vice out of the other. For if they could not do even that which was the less, how could they have done that whereby it was the greater? From these things, as I judge, thou weighest and observest that some things in us we prove by experience, and others assuredly we gather from reason. *The Chaldeans therefore answered before the king and said: There is not a man upon earth that can fulfil thy word, O king.* Behold, now a third time they answer, and at length at some time they manifestly teach their own failure. And that [1239B] we may distinguish by steps the three alternations of the answer, see whether perchance that first answer be of doubt, the second of fear, the third of despair. And at the first endeavour indeed, when we begin something and yet do not finish it, we often begin to doubt of the consummation of what we have begun. But at the second, to dread the more. But at the third endeavour, when we obtain no effect, we are wont utterly to despair.

And note that doubt and dread have an ambiguous answer, but despair has a manifest answer. So assuredly at the first and the second those men rather lessen their own ignorance than speak it. But at the third, they now openly profess the light. Yet let us hear how falsely they speak true things: There [1239C] is not, say they, a man upon earth that can fulfil thy word. They do not say simply, We cannot, which assuredly was true, but, There is not a man upon earth that can, which beyond doubt was false. For Daniel also was a man, and was upon earth, who was able to do this, as the outcome of the matter afterward proved. Yet he was able, not of his own effort, but of divine grace. Who would say that he could not do what he was able to obtain by praying? See in how many ways, and how often, the human spirit deceives itself; but who would suffice to explain this fully? How many things do we often presume that we can do, which yet we altogether cannot; and how many things which we altogether cannot do, do we think that no one can? What is it, I ask, [1239D] that the human spirit, according to the good which it approves in itself, does not at all proclaim others, and yet, according to the evil which it finds in itself, adds others? Behold, what these wise men presumed concerning the interpretation of the dream, they did not yet attribute equally to all in common. But nevertheless, what they could not do concerning the recovery of the dream, they affirm that no one can do. But that we may consider all this according to one and the same spirit: surely we ought neither rashly to presume anything in ourselves, nor rashly to despair. For often what we cannot do in one way, we easily accomplish in another. How many things which we often cannot get by doing, we obtain by praying.



## CHAPTER VI. *How rashly, or how vainly, we presume upon human effort for that which we ought to await from angelic revelation alone, or from divine.*

[1240A]

Yet let us see what these men further add, subtly discussing what they say faultily, or what perchance they say truly. For things uttered incautiously avail for our caution, and things rightly uttered have wherewith to form us unto the zeal of imitation. *But neither doth any of the kings,* say they, *great and mighty, inquire such a word of every soothsayer, and magician, and Chaldean [n: (Dan. II)]*. He is rightly called a king who is exalted unto a kingdom. But what says that King, truly King of kings and Lord of lords? *The kingdom of heaven,* says he, *is within you [n: (Luc. XVII)]*. [var: Vulg. Luc. 17:21 reads *regnum Dei*, "the kingdom of God"] Unto this kingdom surely we can be exalted, [1240B] if we perfectly will it. This kingdom, existing within us, surely has many inhabitants and dwellers without number. But by how much the more each man enlarges such a kingdom, more faithfully dispenses it, more strictly rules it, more prudently orders it, by so much the mightier is he made, by so much the greater is he judged. But unto this kingdom poverty of spirit advances and conducts more than abundance of sense: for *Blessed* are *the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven [n: (Matth. V)]*. He who receives such a kingdom sings confidently, when he says: *But I am appointed king by him [n: (Psal. II)]*. And well is it said of kings of this sort. But neither doth any of the kings, great and mighty, inquire a word of this kind of every soothsayer, and magician, and Chaldean. But in this the said kings are great, and defend their own power for themselves, [1240C] that they presume nothing of their own virtue: how much less those things which are above man? Certainly the king had received that word divinely, and it was altogether such that it could not be known unless from God's revelation. That therefore which could not be known save from God, with what rashness is it presumed of a man, a soothsayer, a magician, or a Chaldean? What therefore is it to be unwilling, and not to be bound, to inquire a word of this kind of any wise man of this sort, unless that those things which are above man ought to be presumed of no human effort or art? Hence it is that it is added, when it is said: *For the word which thou, O king, seekest is grievous, neither shall there be found any one that may declare it in the sight of the king, except the gods, whose conversation is not with men.* Certainly [1240D] what was above man, the king ought not to have demanded of man. But what is more grievous, or what more burdensome, than that a man should demand of a man things impossible for a man, and should wish to wrest from human possibility things that are above the human measure? But the things that are impossible with men are possible with God. Except, say they, the gods, whose conversation is not with men. Rightly enough in this place do we understand by the gods the holy angels. For if because of the participation of the image, or even of the likeness, men have been called gods, how much more rightly the angels? *I have said: you are gods and sons of the Most High [n: (Psal. LXXXI)]*; and angels indeed are engaged among men at every hour, nay at almost every moment, and yet they do not converse with men, because even then, when they are among men, [1241A] they live not in a human way, but in a heavenly, and truly in a divine way. Who would deny or not know that angels have been able to reveal to men many things which are above men, and are wont to reveal them? But that we may still draw a likeness from outward things to our inmost parts, so often the things which we penetrate by no investigation of ours, we come to know from divine revelations and inspirations. But if any one should wish that by the gods there be understood not angels, but men divinely inspired, whose conversation is now not with men (that is, with such as savour of human things), in that they can now truly say, Our conversation is in heaven, nothing truer can be said. For they come to know many things from divine inspiration which exceed human investigation. But if that former sentence be accommodated to this sense, [1241B] nothing in it seems to sound but what is right, where it is said. There is not a man upon earth that can fulfil thy word, O king: as if it were said, None of those who are upon earth, save only those who by a heavenly conversation ascend the heavens.



## CHAPTER VII. *How, after the often illustrious distinctions of its own studies, the mind lays aside the care of doctrines both secular and spiritual; and exposes itself wholly to outward business alone.*

*And when this was heard, the king in fury and in great wrath commands that all the wise men of Babylon should perish. And when the sentence had gone forth, the wise men were being slain [n: (Dan. II)]*. Behold what we have already spoken of above. After the king had despaired of the recovery of his dream, in fury [1241C] and wrath he decreed that all his wise men should perish. As we have already said, this is to destroy his wise men: no longer to seek out, according to the former custom and the accustomed exercise, those keen and subtle apprehensions of knowledge and of wisdom, and to spend no labor at all upon the studies of any teaching whatever, nor to bestow care upon them. The dream that was seen is as it were lost when that grace of contemplation by which the mind was frequently lifted up to sublime things is withdrawn; and then indeed we as it were despair of its recovery, when, laboring long and much and profiting nothing, we distrust that we can any longer recover that delight of our spiritual sights. But it often happens that, when the spirit loses that gazing upon divine revelations which it had been [1241D] wont to love, being now broken by long weariness, it lays aside the care not only of that in whose restoration it failed, but of studies of every kind, and in a manner disposes to destroy all its wise men. In fury, he says, and in great wrath. Fury is a disturbance of the mind wholly devoid of reason. Wrath is a great disturbance of the mind, yet not utterly alien from reason. We are driven and driven about as it were out of fury, when, with no regard to reason, we cast ourselves headlong into that which ought not to be done. Often, moved by wrath, we understand what ought to be done, though it cannot be reined in, if it be great. And so in the first onset of our disturbance we often do not so much as look back to reason; but afterwards we do indeed see reason, [1242A] yet cannot follow it; and at last we both behold it and follow it. Rightly therefore is fury set first, and wrath afterwards.

It is certainly to be noted that those who in this place are commanded to perish are called the wise men of Babylon. I think that the wise men of the Babylonians are one thing, and the wise men of the Jews another. The former, indeed, are occupied about earthly things, the latter about divine. The former follow after the wisdom of the world, which is foolishness with God; the latter search even the deep things of God, being spiritual, and comparing spiritual things with spiritual. What then do we understand by the wise men of the Babylonians, but secular sciences? and what by the wise men of the Jews, but spiritual teachings? So then we as it were consign the wise men of Babylon to condemnation, when we cut off the secular disciplines from our [1242B] studies. Our conscience acquiesces more easily in the cutting off of these, and the more lightly consents to their being cast away, the more it observes them (however useful for something to human salvation) to be in no way necessary. First, then, the wise men of Babylon are slaughtered; whence it is that of them it is said: And when the sentence had gone forth, the wise men were being slain. The sentence goes forth when at length a man manifests in deed what he had deliberated and determined in his mind. That is as it were still within which is still turned over and lies hidden in the mind; and it begins as it were to be already put into practice when it now appears in deed. There follows: And Daniel and his companions were sought, that they might perish. Behold how the evil spreads. We have heard above how the wise men of Babylon were being slain; behold, now the wise men [1242C] of the Jews are sought, that they may be slain. Behold by what steps a studious mind is often loosened from its own liveliness, and slips back little by little from the highest things to worse ones: first it lays aside the care of secular, afterwards of spiritual teachings [sic: *doctrinam*], and exposes itself wholly to outward business alone, and slays within itself as it were all the cultivators of knowledge and of wisdom, while after its contempt for the human arts it utterly forsakes the urgency of contemplation, of meditation, of reading and of prayer.

It is to be noted, however, that of the wise men of the Jews it is said that they were sought for destruction. What, I ask, is it to seek a place where wise men of this sort may be found for destruction, but to snatch at an occasion, [1242D] or even at the opportunity of some excuse, whereby a dissolute mind may the more safely and the more freely, and with a more secure conscience, cast away even the pursuits of sacred instruction? For we often plead infirmity of the body when we cast away spiritual exercises. Often we pretend this to be charity, that, forsaking the contemplative life, we utterly expose ourselves to outward business. In this way an occasion, and as it were the opportunity of a place, is sought, where Daniel with the rest of the wise men of the Jews may be found for slaying. If we consult the deeds of this Daniel, what shall we more rightly find figured in him than the devotion of the heart? See how, under every adversity and in whatever necessity, he always has recourse to the Lord and consults him, implores and receives the divine aid. [1243A] And who does not know that it belongs to true devotion, under every crisis of necessity, to flee to the divine defenses, and in doubtful matters as well as in adverse ones humbly to ask counsel from the one side and aid from the other, and effectually to obtain it? But we know that the mind never prays inwardly and devoutly which does not first rouse itself to devotion by diligent premeditations. For these are the inseparable companions of true devotion: circumspect, discerning and provident thoughts. For without companions and fellow workers of this kind, whatever devotion is ours neither knows nor is able to pray as it ought.

## CHAPTER VIII. *How in every purpose or ordinance we ought to consult the rule of equity, and to call back what has been improvidently decreed to a sounder judgment.*

[1243B]

*Then Daniel inquired concerning the law and the sentence from Arioch, the prince of the king's soldiery, who had gone forth to slay the wise men of Babylon; and he questioned him who had received power from the king, for what cause so cruel a sentence had gone forth from the king's face. When therefore Arioch had made the matter known to Daniel, Daniel went in and asked the king that he would give him time to declare the solution to the king [n: (Dan. II)]*. As in Daniel the fervor of devotion is understood, so by the prince of the soldiery we rightly, as I judge, understand the zeal of rectitude and the rigor of strict severity. Certainly, without the rigor of just severity, not even that kingdom may be possessed in peace or in security in which men are wont to command men, and in which men are wont to disturb the peace [1243C] of those who possess it. What ruler was ever able to enjoy a lasting peace, or to rejoice in it, who was unwilling strictly to judge and strongly to strike the adversaries of peace, when he could and when he ought? But how much more in that kingdom, in which our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against the spiritual things of wickedness in the heavenly places; how much more, I say, in a kingdom of this sort ought we to act strongly, and with strict punishment to strike all the tumults of clamorous thoughts or affections, and whatever disturbers there be of inward peace? Good indeed is this prince of the soldiery (namely rigor; and the severity of justice), whose laws or disciplines whoever does not obey estranges himself [1243D] from that fellowship of the heavenly soldiery. And rightly, as I judge, is this prince of the soldiery called Arioch. For Arioch is interpreted *reducing to solitude*. We know that the kingdom of heaven is within us [var: Vulg. Luke 17:21 *regnum Dei intra vos est*, "the kingdom of God is within you"]. And so this prince of the soldiery ought, whatever kingdom or region he sees rising up or rebelling against this kingdom and not obeying the laws of the eternal King, to overthrow it by a strong assault, and to reduce it to everlasting solitude, and, if it can be done, to blot it out forever. If therefore by Daniel we ought to understand devotion, and by Arioch the zeal of rectitude, what is it for Daniel to inquire of Arioch concerning the law and the sentence of the king, but for a mind stricken with compunction to consult the judgment of equity, and out of great devotion vehemently to examine whether that be perhaps just or unjust which it remembers itself [1244A] to have formerly determined through the impulse of its own spirit? For in the time of compunction and of prayer the mind of man finds many things to be evil and unjust which it had formerly defined out of the impulse of its spirit, and as it were headlong, and which nevertheless it did not perceive at that time to be unjust; and often, out of that same impulse of his spirit, a man dictates many things against his own conscience, and yet afterwards, in the time of his prayer and of his devotion, he tempers that same headlong haste of his spirit, and reforms it to a sounder judgment. And so we ought afterwards diligently to examine those things which we have decreed headlong rather than prudently, and which we greatly fear to be evil, and to search out by shrewd reconsideration whether they be just or unjust, useful or useless; and in this way the office [1244B] of Arioch is as it were inquired of through Daniel concerning the law or the sentence given, when at length, out of great devotion, the rule of true equity and of the highest discretion is consulted concerning any less considered purpose of the mind. But what it is to go forth to slay the wise men can easily be weighed from what has gone before. It is to be known, however, that we often more easily detect, and more fully dread, the determination or the quality of an ill-considered sentence at that time when we now prove by the deed itself, and as it were by experiment, what sort it is. Hence it is that Arioch in this place is consulted about the giving of the sentence then first, when he is already going forth on occasion of it.



## CHAPTER IX *That whatever is wont to befall against us answers, by God's dispensation, to the free will of the mind according to the quality of merits.*

[1244C]

But if by Arioch the strictness of equity is rightly understood, it will perhaps seem strange to someone, and not without reason, how the execution of a sentence of this kind is said to belong to the office of Arioch, since that same sentence is by no means judged just, either according to the history or according to the mystical understanding. Or did the king perhaps, according to the history, being troubled with fury, believe that to be just which was not truly just, in that he might then truly have said: My eye is troubled with fury? Just so, indeed, certain men after the type of this likeness, begetting a zeal of rectitude but not having it according to knowledge, believe it to be right, or feign it to be right, [1244D] that they slay their own wise men, setting before themselves or promising themselves greater gains of merit to be acquired from bodily exercises than from spiritual ones, in which meanwhile they cannot make as much progress, or as easily, as they wish. But if we look still more deeply, and have recourse to the divine judgments, we shall at once see that many things which a man disposes or does unjustly, God permits to be done in no way but justly. Why then should not those things also be said to pertain to the office of Arioch which, according to this consideration, are proved by the equity of the divine strictness to answer to our merits? And he questioned, he says, him who had received power from the king. Mark, then, that this Arioch received power from the king, because whatever [1245A] befalls us, whether profitably or unprofitably, comes down from the merit or the fault of free will. And Arioch receives from the king the power of executing a sentence now profitable, now unprofitable: sometimes from one who knows and wills, sometimes from one who knows and does not will, sometimes from one who does not know and wills, sometimes from one who neither knows nor wills. For, as has been said, what is wont to befall each man answers, by God's dispensation, to the free choice of liberty according to the quality of merits. Whatever therefore is done concerning us is regulated, for the requital of merits and by the right of equity, by the just judgment of God. But that provident gaze of the spirit often, under the onset of its own great disturbance, recognizes the good pleasure or judgment of the Almighty and acquiesces in it. Sometimes it recognizes it and does not acquiesce; but sometimes [1245B] it is so wrought that it desires the will of God alone to be done concerning itself, although meanwhile it does not fully understand it; and sometimes it is so affected that it cannot at all acquiesce in the will of God, even if it had been able fully to know that will (which meanwhile it cannot know). But what wonder if the human spirit cannot always acquiesce even in a divine will that is known, since indeed it often cannot acquiesce even in its own advantage? For often through impatience it dictates a sentence which it is in no way ignorant to be contrary to its own advantage. Therefore that prince of the soldiery which we have named receives from his king the power of executing a sentence not then only, when a king of this sort disposes something justly and usefully, but even now [cj: *nunc*; read *tunc*, "then"] indeed, when he ordains something through shamelessness or even [1245C] through impatience which, by God's disposition and his own preceding merits, answers to the requital of equity; nay, even then, when he does something whereby he incurs a hateful, though just, sentence.

## CHAPTER X. *By what considerations the things that befall us are to be weighed.*

But let us further see what that is which Daniel again inquires of Arioch. For what cause so cruel a sentence had gone forth from the king's face. A fitting order, and diligently to be observed: first he is questioned concerning the law and the sentence, afterwards concerning the cause of that same sentence. Without doubt there must be diligent inquiry [1245D] and vehement examination (in matters doubtful, at all events, and most perilous) first concerning the quality of the action, and consequently concerning the quality of the intention. For often the fault that is contracted from the action is not a little lightened by the quality of the intention. Yet that he inquires concerning the cause of the sentence we can, as I judge, nay we ought, to refer to two things: namely, with what intention it is done, or by what disposition of God it happens to be done. And concerning the action it is asked whether it be advantageous or disadvantageous, just or unjust. But concerning the intention, whether it be perhaps pious or impious, discerning or undiscerning. And concerning God's disposition let each man especially search this out in the investigation of a dread or a hard sentence: whether he strikes us for our profit or for vengeance. For certainly, when he smites us [1246A] or permits us to be struck, he does it now for our instruction, now for our correction, now for our rebuke, now for our condemnation, or in yet some other way whatever. All these things are to be diligently inquired into and subtly examined. All these things strike in a profitable fear, and prick the mind with compunction in prayer. All these things humble the mind, and rouse our devotion, and inflame it to supplication. Thou seest surely how rightly, how discreetly Daniel inquires into all these things before he presses on in prayers or applies himself to supplication. Hence it is that it is said, when there is added: When therefore Arioch had made the matter known to Daniel, Daniel went in and asked the king But what is that aforesaid learning of Daniel from Arioch, but that the devoted mind, the rule of equity having been diligently and devoutly [1246B] and strictly consulted, should at length, after much examination, more fully recognize the quality of the sentence sought and of its cause.



## CHAPTER XI. *How in the time of our disturbance we ought to flee to the remedies of prayer, and to bring a support of this kind into use.*

It remains now to ask what it is for Daniel to go in to the king. Rightly perhaps by the king, who presides and commands over all, we understand in this place the vehement motion of the spirit and the strong impulse of free will, to which any other affection whatever readily yields or gives obedience. And to how many (when they are vehemently affected or sharply moved) does it not occur at all to consult reason or discretion, how much less [1246C] to flee to prayer, or to admit any devotion? But what else do we say this to be, than that none of the wise men dares to appear before the king? Yet often those who are of this sort, after the impulse of the spirit has been settled, when they come back to themselves, have recourse to the judgment of discretion and to the office of devotion, busying themselves to correct the things in which they went beyond measure in the time of disturbance. But if we are diligent about the discipline of the heart, as we ought to be, let us teach and accustom our spirit, under any impulse whatever and in the time of disturbance, to flee to the counsels of discretion; and this is to lose the wise men before the king's sight. But because it often happens that by no attestation of reason can it soothe the headlong impulse of its own [1246D] disturbance, the mind ought, under a crisis of necessity of this kind, to have recourse to the helps of devotion, and to obtain the supports of the divine mercy for the pacifying of the violence of its disturbance; and a remedy of devotion of this kind must be brought into use; and this is for Daniel to go in to the king. For Daniel as it were goes in to the king when, for the pacifying of the impulse of the spirit, devotion lends its support even under the very drive of headlong haste.

But it is to be noted that above he is said to have been brought in, whereas here it is simply set down that he went in. And I think that to be brought in by another and to go in by oneself are one thing and another; as is plain from what has gone before, to have the support of devout prayer ready at hand under every vehement impulse of the spirit, this is [1247A] that Daniel is not wanting in the presence of the raging king. But, as we all in common effect things by carefulness too, other things we obtain by prayers, by praying and beseeching God. When therefore by human shrewdness and by exercise the defense of devotion is made habitual for settling the impulse of the spirit, that Daniel of ours is in a manner brought into the presence of the aforesaid king by another's office. But when this is effected not so much by meditating as by praying, Daniel without doubt goes in to the king by himself. And so we ought by diligent and shrewd premeditation to rouse our mind to devotion; and this will be to bring Daniel in by another's office. Likewise, because often even when necessity demands and presses we cannot pray devoutly, let us pray in the time of the divine visitation and of our own compunction, [1247B] that in the time of necessity we may be able to pray. If, then, the faculty of praying is obtained by prayer, Daniel assuredly goes in by himself. But neither is this to be passed over negligently, that he is read to have gone in during the time of the king's disturbance and fury. For at the time of his being brought in we assuredly receive not even any indication of the king's disturbance. For we must not believe that this king is always angry and troubled with some fury. It is one thing for the impulse of the spirit to be vehement, another for it to be headlong. One thing, I say, to be strong and unconquered, and another to be full of wrath and madness. One thing, finally, to be invincible and almost immovable; but another to be intolerable and plainly irrational. [1247C] But who, I ask, in the time of the royal fury would presume, or would dare, to lead Daniel before the king? I judge it to be above human effort and virtue to apply oneself to prayer in the time of so great and so inward a disturbance, since scarcely, or rather in no way at all, does it happen at that time even to remember it. It behooves therefore, in the manner we have said above, that Daniel go in by himself before the troubled king, if he wishes under the crisis of so great a necessity to fight back against the peril. And so let the mind that is diligent and solicitous about its own salvation, which as yet, when it has been disturbed, does not know how to fight back against its disturbance by praying, and has not yet obtained the practice or the grace of this kind, pray and obtain in a time of tranquillity that the grace of praying in a time of disturbance be given it from God. [1247D] In this way it will perhaps be granted to Daniel at some time to go in to the king by himself, and while he is still raging; and then he will perhaps be able, not once only but often and assiduously, to ask and to obtain a respite for the deferring of an evil sentence, to this end, that he may afterwards utterly blot it out. When, in the time of its inward disturbance, the devoted mind humbly asks and beseeches that the divine goodness not permit him, under the impulse of a roused fury, to do anything through impatience whereof he must afterwards repent, if it obtains what it desires, what else does the Daniel of our devotion seem to thee to do, than to soothe the madness of the raging king? But when it feels itself drawn by the vehemence of its headlong affection to something which meanwhile, under the cloud or the whirlwind of so great a disturbance of its own, it cannot fully recognize whether [1248A] it be right, if meanwhile it asks patience for itself until in the time of its tranquillity it can more rightly discern what is to be done, then, by receiving what it asks, what else does it seem to thee to accomplish, than to ask and receive a respite? Daniel, he says, went in and asked the king that he would give him time to declare the solution to the king. Thou seest surely that devotion piously and profitably presumes often upon the Lord's goodness for things which human effort could by no shrewdness of its own bring about; and how justly we presume great things upon the Lord's goodness, if for love of him, with his help, we conquer our own magnanimity.



## CHAPTER XII *With what meditations the spirit must be inflamed to devotion, and how the urgency of our studies must be reformed.*

[1248B]

But let us see what Daniel did after these things, or what is written of him: *And having gone into his house, he made the matter known to Ananias, Misael, Azarias, his companions, that they might seek mercy from the face of the God of heaven concerning this sacrament, and that Daniel and his companions might not perish with the rest of the wise men of Babylon [n: (Dan. II)]*. By these three, Daniel's undivided companions and inseparable comrades, we understand circumspection, discretion, deliberation; without which we prove by daily experience that the office of true devotion can in no way be fulfilled. For if we wish to pray inwardly and devoutly, the first thing is that we look about upon our own [1248C] life. Let us see with what studies or exercises we have been accustomed to be occupied, or with what we are occupied still, or what purpose we have in these for the time to come. But what does it profit to bring these things into consideration, unless with the same solicitude we busy ourselves to discern each single thing by strong examination, and to separate the good from the bad by watchful shrewdness, that we may know for what things we ought to beseech the Lord, or even to give thanks? But when our good things or our evil ones are known, it still remains to search out by provident deliberation by what occupation or carefulness we may both make satisfaction for past evils, and extricate oneself from present ones, and more carefully exhibit caution concerning things to come. The first belongs to circumspection, the second to discretion, the third to deliberation. It belongs [1248D] to circumspection to bring the measure of our morals into consideration; it belongs to discretion to make judgment in all things; but to deliberation, to seek and to find counsel. Circumspection says: *I will recount to thee all my years in the bitterness of my soul [n: (Isai. XXXVIII)]*. Discretion confesses: *I have done judgment and justice [n: (Psal. XCVIII)]*. Deliberation speaks: *What shall I render to the Lord for all the things that he hath rendered to me? [n: (Psal. CXV.)]* She is called back to the pursuit of circumspection to whom it is said: *Lift up thine eyes round about [n: (Isai. XLIX)]*, and see then where thou hast lain prostrate, harlot [var: Vulg. Jer. 3:2 *vide ubi non prostrata sis*, "see where thou hast not lain prostrate"; the received text carries the negative, which is absent here]. He wished to encourage us to the examination of discretion who said: *If we judged ourselves, we should not indeed be judged [n: (I Cor. XI)]*. The office of deliberation is enjoined, or even commended, when it is said through the wise man: *Do all things with counsel, [1249A] and unto eternity thou shalt not repent [n: (Eccli. XXXII)]* [var: Vulg. Eccli. 32:24 *Fili, sine consilio nihil facias, et post factum non poeniteberis*, "Son, do nothing without counsel, and after the deed thou shalt not repent"]. But who does not see how necessary the offices of these are to true devotion? For who was ever able to pray inwardly and devoutly, if he has put off looking about upon his life, examining it, ordering it? As often therefore as necessity urges us to apply ourselves more vehemently to devout prayer, we must have recourse to the offices of circumspection and of discretion, or even of deliberation, and by such pursuits and busy meditations inflame our spirit to devotion; and this is for Daniel to take up the supports of his companions for the use of his prayer. And so Daniel as it were runs back to the inner chambers of his house, and seeks fellow workers, as it were, for the more perfect fulfilling of the business of his prayer, when, the time of prayer now pressing, or even the crisis of urgent [1249B] necessity, the devoted mind seeks again the accustomed opportunity of its own quiet, necessary for that office, and strives to animate or to inflame its devotion by certain provident meditations, apt for such a use. To his companions, he says, he made the matter known. The matter is as it were made known by Daniel to Daniel's companions, when out of devotion it is brought about that the impending matter is brought into consideration, examination, consultation. But mercy is set forth as a thing to be obtained, if the mind stricken with compunction, in that which it devoutly performs, leans not upon its own merits, but upon the divine mercies.

It is certainly to be noted, according to the history, that Daniel the prophet calls that matter a sacrament; whence who would doubt that a mystical understanding of things lies hidden in it? [1249C] And that Daniel, he says, and his companions might not perish with the rest of the wise men of Babylon. After the example of this thing, when we have seen our mind, after its contempt of secular studies, grow torpid toward the spiritual exercises also, and little by little fail, and the peril of our wise men press upon us, we too ought by all means to ask that of the Lord whereby we may be able to repair or to confirm the accustomed urgency of our studies. But there is, as we alike know, a very great labor both in the pursuit of praying and in that of meditating, and to minds that wander and are restless it is almost intolerable. But in contemplation the delight is wonderful and almost singular. When therefore the grace of contemplation is conferred upon diligent minds, [1249D] that labor of the other studies is by its sweetness lightened or tempered just so far as it is sweetened. If therefore we have not yet received grace of this kind, or grieve that it has been withdrawn, we ought to seek it from the Lord for the confirming or the reforming of our studies. When therefore we do these things, what else, I ask, do we seem to have done than to seek the dreams of divine revelations, that we may have wherewith we can preserve in their integrity those wise men of ours designated above? Then the mystery was revealed to Daniel by a vision in the night. The revelation of a mystery is as it were perceived by night, when the illumination of truth is seen thinly indeed, and in part, and as it were by the light of the moon. We perceive the revelation of a mystery as it were by night, when concerning some [1250A] secret of the Godhead we ourselves indeed understand what is to be thought, but do not yet have ready to hand the reason by which we can prove it to others also. The light of revelation appears as it were in the night and as though in the midst of darkness, when a man is not able to unfold in speech, and as it were to bring forth into the open light, the declaration of the mystery which he sees through understanding. But when afterwards by long reconsideration we bring it to pass that we can declare to others by clear demonstration the received understanding of the truth, which we ourselves formerly could scarcely or but thinly see, what else do we bring forth under the light of day than what we perceived by night? Rightly therefore is no mention made afterwards of night, where Daniel at length speaks openly in the presence of the king what he had formerly received by night.

## CHAPTER XIII. *How at the renewing of understanding we ought always to magnify, not our own effort, but the Lord's magnificence.*

[1250B]

But, the revelation of the mystery having been received, let us further see what Daniel does or says: *And Daniel blessed the God of heaven, and speaking said: Blessed be the name of the Lord from everlasting and even unto everlasting, for wisdom and fortitude are his, and he changeth times and ages, transferreth kingdoms and establisheth them [n: (Dan. II)]*. By this example let us learn what we ourselves ought to do when we receive the light of revealing grace. And so let us busy ourselves, after Daniel's example, to render glory and honor and thanksgiving to him from whom we have it to be wise [1250C] and to understand, and whatever of good it is agreed that we have. For there are many who, when they receive the light of truth, at once ascribe this to their own merits or studies, magnify and exalt themselves, and despise all others in comparison with themselves. A soul of this kind speaks within herself: I have understood above all my teachers. She strives to draw to herself that saying of Solomon, as imprudently as emptily: *I have gone before in wisdom all who were before me [n: (Eccle. I)]*. On the contrary, let us give glory to him from whom we have received understanding. Let us be zealous always, at the very rising of revealing grace, at the very renewing of an illumined understanding, to render proclamations of praise worthy of God. Blow up the trumpet on the new moon, on the notable day of your solemnity. Neomenia, the new moon; the new moon, renewed for the understanding and divinely [1250D] inspired. We know that the moon has not light from itself, but receives it from the sun that it may be able to shine. So indeed the human understanding has received from God, that it may be able to shine back with the rays of the true light. As often therefore as we receive new rays of divine illumination, and know from divine revelation something that exceeds human understanding, we ought at once to rise up into thanksgiving, and with the trumpet of magnificence to resound in the proclamations of the divine goodness: *Magnify,* he says, *the Lord with me, and let us exalt his name together [n: (Psal. XXXIII)]*. Behold how the trumpet has sounded; behold how at the blast of the trumpet he has roused others also along with himself. He wished a blast of such a trumpet to be made at the new moon, or promised that he would make it, when he said: *I will bless the Lord who hath given me understanding* [1251A] [n: (Psal. XV)]. So Daniel, when he received the light of revealing grace, sounded as it were the trumpet of magnificence at the rising of the new moon, when he said: Blessed be the name of the Lord from everlasting and even unto everlasting, for wisdom and fortitude are his.



## CHAPTER XIV. *That the office of true devotion is threefold.*

It is certainly to be noted that the office of true and perfect devotion is threefold. The first is the confession of the crime, the second the request for mercy, the third the glorification of him who shows mercy. The first is the accusing of the fault, the second the supplication for pardon, the third the magnifying of the divine munificence. All these things this Daniel of ours performs magnificently, as is known from his words. It is the confession and the accusing of fault, where in another place he speaks [1251B] to the Lord in prayer: *We have sinned, we have done iniquity, we have acted impiously, and we have departed, and we have turned aside from thy commandments and thy judgments [n: (Dan. IX)]*. It is the supplication and the imploring of pardon, where thou readest, the same man saying: *Hear, O Lord; be appeased, O Lord; attend, and do [n: (ibid.)]*. It is without doubt the glorification and magnifying of his Creator, and of him who shows mercy to him, that thou readest in this place: *Blessed be the name of the Lord from everlasting and even unto everlasting, for wisdom, and fortitude are his, and he changeth times and ages, transferreth kingdoms, and establisheth them [n: (Dan. II)]*. Wisdom and fortitude are indeed goods of the one who receives them, but without doubt they are the goods of God who bestows them, since whoever have wisdom and fortitude, [1251C] whoever have been able to act wisely and strongly, have received them from his gift. *For what hast thou,* says the Apostle, *which thou hast not received? [n: (I Cor. XIV)]*. He, he says, changeth times and ages. We know that all things have their time, and that all things under heaven pass in their own spaces. A time to plant, and a time to pluck up that which is planted. After this manner it can be considered in other things also. And so from the occasion of the time we receive an opportunity, that we may be able to do now these things, now those, more profitably or more readily. And so he changes the times for our uses, when now he accommodates opportunity to the exercises of these virtues, of those. But what, I ask, does it profit to have received the opportunity of the things to be practiced, unless from the gift of that same bounty we receive also the faculty of performing them? But we know [1251D] that different ages are more apt for different effects. Certainly the things we learn in boyhood we retain more deeply and bring forth more readily. In the age of youth the strength of the body is more robust, and the spirit bolder; and therefore that age is more effective for the practice of exercise. Up to a more advanced age both manifold teaching and manifold experience of things increase knowledge by daily advances; and therefore that age, beyond all the rest, is vigorous in counsels and strong in prudence. And so the first of the ages spoken of prevails for learning, the second for practicing, but the third for discerning. After the likeness of years we consider, so to speak, the ages of merits also; and according to the difference of the various advances we know that we have the efficacy of various virtues. [1252A] And so differing efficacies and diverse faculties are in a manner the ages of years. That best governor of merits therefore alternates the measures of times and of ages, who by the dispensation of his goodness administers both the faculty and the opportunity, now of these virtues, now of those. He transferreth kingdoms and establisheth them, when, the tyranny of vices being overthrown, he makes the virtues to reign. Of these peoples of vices or of virtues, and of the destruction of the one as well as the exaltation of the other, it is mystically written, when it is said through the Prophet: *Thou hast brought a vineyard out of Egypt; thou hast cast out the nations, and planted it [n: (Psal. LXXIX)]*. The vineyard is planted when a good purpose is fixed in a good intention. The nations are cast out when, by the edict of confession and the vow of profession, sins are threatened and vices are renounced. [1252B] To the same purport runs that which the same Prophet [sic: *alios*] took heed of concerning the extirpation of vices, or the planting of virtues: *Thou hast cast out the nations, and planted them; thou hast afflicted the peoples, and driven them out [n: (ibid.)]* [var: Vulg. Ps. 43:3 opens *Manus tua gentes disperdidit*, "Thy hand destroyed the nations"; the opening clause as printed here is that of Ps. 79:9 just quoted, whose object is the vine, *eam*]. That hateful people of vices is driven out by the greatness of affliction, when at length the soul, long and much oppressed, is set free from the dominion of carnal desires as much by contrition of body as by compunction of heart. And so in this manner the author and protector of our salvation, while he destroys the dominion of vices in us and restores the virtues in their place, transferreth kingdoms and establisheth them. And rightly indeed, for the kingdom is the Lord's, and he shall rule over the nations: *He giveth,* he says, *wisdom to the wise, and knowledge to them that understand instruction. He revealeth [1252C] deep and hidden things, and knoweth what is set in darkness, and light is with him.* Let no one, then, presume upon his own genius; let no one ascribe the knowledge of inward or of outward things to his own studies or merits. For it is he who gives wisdom to the wise, he equally who gives knowledge to them that understand instruction. To the same purport without doubt goes he who says: *All wisdom is from the Lord God, and hath been with him always, and is before all time [n: (Eccle. I)]*. With both agrees he who says: *Every best gift, and every perfect gift, is from above, coming down from the Father of lights [n: (Jac. I)]*. He revealeth deep and hidden things, and knoweth what is set in darkness. For those things which are truly deep, and exceed the measure of human understanding, the Apostle cries out [1252D] when he says: *O the depth of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God, how incomprehensible are his judgments, and his ways past finding out! [n: (Rom. XI.)]* [var: Vulg. *O altitudo divitiarum sapientiae et scientiae Dei*, "O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God"] Yet of these very sublime and deep things he does reveal, through his Spirit, as much as it behooves us to know, or is expedient for us. He reveals therefore the deep things and the secrets of his own hiddenness; nor these only, but also the hidden things of another's counsel, which an alien malice conceals from us, that it may the more easily deceive us. Thou hast heard what we ought to desire or to hope for concerning his revelation; hear further what we should fear concerning his knowledge. He knoweth what is set in darkness; he knows indeed our inmost things and whatever is hidden of our heart, and not only those things which we alone know of ourselves and wish to be hidden from others, but also those which we ourselves are not able to penetrate in the hiding places of our conscience. He reveals therefore his own things, he reveals [1253A] another's, he knows ours. He reveals his own secrets, he reveals another's frauds, he knows our hidden things. He reveals the deep things of his own dispensation, he reveals the hidden things of the devil's fraud, he knows the dark things of the human conscience. He reveals his own deep things, that we may know what we ought to believe of him, what to hope from him. He reveals another's hidden things, that we may know what we ought to fear, what to beware of. He knows our dark things, lest we believe that anything can lie hidden from him, and deceive ourselves with a vain hope. He revealeth deep and hidden things, and knoweth what is set in darkness: *The uncertain and hidden things of thy wisdom thou hast made manifest to me [n: (Psal. L)]*. Behold the revelation of deep things; and elsewhere he prays to the same effect: *Unveil mine eyes, and I will consider the wondrous things of thy law [n: (Psal. CXVIII)]*. He feared another's hidden things who said: *Thou wilt bring [1253B] me out of this snare which they have hidden for me [n: (Psal. XXX)]*. To the same thing looks what he sings elsewhere: *With their tongues they acted deceitfully; the venom of asps is under their lips [n: (Psal. XIII)]*. Did they not wish to hide the venom which they carried under their tongue? He believed that our lurking places could not lie hidden from him, who said: *But all things are naked and open to the eyes of God [n: (Hebr. IV)]* [var: Vulg. Heb. 4:13 *oculis ejus*, "to his eyes"]. It is Solomon's judgment that he alone knows all things, or knows all the hearts of the sons of men [n: (Sap. IX)]. With whose judgment he agrees who says: *God searcheth the hearts and the reins [n: (Psal. XII)]*. But what did he mean by saying, and light is with him. Without doubt God is light, and in him there are no darknesses at all. Why then does he not say what he could truly have said, that God is light, but says, and with him is light? Or did he perhaps wish to teach us this, [1253C] that where he himself has abided through indwelling grace, the light of necessary knowledge cannot be lacking? For the light indeed which he himself is, as it is in itself, we certainly cannot meanwhile see in this life; but the light which is with him we have been accustomed to receive, not only for solace, but also for support. But of what sort do we say this light to be, through which we recognize what we ought to do, what to avoid, what to love, what to hold in hatred, what to believe or to hope? Of what sort, I ask, is that light which knows deep and hidden things, he indeed revealing, he finally inspiring, who gives wisdom to the wise, and knowledge to them that understand instruction? Thus far Daniel has glorified God for the common good; but now for the special benefit specially bestowed [1253D] upon himself and upon his companions. *To thee,* he says, *God of my fathers, I confess, and thee I praise, because thou hast given me wisdom and fortitude, and now thou hast shown me the things we asked of thee, because thou hast opened to us the word of the king.* [var: Vulg. Dan. 2:23 *Deus patrum nostrorum*, "God of our fathers"] Above he said, he giveth wisdom to the wise. But here he says: Because thou hast given me wisdom and fortitude; and again: Because thou hast opened to us the word of the king. The chief order of charity, to prefer common goods to private ones. For charity seeketh not the things that are her own, but the things of others. He therefore who by the instinct of charity set common goods before his own, what wonder if he first offered the sacrifice of praise for those things which he loved more?

But it is to be noted that those three things which we assigned above to Daniel's office we can equally [1254A] mark in this one verse. Mark the voice of confession and of glorification in that which thou readest: To thee, God of my fathers, I confess, and thee I praise; and he shows that he offered the prayers of supplication in that which he says: And now thou hast shown to us the things we asked of thee. [var: Vulg. Dan. 2:23 has "hast shown ME" here, and the lemma printed above has it so too; this re-quotation gives "to us"] But in these three, unless I am mistaken, the office of true devotion is contained or fulfilled.



## CHAPTER XV. *How we ought to consult the rule of equity the more strictly, at that time above all when some office of sublimity must be fulfilled.*

*After this Daniel, going in to Arioch, whom the king had appointed to destroy the wise men of Babylon, spoke to him thus: Destroy not the wise men of Babylon; bring me in before the king, and I will tell the king the solution* [1254B] [n: (Dan. II)]. If by Daniel the fervor of devotion is rightly understood, and by Arioch the strictness of equity, what else will it be to wish to go in to Arioch than to seek out more deeply the [sic: *secretioria*] secrets of equity, and to wish to discern by innermost searching what strict justice demands? Now this business is rightly ascribed to Daniel at that time when the human mind is urged to this very thing out of a great devotion of spirit. Daniel therefore goes in to Arioch when devotion seeks out the counsels of equity. There is also yet another cause for going in to him (and perhaps not a less necessary one), namely when we wish to pour into him, to the very marrow, what we have recognized from divine revelation as needing correction in his senses. There we go in to him that, from much investigation and examination of justice, we may recognize what is right; here we enter in to him [1254C] that what has been divinely recognized as right we may press home the more strictly with a zeal for rectitude. There, then, we enter for the sake of learning, here for the sake of teaching; or there for the sake of inquiring, here for the sake of persuading. But we perceive the cause of his entering the sooner if we attend to what he says: Destroy not the wise men of Babylon. Behold, what the king in his trouble commanded to be done, Daniel, divinely enlightened, forbade to be done; and it often happens that what, being troubled and carried by an impulse of the spirit, we discern as though it were right, and presume can or ought to be done as by the office of Arioch, afterwards, having turned to prayers and supplication and been divinely enlightened amid the tears of our compunction, we find to be unjust, which before we thought right. So devotion often finds that to be iniquitous, and forbids its being done, which a violent impulse of the spirit had decreed should be done as it were [1254D] under a royal fury: Destroy not, he says, the wise men of Babylon. And he adds: Bring me in before the king, and I will tell the king the solution. Why, I ask, does he in this place beg to be brought in by another, who already above entered before the king's sight by himself? But above he entered that he might make supplication to the king; here, however, that he might teach the king. That was of humility, this of great sublimity. Of great sublimity, I say, was it to teach the king that which he could have learned from no one else. To the services of humility, therefore, he thrust himself willingly; to the offices of eminence he declined to thrust himself shamelessly. By his example let us learn what we ought to do in matters of this kind. When the place of mastery must be looked up to, whether from a command or for an office, [1255A] let the mind first enter in to Arioch. Let it seek out the counsels of justice, and by anxious examination let it look ahead, that it may carry out a good work well and justly. Do the good well, he says. The good is then done, when a good work rises from a good intention and proceeds in a fitting manner. It is easy for ambition or vainglory to drive us to a conspicuous and illustrious work. It is easy for the leaven of the Pharisees to corrupt the whole lump of our good work. In no way are we brought in by Arioch when we are driven to a good work by a sinister intention. As often, therefore, as we take up the place of teaching, let us look ahead to how justly, how orderly we are to fulfil the office we have taken up. Let us see to it that we say nothing false or frivolous, nothing inept or disordered. This rule of learning and of teaching, unless I am mistaken, [1255B] he keeps to whom that word of the Psalmist could apply: *Pleasant is the man who has mercy and lends; he shall order his words in judgment [n: (Psal. CXI)]*. And perhaps this will be to consult Arioch outwardly: to fortify ourselves beforehand with counsels of rectitude against the vices of speech or of work. But he is consulted as it were inwardly when inquiry is made concerning inward things, and the soul is fortified beforehand by the ordinances of justice against the corruption of thoughts or of afflictions. Above all at that time ought we to go in to Arioch, and to seek his leading by the hand, and to do nothing without the forethought or the fortification of justice; above all, I say, at that time when we must appear in a place of eminence, or fulfil an office of sublimity. Bring me in, he says, before the king, and I will tell the solution [1255C] to the king. Now our Daniel truly uses the leading by the hand of the said Arioch when, from the recollection of the divine strictness and the consideration of true justice, the spirit is pricked with compunction. And then he is brought in as it were before the royal presence by such a leader, when under any impulse of the spirit whatever, and as it were in the presence of royal power, the heart of man is easily inflamed to devotion by the regard of a strict examination.



## CHAPTER XVI. *By what steps the knowledge of mysteries advances, and to how great a perfection of learning the spirit often ascends by the merit of devotion.*

And I will tell the king, he says, the solution. What is this solution of the mystic vision, but the easy unravelling and ready [1255D] explication of the divine sacraments and mysteries? But if by the king we must understand the power of free will, what else will it be for such a solution to come to the royal cognizance, than to have the account of the divine mysteries openly and ready at hand? If therefore we have it free and ready and in our own power to bring forth in common the unravelling of hidden things whenever we will, we do not doubt that the learning and unravelling of the divine mysteries is already in our own choosing, and has already come, as it were, to the royal power. Now so great an enlargement of learning or of teaching is rightly ascribed to Daniel at that time when such grace is acquired and possessed by the merit of devotion. Let us see, then, by what steps of advancement the knowledge of divine things is enlarged. First of all Daniel received cognizance of the mystic vision from divine [1256A] revelation. Afterwards the same thing became known to his companions also, and at last the learning of that same thing came even to the king's cognizance. Of the first it is said: *Then to Daniel the mystery was revealed by a vision in the night.* [var: Vulg. *per visum nocte*, "by a sight in the night"] But afterwards Daniel professes, as much for himself as for his companions: *Because the word,* he says, *of the king thou hast opened to us.* And now the same man promises concerning the publishing to the king of the cognizance of that same thing. Bring me in before the king, and I will tell the king the solution. And that I may briefly discharge what I think upon these things: some in their prayer, some in their meditation. and others often in their very speaking, receive divine revelation, and come to know whatever things are sublime and profound out of divine inspiration.
