Nevertheless not only that which we penetrate subtly by praying, but that also which we penetrate by meditating [1256B] or by speaking, we then rightly attribute to Daniel, when we acquire any of these by the merit of devotion. There are certain men, then, who can never ascend to the contemplating or the penetrating of sublime things save after inward compunction and as it were after a cleansing of the heart; whose person Job expressed in himself when he says: *Before I eat I sigh, and like overflowing waters, so is my roaring [n: (Job. III)]*. He must needs sigh before he eats, who in no way can reach the inward refreshment of the soul and the pastures of truth save through the grace of compunction and after a pouring out of tears. Others in their meditations abound copiously [1256C] in divine revelations; and perhaps there are still such as cannot at all, without premeditation, either penetrate subtle things or discourse subtly. Those former, then, kindle for themselves the fire of divine revelation by their prayers, but these by their meditations: *And in my meditation a fire shall flame out,* says the Psalmist [n: (Psal. XXXVIII)]. The fire flames out in meditation when the spirit advances, even by its own investigations, to the light of divine revelation and to the manifestation of hidden things. The fire flames out in meditation when, out of its own inquiry, the spirit grows white-hot toward the knowledge and the love of truth. But it is agreed that some have advanced to so great an instruction that they can at every hour discourse subtly upon any subtle matters whatever, and can answer sufficiently, almost always, to whatever is asked them (without any premeditation [1256D]), being always ready, as it is written, to give satisfaction to everyone that asks a reason, and with that faith and hope which is in us [n: (I Petr. III)] [var: Vulg. *de ea, quae in vobis est, spe*, "concerning that hope which is in you"; the received text has no word for faith here, and reads "in you" for "in us"]. But certain of those who are of this kind have the light of divine revelation so familiar that many things are revealed to them even while they are speaking, out of those things which they themselves before knew not. As long, therefore, as the spirit obtains divine revelation through compunction of heart alone, Daniel as it were alone has thus far the cognizance of the mysteries. But when so divine a revelation occurs to our meditations, then the recognition of the mystic vision has come even to Daniel's companions. But when the mind has begun to have the illuminating grace so familiar and as it were at hand that [1257A] it can, at its own choosing and will, whenever it please, be sufficient at almost every hour for whatever things are to be discussed, established, defended, then the unravelling of hidden things begins to enlarge itself even to the royal cognizance. Is not the learning, or the instruction, of deeper things possessed as a faculty by a kind of royal right, when at the choice of the will one discourses easily and without any difficulty upon whatever mystic and profound matters? Behold to how great a perfection of learning the spirit is often led by the merit of devotion; behold what fruit often follows true devotion. This fruit of its devotion the provident mind often and prudently foresees before it obtains it, and confidently awaits. Whence it comes above all that it presses the more vehemently upon the zeal of devotion. I will tell the king, he says, the solution. And it is added: [1257B] *Then Arioch in haste brought Daniel in to the king, and said to him: I have found a man of the sons of the transmigration of Judas, who may signify the solution to the king.* [var: Vulg. *annuntiet*, "may announce" — the reading Richard's own exposition re-quotes twice at 1257D and again at 1259A] Behold, as thou hearest, when the promise of that solution which the king greatly desired had been received, Arioch brought Daniel in to the king. As was said above, Daniel is led by the hand to Arioch when, from the sight of strict equity, the fervor of devotion is inflamed. Now the human spirit is pricked with compunction in many ways and in many regards. But almost the best mode of compunction is that which rises from the consideration of the strict examination. Daniel therefore is then brought in not by anyone whatever, but as it were by Arioch, when from the consideration of true justice too little kept, the spirit is inwardly pricked with compunction. He is brought in to the king [1257C] and stands as it were beside the royal power, when true devotion is possessed out of virtue, and the spirit uses it at its own choosing. He is brought in in haste when easily, and without delay when need requires, the spirit is softened to contrition of heart. Let him therefore be zealous to have such a faculty, or facility, of compunction and of devotion, who desires to attain to that enlargement of learning which we assigned above. For it comes first that Daniel enter in through Arioch, and with haste, before the desired word becomes known to the king.



## CHAPTER XVII. *That he attains the highest summit of devotion who ascribes to his own merits whatever trouble befalls him, even beyond his desert.*

I have found, says Arioch, a man of the sons of the transmigration [1257D] of Judas, who may announce the solution to the king. That is found by Arioch which by the judgment of equity is discerned to be just and right. Arioch therefore found Daniel fit, and worthy to receive so great a grace, to perceive the revelation of the mysteries from God, to announce the solution to the king. And perhaps the fact that he was of the sons of the transmigration of Judas, and bore that long captivity patiently, helped Daniel's merit toward this very thing, and showed him the fitter for the receiving of so great a grace. This Daniel had assuredly been carried captive from Jerusalem into Babylon, and perhaps had committed nothing such as to incur a captivity of this kind, save that the common lot enfolded him and another's malice unjustly oppressed him. Nonetheless he ascribed to his own merits the captivity [1258A] which he bore without guilt. *We have sinned,* he says, *we have committed iniquity, we have done wickedly, and we have departed, and we have turned aside from thy commandments and thy judgments [n: (Dan. IX)]*. Rightly, then, is he said to be of the sons of the transmigration of Judas, who even amid the scourges of an undeserved oppression humbly confesses to the Lord. For Judas too is interpreted *confessing*. See therefore how rightly he deserved to be divinely glorified, who in so great and such an affliction sought the divine glory (not his own) by living and by confessing. How many incur the mark of suspicion not so much by their own fault as by another's malice, and pass as it were from Hierusalem to Babylon, and as though from a place of peace and quiet to a place of confusion and captivity. For Hierusalem is interpreted *a vision of peace,* Babylon *confusion*. What, then, is it to pass unjustly, as a captive, from Jerusalem into [1258B] Babylon, but to labor under a sinister, yet false, suspicion? It belongs to the depraved always to tear at the life of the good, and, when they cannot do it with true charges, to assail them nevertheless with false accusation; and when they fail at the defaming of their works, they overspread that simple eye of their intention, if they can, with the mark of a sinister suspicion. Just so, therefore, after the manner of Daniel, the mind of the just man is held under an unjust captivity at Babylon, when, laboring under a false suspicion, it is afflicted as shamelessly as irreverently by the reproach of an unjust confusion. Was he not groaning under a Babylonian affliction, so to speak, who said: *All the day my shame is against me, and the confusion of my face has covered me [n: (Psal. XLIII)]*. Consider [1258C] nevertheless that captivity of his confusion which he then bore, which at that time he carried without guilt, who with a secure conscience could say: *All these things came upon us, and we have not forgotten thee, and we have not dealt unjustly in thy testament [n: (ibid.)]* But when, amid pressing scourges, we detect in ourselves no present fault, not even then ought we to be secure. To this he instructed us by his own example who says: *I am conscious to myself of nothing, but I am not hereby justified [n: (I Cor. IV)]*. For often we are struck for a preceding fault, often for a present but hidden one, and indeed for such a fault as we believed to be no fault at all, or perhaps blotted out by satisfaction. And indeed, as must be altogether confessed, we are not always struck for correction or for purgation. But we are scourged now for instruction, [1258D] now for testing, or in some other way whatever. But it belongs to true and perfect devotion always to ascribe to its own merits the punishment it suffers, and to fear from what is hidden the fault which it does not detect in itself. That fervor of devotion, therefore, has already reached as it were the highest summit of perfection, which ascribes to its own merits any unjust reproach of confusion, and whatever befalls it even beyond its desert; which glorifies the Lord in all its affliction, and accuses itself in all things without pretense. How rightly is that fervor of devotion reckoned among the sons of the transmigration of Judas, which amid whatever ignominies of unjust reproach always humbly confesses to the Lord. But often those who are of this kind, who seek the divine glory before all others, who see themselves [1259A] without glory and do not shrink from being so seen, receive grace from God above the rest. I have found, he says, a man of the sons of the transmigration, who may announce the solution to the king.



## CHAPTER XVIII. *That we often presume less upon the virtue of devotion than we ought, and that the gift of mystic understanding is one thing, and the gift of mystic teaching another.*

*The king answered, and said to Daniel, whose name was Balthasar: Thinkest thou that thou canst truly tell me the dream which I saw, and the interpretation thereof?* For the king to answer Daniel and to show his own diffidence is nothing else than that such a vice of the spirit cannot lie hidden from true devotion. For often certain vices which at another time we cannot detect, we detect easily [1259B] in the hour of our compunction and amid the tears of our devotion. For perfect devotion sifts all things, discerns all things. For the spiritual man discerns all things, and he himself is judged by no one.

It is surely to be noted that Daniel, while he seeks out things profound and mystic, when he promises things sublime and subtle, is called Balthasar, which is interpreted *a hair of the head*. Now a hair of the head, as you know, is exceedingly long and subtle. What, then, is a hair of the head, but the subtle profundity and the profound subtlety of the mind? And perfect devotion assuredly both illuminates the mind unto profundity and sharpens it unto every subtlety. And a hair of the head is also an ornament; and the mind of man, assuredly, out of true devotion, in [1259C] so far as it is purged from vices, in so far as it is illuminated unto truth, in so far as it is inflamed unto virtue, in so far without doubt is it adorned, or ornamented. Note therefore that even he distrusted Balthasar's promise who had laid such a name upon him. For it was from the king assuredly that he received such a name. And it does happen that the mind feels and understands itself to be sharpened unto a wondrous subtlety out of much devotion, and yet in a time of necessity presumes less upon the virtue of devotion than it is able, or than it ought. Thinkest thou, he says, that thou canst truly tell me the dream which I saw, and the interpretation thereof? And Daniel above: Bring me in before the king, and I will tell the king the solution. Behold: where Daniel presumes and confidently promises, the royal [1259D] anxiety distrusts. All this is often enacted within one and the same spirit; and by almost as many affections as it is touched, by so many opinions is it varied. One and the same thing it now hopes for, now despairs of, and according to its various effects or regards it alternates the opinions of its estimation. But this fluctuation of alternating vicissitudes is at last concluded with a useful issue and a best end, when what is despaired of from human effort is at length, by the mastery of devotion, wholly presumed upon from divine grace. For what is Daniel's answer, but the mastery of true devotion? *And Daniel, answering before the king, said: The mystery which the king asks of, the wise men, the magi, and the soothsayers, and the diviners are not able to tell the king. But there is a God in the heavens revealing mysteries, who has shown to thee, Nabuchodonosor, what things [1260A] are to come in the last times.* [var: Vulg. *tibi, rex Nabuchodonosor* — the royal title is absent here, though Richard's own re-quotation at 1261A restores it; the received text also has the singular *in caelo*, "in heaven"] But because Daniel had already recognized the mystic vision which the royal anxiety was still seeking, someone perhaps desires to have it shown him more openly how one and the same thing can, by the same spirit, in one respect be known and in another respect not be known. But it is one thing to grasp the depths of the mysteries by understanding alone, and another to be able to explicate and expound them easily as often as thou shalt wish. See how rare they are who are able to penetrate the mystic things of the Scriptures without another's labor and exposition; yet far fewer are they who can publish the exposition of them, by word or by writing, to the cognizance of others. Thou weighest therefore, as I judge, that the gift of mystic understanding is one thing, and the gift of mystic teaching another. Some are strong in the one, some in the other, [1260B] but others are eminent in both. If upon this point we consult what is said of Moses, we recognize that he stands pre-eminent in wisdom, and his brother in eloquence. If we look to David, we shall be able to find both in one: *The uncertain and hidden things of thy wisdom thou hast made manifest to me [n: (Psal. L)]*. Behold, for the one. And likewise for the other: *I will open my mouth in parables, I will utter propositions from the beginning [n: (Psal. LXXVII)]*. But certain men have already received the first, and yet utterly distrust as to the second. Jeremiah had already known the mystic vision, who, being questioned upon this very thing, said: *I see a rod that watches;* and likewise: *I see a pot set burning, and the face thereof from the face of the north [n: (Jer. I)]*. Behold, thou already hearest him professing concerning the one gift; hear the same man still distrusting concerning the other: *Ah, ah, ah, [1260C] Lord, I know not how to speak.* Such a diffidence, surely, is expressed when it is said to one who already knows the vision. Thinkest thou that thou canst truly tell me the dream which I saw? Such diffidence is refuted, and it is shown whence such a grace ought to be despaired of, or hoped for, when it is said: The mystery which the king asks of, the wise men, the magi, and the soothsayers, and the diviners are not able to tell the king. But there is a God in the heavens revealing mysteries. Our Daniel therefore teaches us in these words utterly to despair of human effort as to those things which are above man and exceed human sense, and to look for them from the Lord's revelation alone. But in saying that there have been shown to him the things that are to come in the last times, he seems without doubt to look to that [1260D] which is added at the end of the vision after the rest: But the stone which had struck the statue became a great mountain, and filled the whole earth. How great, and how profound, and how worthy of much veneration are those things which this vision speaks according to the allegorical, nay almost according to the historical sense, no one skilled in the Holy Scriptures is permitted to be ignorant. But we sift these things according to the moral sense, for our own edification or that of others, in such a way that we presume to diminish or to weaken nothing of the authority of so great a mystery according to its more sacred understanding. This therefore presents itself as astonishing and worthy of much wonder: how widely there lies open to the eyes of contemplation the man who, by the cooperation of divine revelation, enlarges himself even to the surveying of those things which come to pass at the last. [1261A] Who has shown to thee, king Nabuchodonosor, what things are to come in the last times: he does not say, what things are to come to thee, but what things are to come in the last times.

It must therefore be asked whether perhaps something lie hidden in these words which may in some respect fit not one man only, but many, or even almost all prefects. For the kingdom of heaven is not raised up anywhere else than among the elect. A kingdom which, according to Daniel's word, is not scattered for ever; a kingdom which is said to be within us: *The kingdom,* says the Lord, *of heaven is within you [n: (Luc. XVII)]* [var: Vulg. *regnum Dei*, "the kingdom of God" — the received text of Luke 17:21 does not read "of heaven"]. This kingdom assuredly the Lord raises up in his elect at their last, in whatever manner he may permit them in their beginnings to waver [1261B] through various trials.



## CHAPTER XIX. *That we recover a lost grace of contemplation better by devotion than by investigation, and that we obtain freely that also which we acquire by the merit of devotion.*

But behold, Daniel now comes to the narration, or the exposition, of the vision, when he adds: *Thy dream, and the visions of thy head upon thy bed, are of this kind [n: (Dan. II)]*. Because by the dream the bodily sense is lulled, we rightly understand by it the excess of mind, and by the dream those things which we see through the excess of mind. The head is the highest and chief member of the body, and the mind is the principal part of the inner [1261C] man. The visions of the head, therefore, are the contemplations of the mind. Now in a bed we are wont to rest, and therefore in it we rightly understand the leisure of rest. In this bed our inner man is laid as it were to rest, when the spirit is composed to the highest tranquillity. In this bed a dream is then in a manner seen, when amid the leisures of its inmost rest and highest tranquillity the mind is lifted up to the contemplation of sublime things. Thy dream, he says, and the visions of thy head are of this kind. It is nothing else for our Daniel to say these things, and to go over again the lost dream, and to teach the king, than that the devout mind, often after the grace of contemplation has been lost, calls back to memory what that grace once was in it, and by much insistence of compunction [1261D] repairs it again, and at last possesses it more firmly and more perfectly. For the king came to know his vision more firmly and more perfectly through Daniel's office than he had before received it by himself. For to this end such grace is often given to some in their beginnings, and withdrawn, that they may recognize by experience what they ought to seek after, and with how great avidity. To this end again it is granted to be recovered (yet not without great labor), that from it may better become known how strictly it must be guarded. But that we may pass on to what follows: behold, before Daniel explicates the vision, he is zealous to set down two things first, namely how the king had first obtained it, and how Daniel himself might afterwards recover it. And of the first: *Thou, O king,* he says, *didst begin to think [1262A] upon thy bed what should be after thee. And he that reveals mysteries showed thee what things are to come.* [var: Vulg. *post haec*, "after these things"] As if he said openly: Because thou didst diligently seek concerning things to come, thou hast deserved to receive a revelation of things to come. Of the second also he adds: *To me* moreover *too, not in the wisdom which is in me above all living, has this sacrament been revealed, but that the interpretation might be made manifest to the king, and that thou mightest know the thoughts of thy mind.* As if he said to the king more openly: To me also it has been revealed, not through my own sense, not on account of my merit, but for thy advancement. And I think this very thing is plain to all, how much it pleases according to the history, that he in no way ascribes to his own effort or to his merits that other thing which he had obtained by prayers. Thou, O king, he says, didst begin. And do thou consider, and [1262B] consider well, if thou art able, how much the thought of things to come avails with God, which is wont to be divinely rewarded with a revelation of things to come. Hear a man anxious concerning things to come, and vehemently occupied in thoughts of this kind: *Will God then cast off for ever, and will he not add that he be more favorable yet? Or will he cut off his mercy unto the end, from generation to generation? [n: (Psal. LXXVI.)]* Hear the same man taught concerning such things, and deeply enlightened as to those things which he had sought: *The Lord is compassionate and merciful, long-suffering and very merciful; he will not be angry for ever, nor will he threaten unto eternity [n: (Psal. CII)]*. Perhaps he had then lost the revelation of things to come, and grieved to have lost it, when he said: *There is now no prophet, [1262C] and he will know us no more [n: (Psal. LXXIII)]*. And likewise: *And the light of the eyes, even that is not with me [n: (Psal. XXXVII)]* [var: Vulg. *lumen oculorum meorum*, "the light of my eyes"]. He was aspiring, unless I am mistaken, to the former grace, who said: *Who will grant me that I may be according to the former days? [n: (Job. XXIX.)]* [var: Vulg. *Quis mihi tribuat, ut sim juxta menses pristinos*, "the former months"] He was seeking again the accustomed revelation of mysteries, who asked of the Lord: *Unveil mine eyes, and I will consider the wondrous things of thy law [n: (Psal. CXVIII)]*. Thou too who hearest or readest these things, if thou feelest that thou hast fallen from such grace, attend diligently to what thou dost silently within thyself; consider with what thoughts thou art vehemently occupied. If thou meditatest on empty things alone, on pressing things alone, what wonder if thou art cheated of the revelation of deep things, of things to come? In the beginning of thy conversion, when thou didst think on eternal things alone, on spiritual and future things alone, when thou didst sigh after sublime things alone, [1262D] what wonder if thou didst deserve to be consoled according to thy desire? The Lord has heard the desire of the poor. Thou hast now ceased to sit and rest at the Lord's feet, after the likeness of Mary. Thou art now troubled about many things, after the likeness of Martha. Remember therefore whence thou hast fallen, and do penance, and do the former works. If thou desirest to restore that former grace, if thou seekest to recover the visions of thy head upon thy bed, run back to Daniel, renew thy devotion. For the renewal of the heart, surely, for the restoration of a lost grace, thou advancest better and art promoted more swiftly by inward devotion than by profound investigation, unless perhaps thy investigation be about thy own declines, and the remedies of those declines. That saying of Daniel agrees with these words. To me also, not in the wisdom [1263A] which is in me above all living, has this sacrament been revealed. Assuredly the king, inquiring after every word of wisdom and of understanding, found in Daniel tenfold above all the soothsayers and magi. Nevertheless a man of so great wisdom obtained what he sought not so much by investigation as by prayer. Let no one, therefore, seek through human wisdom those things which are above human understanding. It calls us perhaps to a deeper understanding, that Daniel does not ascribe to himself even that which he had obtained by the merit of devotion. But that the interpretation, he says, might be made manifest to the king. Perhaps that also is obtained freely which is acquired by the merit of devotion. For devotion itself indeed we have not from ourselves, but we receive it from the gift of the bestower: *For what hast thou,* says the Apostle, *which thou hast not [1263B] received? [n: (I Cor. IV)]*. Therefore both by devotion, and indeed by grace: *Freely,* he says, *you have received, freely give [n: (Matth. X)]*. If therefore by devotion we receive freely, that too is gratuitous which we obtain by its merit. When grace is bestowed for grace, then, just as the first, so also the second gift is obtained freely. We do not therefore receive the gifts of God because we have deserved them, but that from them we may be able to advance, or to profit others. And the understanding of truth indeed we receive for our own advancement, but the teaching of truth for the advancement of others. Now by both is free will helped toward the good, and both are divinely bestowed upon it for a cooperation in the good. But by the king, as we have said, we understand the liberty of the will. To Daniel, therefore, the interpretation [1263C] of perplexed things, the account of the divine judgments, is given as it were for this end, that it may be made manifest to the king, when devotion is for this end illuminated unto truth, that free will may have and recognize wherein it ought to exercise itself, what to beware of, what to choose.



## CHAPTER XX. *A concise recapitulation of what has been said, with the attestation of a likeness.*

It is profitable at this point to bring into consideration how this reading and the Gospel reading seem to accord together in a mystical manner of speech. Luke the evangelist relates how the Lord willed to show his presence to the disciples on their journey in the appearance of a stranger, and [1263D] afterwards to withdraw it; but to remain with them as they asked, to enter in to them as they constrained him, and at last, amid the feast, to show that appearance which they might recognize [n: (Luc, XXIV)]. What then is it to have Christ, that is, the Wisdom of God, present in the appearance of a stranger, but to see the truth not in its own simplicity, but through a glass, or in an enigma? But this vision is shown outside the house and as it were on a journey, when the contemplation of sublime things is seen through an excess of mind and as it were in passing. There are, as it were, two going out, who also as they walk behold such things, when reason and intelligence, exceeding the human measure, run through the spectacles of sublime things, stealthily indeed and hurriedly. But then the Lord feigns to go further, and yet does not wholly withdraw, [1264A] when the grace of contemplation, which he is wont mercifully to bestow, he withdraws for a time, no less profitably, that he may better teach by experience with how great eagerness it ought to be sought and to be held fast. And he is constrained to remain and to enter in to them, when by much instancy of prayers the lost grace is repaired, so that he may draw inward the vision offered outwardly, and that the spirit, returned to itself, may retain in memory the things seen through excess, and thereafter possess the grace of contemplation more familiarly. We set before him such foods as the Lord loves and is wont to be delighted with, when, for the recovery or the accumulation of grace, we praise, honor, and magnify him in the voice of exultation and of confession: *In the voice,* he says, *of exultation, and [1264B] of confession the sound of one feasting [n: (Psal. XLI)]*. Amid these hymns of our exultation and confession the bosom of the mind is often enlarged, the sense is sharpened, and the intelligence is enlightened for penetrating mystical things, and for often searching out even the secrets of the Godhead: *The sacrifice,* he says, *of praise shall honor me, and there is the way by which I will show the salvation of God [n: (Psal. XLIX)]*. [var: Vulg. *ostendam illi salutare Dei*, "will show him the salvation of God"] Beyond doubt the bread is broken before us by the Lord, when the profundity of the mysteries is opened by mystical interpretation, and is known by his own revealing. From this breaking of bread and revelation of the mysteries it comes about that the Lord is recognized in his own appearance, and that Truth itself (the veil of figures being removed) is discerned in its own simplicity, and the Lord's presence is weighed from [1264C] the infusion of his grace. But the Lord (who is also the Wisdom of God) vanishes from the eyes of those beholding, when, from the contemplation and admiration of the divine wisdom, it becomes known to the spirit of him who contemplates and admires how far its incomprehensibility exceeds every human intelligence: *O the depth,* he says, *of the riches, of the wisdom, and of the knowledge of God: how incomprehensible are his judgments, and his ways unsearchable [n: (Rom. XI)]*. For the human spirit, the more subtly it is enlightened for contemplating the wisdom of God, so much the more strongly is it beaten back upon itself by the immensity of that light; and this is to vanish from the eyes of the beholder, and, as it were, in showing itself to withdraw itself. From these things, therefore, one may weigh with how great a proportion of likeness this twin reading seems [1264D] to answer to itself. For that the Lord showed himself in the appearance of a stranger, this is that Nabuchodonosor received the revelation of the truth under a mystical veil. That there the Lord feigned for himself a longer journey, this is that the vision shown to the king withdrew itself for a little from his memory. That there he who had appeared is constrained to remain and to enter in, this is that here the withdrawn vision is sought with much instancy, and at last, by Daniel's solicitude, is perceived and retained far more profoundly, far more perfectly. That he who had appeared there is at length known in a manifest vision, this is that in this place the clouded truth of the vision taken away is at last made manifest by prophetic interpretation. In these things, and in certain others, he will see this twin reading to accord with itself, [1265A] if there be any who is willing to search these matters out more deeply. Yet that reading has certain things proper to itself, and this one too, of which there is no need to speak now one by one. These things, therefore, having been shaken out by way of digression, and brought together for the attestation of the likeness, let us return to the explication, or explanation, of the vision.



## CHAPTER XXI. *How everyone who desires one day to remain fixed in true stability must subside from the height of his own presumption.*

*Thou, O king, wast seeing, and behold, as it were one great statue that statue, the great one, and lofty in stature, stood over against thee, and its look was terrible. The head of this statue was of the finest gold. But the breast and the arms of silver. Further, the belly and the thighs of bronze, but the shins of iron. [1265B] A certain part of the feet was of iron, a certain of earthenware. Thou wast seeing thus, until a stone was cut out without hands, and struck the statue upon its feet of iron and of earthenware, and crushed them. Then were crushed together the iron, the clay, the bronze, the silver and the gold, and were reduced as it were into the cinders of a summer threshing-floor, which were carried off by the wind, and no place was found for them. But the stone which struck the statue became a great mountain, and filled the whole earth. This is the dream [n: (Dan. II)]*. [var: Vulg. *abscissus est lapis de monte sine manibus*, "was cut out of a mountain without hands"] Behold, as thou canst see, that image which is discerned through the vision is by manifold change always led into worse things; and that which in the dream begins from the most precious material, running down through manifold declines, at last ends in the vilest material. For what is begun from gold is at [1265C] the last consummated in mire. That I may therefore briefly touch upon what I think concerning these things, according to a certain general consideration: I judge that everyone must, according to the form set forth of the vision shown, decrease within himself from his own estimation, and fail more and more in confidence in himself, and temper his presumption, if he desires the kingdom of heaven to be built within him, and that kingdom indeed which can never be ended. Every man naturally loves and approves himself, and assuredly, in so far as he loves, so far also does he esteem himself great. But always the measure of esteem hangs upon the greatness of love; because the mode of love is without mode, the greatness of his own esteem is without measure. O how rare it is that a man can be found [1265D] who does not think himself, against the Apostle's sentence, to be something, when he is nothing! But is he at least something small? Nay, truly great, and exceedingly great beyond measure, and, that I may speak figuratively, almost more than golden, while in truth he is vile mire. Why art thou proud, earth and ashes? *If thou be exalted as an eagle, and if thou set thy nest among the stars of heaven, thence will I draw thee down, saith the Lord [n: (Abd. IV)]*. [var: Vulg. *et si inter sidera posueris nidum tuum*, with no *coeli*, "among the stars"] It behooves him therefore who still swells immeasurably within himself to subside from that enormous height of his own esteem, and to descend by steps to the depths of true humiliation, and at length to reckon himself as a nothing and a void: to trample himself in contempt as vile mire, and to look upon himself every hour as cinder and ashes, if he desires that kingdom of eternal stability to rise up within himself. [1266A] He accords with this sentence to whom there was none like upon the earth: *I am compared to mire, and am made like to cinders and ashes [n: (Job XXX)]*. But do you wish to hear yet more plainly how utterly he was cast down from all confidence in himself, who appeared great among all the men of the East? *I have despaired,* he says, *by no means shall I live any longer now [n: (Job VII)]*. He says that he has despaired, but perhaps thou doubtest of what: of the Lord, or of himself? Hear therefore what he says elsewhere, and know how strongly he remained fixed in confidence in the Lord: *Even if he slay me, I will hope in him [n: (Job XIII)]*. He hoped, therefore, but of the Lord. He despaired none the less, but of himself. O how great a perversity, to presume of oneself and to despair of the Lord's mercy! If thou trustest much in thine own virtue, there thou raisest thyself on high, and [1266B] swellest up after the likeness of a mountain, where thou oughtest to have lowered thyself and made thyself as a valley. It is good therefore to say to this mountain: be lifted up, and be cast into the sea. Because of such mountains the earth shall be troubled, and mountains shall be carried into the heart of the sea. On the contrary, if thou distrustest the Lord's protection, there beyond doubt thou makest, wickedly and perversely enough, a valley where thou oughtest to have had a hill, nay a mountain, and a mountain exceeding high. That therefore the crooked things may be made straight, and the rough ways plain, every such valley shall be filled, every mountain and hill shall be brought low, and at that time the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be raised above the top of the mountains. O how great a height of mind! o how great a fortitude or firmness, to trust in the Lord's mercy alone, and to remain fixed in such [1266C] confidence! This is that mountain which, after the casting down of the statue and the attenuation or extermination of confidence in oneself, grows from small to immense, so that it cannot be moved for ever: *He that trusteth,* he says, *in the Lord, as mount Sion, shall not be moved for ever, he that dwelleth in Jerusalem [n: (Psal. CXXIV)]*. [var: Vulg. *Qui confidunt in Domino*, plural, "they that trust in the Lord"] This is the mountain which must fill the whole surface of the earth, so that a man may dare nothing of his own effort, may presume nothing at all save of the Lord's virtue. I think that a city set upon this mountain cannot be hid. If thou believest me, thou wilt build for thyself on this mountain that structure which is built as a city, whose participation is in itself, that there may be a firmament in the earth on the tops of the mountains. On this eminence assuredly the kingdom of charity ought to have its metropolis and the seat [1266D] of its empire, and of its kingdom there shall be no end. For the kingdom of charity, if I mistake not, is that kingdom which, according to Daniel's sentence, shall not be destroyed for ever. Behold what the raising up, or the casting down, of this statue sets before thee; behold what things, and how great, it represents to thee by way of likeness.



## CHAPTER XXII. *On the measure of the human condition, or of human corruptibility, and that on any summit of virtues one must fear the ruin of morals.*

What is a statue, but a human effigy? What then is it to discern a statue, that is, a human likeness, through a vision, but to look upon the measure, or the order, of human life as through a glass, and in an enigma, [1267A] with the eye of contemplation? *Thou, O king,* he says, *wast seeing, and behold, as it were one great statue [n: (Dan. II)]*. If thou wouldst search out the measure or the quality of human life, if to the dignity of its condition, if to the ease of its reparation, to whichever of these thou turn thyself, thou wilt see that thou failest in each, and canst not fully comprehend any of them. See therefore how great that is in the eyes of the beholder which cannot at all be comprehended by his own sight: *That statue,* he says, *the great one, and lofty in stature, stood over against thee, and its look was terrible.* But rightly, after he said "great," he perhaps adds "lofty" also. For it is one thing to be great, and another to be high. For a field also is called great which yet is raised by no height. So indeed some things are almost incomprehensible [1267B] which yet are not worthy of much investigation or admiration. But that we have heard this statue to be great, lofty, terrible, we can rightly accommodate to a threefold consideration. For the condition of human life, which is figured in this statue, although each of these is found in some respect in each, is yet more especially and more expressly found great from one thing, lofty from another, and terrible from another. One consideration therefore of the human condition is monstrous, on that side by which it lies subject to corruption; and it is lofty on that side by which it is reserved for reparation; and terrible on that side by which it lies open to perdition. Do you wish to hear how great is the monstrousness of corruption? *To what shall I compare thee, or to what shall I [1267C] liken thee, O daughter of Jerusalem; to what shall I make thee equal, and comfort thee, O virgin daughter of Sion? Great as the sea is thy crushing. Who shall heal thee? [n: (Thren. II)]*. [var: Vulg. *magna est enim velut mare contritio tua*, "for thy crushing is great as the sea"] Do you wish to know how great is the loftiness of reparation? *For whom he foreknew, he also predestinated to be made conformable to the image of his Son, that he himself might be the firstborn among many brethren. Whom he predestinated, them he also called; and whom he called, them he also justified; but whom he justified, them he also magnified [n: (Rom. VIII)]*. [var: Vulg. *glorificavit*, "glorified"] Do you wish to know this also, how great is the terror of the divine stroke? *Who,* he says, *knoweth the power of thy wrath, and for fear of thee can number thy anger? [n: (Psal. LXXXIX)]*. For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and injustice of those men who detain the truth of God in injustice. Consider therefore the greatness of our statue [1267D] in the consideration of fault; its height, in the consideration of grace; its terror, in the consideration of punishment. Seek the greatness of fault both according to original fault and according to actual fault. And for original fault, hear what is said of man to man: *Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he is compared to senseless beasts, and is become like to them [n: (Psal. XLVIII)]*. And concerning actual fault, receive the voice of reproach: *On every high hill, and under every leafy tree thou didst prostrate thyself, a harlot [n: (Jer. II)]*. Whence it is that it is said to her: Lift up thine eyes round about, and see where thou now liest prostrate, a harlot. O truly the height of grace, both according to justifying grace and according to confirming grace, and according to glorifying grace! [1268A] Measure, if thou art able, the loftiness of that sublimity, according to justifying grace: *For as far as the rising is distant from the west, so far hath he put our iniquities from us [n: (Psal. CII)]*. Receive also the height of eminence, according to confirming grace. For according to the height of heaven from the earth, he hath strengthened his mercy over them that fear him. Estimate, if thou canst, the sublimity of dignity, according to glorifying grace: *For whosoever are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God. And if sons, heirs also. Heirs indeed of God, but joint-heirs with Christ [n: (Rom. XIV)]*. O the aspect of our statue, truly terrible according to the adjudging of punishment; terrible according to the judgment of corruption; terrible according to the judgment of reprobation; terrible according to the judgment of damnation! O the aspect [1268B] of terror, according to the judgment of corruption! For evils without number have surrounded me; my iniquities have overtaken me, and I was not able to see. They are multiplied above the hairs of my head. O the aspect full of horror, according to the judgment of reprobation! *And as they did not approve,* says the Apostle, *to have God in their knowledge, God delivered them up to a reprobate sense, to do those things which are not fitting, being filled with all iniquity, malice, fornication, avarice, wickedness [n: (Rom. I)]*. O the aspect full of terror, full of horror, according to the judgment of damnation! For there is, according to the same Apostle, a certain terrible expectation of judgment, and rage of fire which shall consume [1268C] the adversaries. For their fire shall not be extinguished, and their worm shall not die. Of those, namely, who lead their days in good things, and in a moment go down to hell. From all these things, as I judge, thou weighest how horrible it is to fall into the hands of the living God. What can be said more terrible than these, what more horrible can be devised? And its look, he says, was terrible. But that which is said of the statue, it stood over against thee, needs no long exposition. Then beyond doubt is such a statue raised up against any single man, when the foulness, the infirmity, the calamity of the beholding spirit is thrust upon his eyes, and it is shown him by revelation what he is, or what he may yet become, so that his shamelessness, his pride, his hardness may be confounded, humbled, crushed: *I will reprove thee,* [1268D] he says, *and I will set thee against thy face [n: (Psal. XLIX)]*. He is divinely reproved, when the spirit, already touched by divine inspiration, is confounded by the accusation of his own conscience. And the transgressing soul is set as it were against its own face, when in the consideration of its own foulness it seems to serve against itself by rebuke. A statue therefore is in a manner set against the spirit of him who beholds, when, for his own confusion and humiliation, by a certain divine nod the image of his own corruptibility is set before him. Learn therefore, O man, learn to lay aside confidence in thyself (if suddenly and at once thou canst not, then at least by degrees and through intervals of time); be earnest to do it; be busy to think of thyself ever more and more humbly, that thou mayest attain, even [1269A] late, to true and perfect humility. These are the unshaken foundations of consummate charity; these are the firm defenses of the eternal security of the reigning soul. Lay aside arrogance, press down pride, crush that perverse trust in thine own virtue, cast thy care upon the Lord. Reckon all thy virtue, all thy fortitude, all thine effort as ash and cinder. What else has marked the cinder than to yield to every whirlwind, nay, to fly apart at any breath, however slight, and to forsake the place of its rest? A form fitting enough for our corruption, and an image suitably expressed in ash and cinder. See, whoever thou art, lest perhaps it behoove thee, willing or unwilling, to be such perhaps at some time inwardly or outwardly: inwardly with thyself in thine own estimation, or outwardly also before [1269B] others in thine action. Inwardly, I say, from the purpose and zeal of the will, or outwardly from the failing and the fluctuation of human corruptibility. And how many there are who in no way come down from the height of their own estimation, save then first, when outwardly they fall shamefully in action. For to this end beyond doubt are some permitted to fall deformedly in action, and to change their gold into silver, silver into bronze, bronze into iron, iron into clay, that from their own failing, and as it were by experiment, they may learn what they ought to think of their own virtue and fortitude. Let us see therefore how it befalls some, according to the form of the image shown, to fall as it were from the highest goods almost to the utmost evils through the various failings of corruptions, [1269C] and to end a head of gold, as it were, in feet of clay; that we may learn, on any summit of virtues, to fear the ruin of morals, and may be busy always and everywhere to keep the form and the measure of true and perfect humility.



## CHAPTER XXIII. *That from a great summit of virtues the human mind is often wont to fall by degrees into the depths.*

*He that standeth,* says the Apostle, *let him take heed lest he fall [n: (I Cor. X)]*. [var: Vulg. *qui se existimat stare*, "he that thinketh himself to stand"] From however lofty a summit one may easily fall into the depths, or be plunged into the deep; nay, beyond doubt, the higher the step, the worse the fall. That dream of Nabuchodonosor ought always both to render us cautious and to make us solicitous. See, I beseech thee, the statue of his vision; [1269D] see, I say, from how great a loftiness it begins, and to what an end it is at last brought down. It has indeed a head of gold, and an end of clay. What is dearer than gold, what viler than clay? Note this also, how by degrees it inclines to worse things, and at length makes its end in a most foul ending. The first part is described as of gold, the second of silver, the third of bronze, the fourth of iron, and the fifth of clay. In the gold is understood charity; in the silver, truth; in the bronze, pretense; in the iron, cruelty; in the earthenware clay, fragility. For clay is easily broken, and by it the fragility of impatience is rightly figured. Iron, which crushes and tames all other metals, fittingly designates the violence of cruelty, which presses upon whatever resists, that it may crush it. But bronze imitates silver [1270A] in sound, yet is much at variance in price. So simulation has the sweet ring of flattery in speech, and resounds sweetly, and echoes pleasantly in work; but as much as by word and practice it soothes without, so much by counsel and desire it grows pale within. Silver too, the more frequent the use by which it is worn, so much the brighter is it made: so truth, the more it is shaken by vehement discussion, so much the better is it commended, if the counsels of truth, made more certain by the use of experience, are thereby rendered the brighter. The splendor of gold expresses the brightness of charity, which blazes with the fire of heavenly desire; and as gold is preferred to the other metals, so charity surpasses the other virtues. O how great is the distance between clay and gold, between the end of the statue and the beginning of the statue! The statue which begins from gold ends in clay. [1270B] I think that no one becomes most base of a sudden. But he who neglects the least things slips away little by little. As one climbs to the heights by certain steps of progress, so again one descends by degrees to the depths. Note how in this statue there is first gold, afterwards silver, and after these, with bronze between, iron also follows. O how great the difference of gold and iron! O how greatly do charity and cruelty differ from one another! Yet what says the Truth concerning these? *Iniquity shall abound,* he says, *and the charity of many shall grow cold [n: (Matth. XXIV)]*. [var: Vulg. *quoniam abundavit iniquitas*, "because iniquity hath abounded"] See, I pray, from whence one comes to what: from the abundance of charity to the abundance of iniquity. Charity belongs to gold, iniquity belongs to iron. O the wonderful (nay, the detestable) change from charity to iniquity! *If the just man,* he says, [1270C] *turn away from his justice, and do iniquity, all his justices which he had done shall not be remembered [n: (Ezech. XVIII)]*. A detestable work, and worthy of confusion, which is begun from gold and consummated in clay and iron. For thus is described a part of the feet as of iron, and a certain part as of clay. O shameful workmen, who at the beginning of their conversion begin their work from gold, and at last consummate it in mire. We know that often, when the unclean spirit has gone out of a man, seeking rest and not finding it, having taken with him seven other spirits more wicked than himself, he returns into his house, and entering in dwells there, and the last things of that man become worse than the first. How many do we see at the beginning of their conversion rejoicing in hope, fervent in spirit, patient in tribulation, solicitous in work, [1270D] studious in reading, devout in prayer. What do these seem to thee to do, but to work in gold, and to be initiated in charity? *For charity,* as it is written, *is patient, is kind, beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things [n: (I Cor. XIII)]*. Does he not seem to thee to work in gold, to whom it was said by the Lord: *I know thy works, and thy charity, and thy faith, and thy ministry, and thy patience? [n: (Apoc. VIII.)]* [var: Vulg. *et fidem, et caritatem tuam*, faith before charity] But there are many who believe for a time, and in the time of temptation fall away. Yet those who are such do not at once plunge themselves into the lowest things, but fall first from the good into the worse, then from the less good into the bad, and at last from the bad into the yet worse. For a falling mountain slips away little by little, and the earth is consumed by a flood. For such as these begin little by little to grow lukewarm from their former desire, [1271A] and to fail more and more from their earlier fervor.



## CHAPTER XXIV. *How, or by what steps of corruption, the human spirit often falls from the highest things into the lowest.*

Yet they do not at once forsake what they have begun, but still do the good things they can. For when charity has grown cold, they do indeed work good things out of deliberation. Yet what do we think there is between that former state and this second one? Much in every way. It is one thing to follow the good out of desire, and another out of counsel alone. It is one thing, I say, to work the good with great delight, and another out of deliberation alone. This is good, but that is best. This belongs to silver, that belongs to gold. A precious [1271B] metal indeed is in silver, though it be far viler than gold. Let him therefore study to work in silver who perchance lacks abundance of gold: if he cannot do good things out of delight, yet do it at least out of truth, and the truth shall make thee free. But do you wish to know the work that is made out of such silver, how it shines, or how much it pleases, and how rich or how secure it renders its possessor? *Everyone,* he says, *that doeth truth cometh to the light, that his works may be made manifest, because they are good [n: (Joan. III)]*. [var: Vulg. *Qui autem facit veritatem … quia in Deo sunt facta*, "But he that doeth truth … because they are done in God"] It is good therefore to abound in silver of this kind, but no less foolish to change one's gold into silver. For every man that putteth his hand to the plough and looketh back is not fit for the kingdom of God. But do you wish to know how the divine word strikes with rebuke [1271C] him who had changed a golden work into silver? *I know,* he says, *thy works and thy labor, and thy patience [n: (Luc. IX)]*. Behold a good work; behold the arms, behold the breast of silver. But let us see what follows, when afterwards it is subjoined: *But I have,* he says, *against thee, that thou hast forsaken thy first charity [n: (Apoc. VIII)]*. He therefore who still does good is reproved because he has left his first charity, and has bent the golden head down into a breast of silver. Whosoever thou art that judgest thyself to be of this kind, be mindful whence thou art fallen, and do penance, and do the first works. Otherwise fear that which follows, which the divine word threatens against him who by no means comes to his senses: *But if not,* he says, *I come to thee, and will move thy candlestick out of [1271D] its place, unless thou do penance [n: (Apoc. II)]*. Fear therefore, unless thou return the more speedily to thy former good things, lest thou fall yet into worse. Choose which thou wouldst rather, to ascend or to descend. For a man cannot stand fixed in the same state for long. For he flees as a shadow, and never continues in the same state. Hold it in memory, and fear it not moderately, that he who does not return to his first charity, his candlestick is quickly moved out of its place. What is meant by the candlestick, the bearer of light, but a good work, a work of truth? Such a candlestick stands in its place, when a good work rises out of a good purpose. But such a candlestick is moved out of its place, when the good intention of a good work is changed into an evil one. So a work of silver passes into one of bronze. And this evil is indeed frequent [1272A] among the sons of men. For often what one formerly did out of truth, being dissolved toward the praise of men, he afterwards keeps doing for human favor: *O my people,* he says, *they that call thee blessed, the same deceive thee, and destroy the way of thy steps [n: (Isa. III)]*. He therefore who shows himself bland in speech, kind in work, but crooked and perverse in thought and in will, he assuredly, having cast away silver, works now in bronze. For after the manner of bronze he rings sweetly without, but by the depravity of his will he grows pale within. Does not the work of those seem to thee to be such, who speak peace with their neighbor, but evils are in their hearts. In such a work, as I judge, he sweated whom the Lord reproved in rebuking him, when he says: *I know thy works, that [1272B] thou hast a name that thou livest, and thou art dead [n: (Apoc. III)]*. But whosoever thou art that art such, do not think that thou canst long lie hid: *But if thou be exalted as an eagle, and set thy nest among the stars, thence will I draw thee down, saith the Lord [n: (Abd. I)]*. One day thou must hear the prophetic, nay the Lord's, voice: *Uncover thy shame, lay bare thy shoulder, make bare thy legs, pass over the rivers. And then shall thy ignominy be revealed, and thy reproach shall be seen [n: (Isa. XLVII)] [var: Vulg. Isa. 47:3 runs on without *Et tunc*, *transi flumina, revelabitur ignominia tua*; the same verse is printed at 1361A of this work without the added words]*. But when thy shame has been uncovered, when the belly and the thighs of bronze have begun to appear, thou wilt soon begin to grow foul to thy praisers, nay now to thy mockers, and from day to day to grow viler and viler. Then wilt thou begin to be angry with them, to be indignant, to detest them and cruelly to persecute them, whom [1272C] before thou hadst studied much to please. And as bland as thou wast before, so harsh and hard wilt thou be afterwards. So thy bronze shall be changed into iron, and it shall be said to thee: *How art thou turned into bitterness, O strange vine? [n: (Jer. II.)]* [var: Vulg. *conversa es mihi in pravum*, "turned unto me into that which is depraved"] There is no doubt that he has changed a work of bronze into iron. Gentleness into severity: whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness, who before dealt deceitfully with their tongues, the venom of asps under their lips. You who before showed yourselves so bland, so kind, whence now are wars and quarrels among you? Now you have bitter zeal, and contentions among you. You kill and you envy, you go to law and you make war; and whence is this so savage cruelty and hardness of iron in you? What thinkest thou is the cause that their feet are so swift [1272D] to shed blood, unless that they have shins and soles of iron, who rejoice when they have done evil, and exult in the worst things? But this in them is above all wonderful, nay above all things pitiable, that as they are prompt and bold in inflicting evils, so are they faint-hearted and beyond measure impatient in bearing the evils inflicted; so that thou mayest rightly wonder in what manner iron can agree with clay, so great a cruelty with so great an impatience. Behold to what an end our statue comes, which after a head of gold received soles of earthenware. The noble sons of Sion, and clothed with the finest gold, how are they esteemed as vessels of clay, the work of the potter's hands? What is more precious than gold, what viler than clay? How then is the gold become obscured, the finest color changed? [1273A] What is more tractable than gold, what more fragile than clay? How does charity permit herself to be handled; how to be drawn thin, she who beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things? But what is more contemptible than the will, what more abject than a delicate mind, which both above and in prosperous things is dissolved through concupiscence, and in adverse things is broken through impatience? *Woe to them that have lost endurance, that have forsaken the right ways, and have turned aside into crooked ones [n: (Eccle. II)]*. For crushing and unhappiness are in their ways. Crushing, because of the corruptibility of clay; and unhappiness, because of the rigor of iron, in that a certain part of the feet is of clay, but a certain part is of iron. But what is it that men of this kind are turned again to their own desires, that after the works of bronze and of iron they are drawn to [1273B] the work of the potter, unless that they have not (save in their own concupiscences) wherein to be delighted, because by simulation they first lost the joy of a good conscience, and afterwards, by cruelty, the glory of reputation. But that we may recall to a summary the things we have now said more diffusely: in the head of gold is understood devotion; in the members of silver, discretion; in those of bronze, simulation; in those of iron, indignation; in those of clay, dissolution.



## CHAPTER XXV. *On the difference of the aforesaid steps, and the quality of each.*

It is indeed to be noted what is said of which members, and of what sort each of them is described. Now there is described [1273C] a golden head, a silver breast, silver arms too, a belly and thighs of bronze, iron shins, feet of iron, or in part of clay. By the head the whole body is ruled, whence by it intention is rightly signified, because by intention the whole body of our action is led to an end, whether good or evil. Counsel belongs to the heart, and the heart lies hidden beneath the breast. With the arms we carry out our works, when we will something to be done by us. The belly, the more tender part of the body and the covering of foulness, portends the service of compassion. The thigh is set beneath the shameful parts, and humility, which bends down to base and unworthy things, wishes to be seen as perfect. The shins carry bones longer and sturdier than the other members, whence they also rightly signify the rigor of severity. With the feet we touch the earth, even when we [1273D] stand upright; and however much the mind stretches itself out toward heavenly things, without the supports of this life it does not sustain its own necessity. By the head, therefore, as has been said, intention is understood; by the breast, deliberation; by the arm, exercise; by the belly, compassion; by the thigh, humility; by the shin, severity; by the foot, necessity; by the head, the desire of intention; by the breast, the zeal of deliberation; by the arm, the exercise of action; by the belly, the service of piety; by the thigh, the servitude of subjection; by the shin, the scourge of severity; by the foot, the support of necessity. If then the head is intention, and gold devotion, what else is a golden head but a devout intention? If the breast is deliberation, the arm action, and silver discretion, what else will a silver breast and silver arms be than [1274A] discreet counsels and works? In the belly, compassion; in the thigh, subjection; and in the bronze, simulation. What else, then, is a bronze belly and bronze thighs but feigned piety and feigned humility? If by the shin severity, if by iron cruelty, what else is understood in iron shins but a cruel severity? The foot signifies necessity, the clay pleasure. The clay sole, therefore, signifies voluptuous superfluity. But the foot is described as in part of iron and in part of clay, because the pampered mind is now hardened into hatred of those by whom it is perhaps restrained from its own desires, and now, when the things it has coveted are at hand, is dissolved in the luxury of them. What, then, is the gleam of the golden head but the fervor of heavenly desire? The brightness of the silver breast and of the silver arm is the certainty of right counsel and the rightness of a certain work. The resonance [1274B] of the bronze belly and thigh is the allurement of false piety and of feigned humility. The strength of the iron shin is the rigor of immoderate discipline; the fragility of the clay foot, the unbridling of superfluity. The golden head, therefore, holy desires make; the silver breast and arm, right counsels and works. The bronze belly and thigh, feigned services and servitudes; the iron shins, savage scourges; the clay sole, dainty supports.

## CHAPTER XXVI. *It has been said how a man often flows down from good into evil; now it is said how he often falls headlong from evil into evil and from vice into vice.*

But if anyone should wish to take the whole of what is said of the statue in an evil sense, I readily yield, without doubt, [1274C] to his assertion. Yet let him who is of this mind be zealous so to approve his own meaning that he by no means dare to condemn what has been said before, in that the Holy Spirit is often wont to signify many things in the one thing he speaks. For as there is something in this writing which is more easily fitted to that reading, so also something is found in the same which is more lightly applied to this one. For the gold of this statue indeed, since it is read as the best, seems able to be taken more fittingly in the better sense. But as this is rightly taken, according to the aforesaid reading, in keeping with the truth of the matter, so in this reading it can indeed be referred suitably enough to the estimate which the soul that is proud of itself makes of itself. So the fact that what is beheld through the revelation is described as a statue and not as a living creature smiles the more eagerly [1274D] upon this second reading, where it is pleasing to take the whole of what is said in the evil sense. For what else is such a statue but a human figure, or a human life? And what else is a human figure without a rational soul but a fitting action without a right intention? So often, therefore — I will not say a living creature is nourished, but a statue is fashioned after the human likeness — as often as a man in an order regulates his manner of life according to the prudence of the flesh (which is an enemy to God). Let us see, then, what sort of members the divine discourse describes for such a statue, when it says: the head of this statue was of the best gold, and so on. According to this acceptation, then, by which we refer the whole to the evil sense, by gold arrogance can be understood. by silver boastfulness, by bronze obstinacy, by [1275A] iron savagery, by clay impatience. For gold goes before all metals in the dignity of its price, and the proud mind despises all others in comparison with itself. Silver has a sweet and exceedingly pleasant sound, and boastfulness shows itself soothing and delightful in the proclamation of its own praise. Bronze, in that it is exceedingly durable, figures obstinacy rightly enough, which can scarcely or never be turned aside from its own counsel or purpose. Iron, because it is wont to tame the other metals, suitably enough signifies savagery, which is wont to crush others. But by clay, which is easily broken, impatience is rightly enough signified. He therefore fashions a golden head for himself who arrogates holiness to himself. He is seen to carry about a silver breast and silver arms who glories in the rightness of his own counsel and [1275B] work. He has, as it were, a belly and thighs after a manner of bronze who remains obstinate even in those things which he ought to despise for their baseness, or to blush at for their dishonor. He shows himself to have iron shins who both raises himself against his superiors through boldness and crushes his inferiors through savagery. He leans upon clay soles who, bearing down too immoderately upon the love of earthly things, is unbridled into impatience.

It is indeed to be noted by what steps of corruption our failing takes on an evil increase, how, sinking gradually toward worse things, it descends even to the lowest. See how boastfulness follows arrogance; obstinacy, boastfulness; savagery, obstinacy; impatience, savagery. Arrogance indeed goes before boastfulness, because unless the mind, lifted up, first thought lofty things of itself, [1275C] it would never so shamelessly boast of its knowledge or of its holiness. But when it believes that what it thinks within itself of its own knowledge or holiness has been persuaded to others as well, what wonder is it now if it has stood obstinate in its own counsel or purpose? But unless it first persisted obstinately in its own counsel or purpose, it would never rage so wickedly against others in their defense. Savagery begets impatience, because by how much the less each man loves his own neighbor, by so much the less, assuredly, does he bear weak things the more troublesomely. But we know that the channel of love, the more it is blocked outwardly toward the neighbor, the higher it swells inwardly toward itself. And by how much the more wretchedly each man languishes in himself through private love, by so much the more troublesomely [1275D] does he endure his own troubles, and by so much the more hardly does he restrain his own desires. Hence it is that, severe toward others and slack in himself, so long as [cj: *dummodo*; read *modo*, "now"] he rages against others, and now grows torpid in himself, he walks with feet in part of iron and in part of clay. And indeed certain ones often become so enormously empty of the great efforts which at the beginning of their conversion they boldly presumed upon, that in the great dissolution in which at last they live so nervelessly they cannot patiently hear even a slight word, I will not say of reproach, but not even of correction, nay, of gentle admonition: Woe to the wretched. What, I ask, can now be done with these, or what hope can now be had hereafter, who by reason of arrogance can in no way be cast down from their swelling, [1276A] nor by reason of obstinacy be convicted of their error, nor by reason of the hardness of iron be turned aside from their rigor, nor by reason of their clay fragility be reproved concerning their own body?



## CHAPTER XXVII. *By what steps of repair the mind that falls from great goods into the lowest often rises again by divine working.*

But neither ought we for all that to despise the iron or stony hardness of these men, for the Lord is able of these stones to raise up sons to Abraham. For the things that are impossible with men are possible with God. For see what follows: *Thou wast beholding,* he says, *thus, until a stone was cut out without hands, and struck the statue upon its feet of iron and of earthenware, [1276B] and broke them small [n: (Dan. II)]* [var: Vulg. adds *de monte* after *lapis*: the stone is "cut out of a mountain"]. Behold, a stone is cut out without hands, whereby the hardness of iron may be crushed; and rightly indeed. For what hand could cut down, or even cut out, such a stone as would be strong enough to crush or to break iron small? But what human work, or any human effort whatever, cannot do is done by the divine will alone. It is assuredly God alone who, without any exertion, without any motion of himself, can work as often and whatsoever he will, and, remaining stable, grants all things to be moved. But what, I ask, is it, that he who was able and willed to do this, by no means willed to accomplish these things with hands? Or does he perhaps work better in such iron and hardened minds by inspiration than by striking, and is he often corrected by an inward illumination whom scourges cannot correct? *I have struck,* [1276C] he says, *your sons, and they grieved not; they refused to receive discipline [n: (Jer. V)]* [var: Vulg. Jer. 5:3 reads *Percussisti eos … attrivisti eos, et renuerunt accipere disciplinam*, "Thou hast struck them … thou hast bruised them"; the opening words are those of Jer. 2:30]. But although with us it is much lighter to say than to do, yet often even in those minds in which the work of the striking hand seems to have failed, he works indeed in a wondrous and incomprehensible manner by his own inward word or whisper: *The word,* he says, *that shall go forth from my mouth shall not return to me void, but shall do whatsoever I have willed, and shall prosper in those things for which I have sent it [n: (Isa. LV)]*. So too the Holy Spirit breathes where he wills. For by the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and all their power by the spirit of his mouth. The stone, therefore, cut out without hands is the fear of the Lord divinely inspired; at the stroke of this stone the statue is cast down, and the monstrous work is destroyed. [1276D] As by fear the mind is cast down from a good purpose, so by fear indeed it is shaken out of an evil purpose. For as pride is the beginning of every sin, so the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. By such a stone, then, the statue is shaken, that the mind that can be confounded may be confounded and humbled. What is such a striking but inward compunction? And what is the breaking small of the stricken statue but the contrition and humiliation of a heart pierced with compunction? But we know that God will not despise a contrite and humbled heart [var: Vulg. Ps. 50:19 addresses God, *Cor contritum et humiliatum, Deus, non despicies*, "thou, O God, wilt not despise"]. It is therefore indeed better to be crushed upon this stone than to stand erect and to be high-minded. It struck, he says, the statue upon its feet of iron and of earthenware, and broke them small. The statue, assuredly, is shaken in its lower and worse parts, when the mind, lifted up and [1277A] perverse, is beaten back by the spirit of the fear of the Lord to the consideration of its own iniquity and weakness. This loving striking of the Lord is threatened as mercifully as it is profitably completed in us in this life, when it is said: *I will reprove thee, and will set against thy face [n: (Psal. XLIX)]*. In this manner assuredly he had been reproved and struck in the weak part of himself, and by such a striking had raised himself against himself, who said: *For I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always against me [n: (Psal. L)]*. But after the iron and the clay are shaken, the rest also are crushed. *Then were broken in pieces together,* he says, *the iron, the clay, the bronze, the silver, and the gold.* Thou hast seen above by what steps goodness failed and perversity grew. See now how the foundation of all goodness, humility, [1277B] advances step by step: first we blush at true evils, afterward at feigned goods. Last of all, at true goods also, since they are imperfect and unconsummated. So indeed first the iron and the clay are crushed, then the bronze members, last of all the silver and the golden. Among evils we blush more easily at iniquity than at weakness. But among goods we blush more quickly at imperfection than at interruption. Hence it is that in the lowest members the iron is crushed before the clay. But higher up the silver members are broken small more quickly than the golden. First, therefore, in the crushing of the iron we condemn the evils which we have committed through iniquity. But in the crushing of the clay, those things which we have contracted through weakness. And what is the crushing [1277C] of the bronze but the reprobation of a simulated good? In the silver members this is what pleases us less, and what ought least to please, not that they are good, but that they are not the best. For in the golden work this alone is indeed discerned as blameworthy, that the beginning of the best work is not carried through even to the heel of a worthy or due end. In the crushing of the silver, therefore, the imperfection of a good work. But in the crushing of the gold the interruption of the best work is arraigned. This we have now already said concerning the crushing of this statue, according to that reading which we set down first, where we took it partly in a good and partly in an evil sense.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. *By what steps of advancement the mind that slips from great evil into worse things is often divinely repaired.*

[1277D]

But now let us say something according to that reading which is set in the second place. As there is nothing at which we blush more easily than malice, so there is nothing which we acknowledge or blush at more hardly than arrogance. For arrogance clouds over or blinds the eye of the mind, so that it cannot even recognize itself. For such as the mind lifted up feigns itself to be by its own estimate, such, beyond doubt, it believes itself truly to be. See then how difficult it is for us to reprehend in ourselves, and to arraign, and by rebuke and reprobation to crush, those things in which we have long believed that we truly ought to please others also. But since boastfulness, while it is zealous to spread its own glory abroad, mixes false things with true, and persuades others, concerning the estimate of itself, not only [1278A] of those things which it knows to be true of itself, but even of those which it knows to be false. There beyond doubt it is more easily cast down into confusion, where concerning its false ostentation it is convicted even by the proper testimony of its own conscience. Whence assuredly it comes that the silver of boastfulness, rather than the gold of arrogance, is worn away the more quickly by how much the more easily. But as we blush at arrogance much more hardly than at boastfulness, so we blush much more laboriously at boastfulness than at obstinacy. For we do not doubt that our reputation has often grown from boastfulness, but has always decreased from obstinacy. For we call nothing else obstinacy, save when we shamelessly persist in our own opinion against the counsels of others. But who would not blush more easily at that evil in which he is by no means ignorant that he has greatly displeased others as well? [1278B] Rightly, therefore, is the bronze described as crushed before the silver, because, as has been said, the mind is more easily confounded over obstinacy than over boastfulness. But to the crushing of the clay belongs the confusion that comes of the consideration of one's own weakness and impatience. But when the perverse mind has come to such weakness and impatience that it cannot at all resist its own passions, even when it has willed to, who would not see how easily it blushes in this consideration of its own fragility? But more easily, as has been said above, do we excuse those things which we contract through weakness than those which we commit out of malice alone, whence also we blush at them the more quickly. Rightly then, as it is read, the iron is broken small before the [1278C] clay, just as after these the bronze, the silver, and the gold are rightly described as broken small. Such an order of crushing, then, is described when it is said: Then were broken in pieces together the iron, the clay, the bronze, the silver, and the gold. Where also it is brought in: *and they were reduced as it were into the ashes of a summer threshing-floor, which were carried away by the wind; and no place was found in them.* [var: Vulg. *nullusque locus inventus est eis*, "no place was found for them"; chunk 0016 of this work prints the verse without *in*]



## CHAPTER XXIX. *How, and to how great a perfection, a man often rises again after a manifold lapse by divine working.*

What do we understand by the summer season but the fervor of the spirit, and what by the threshing-floor but the prudence of the spirit? What, then, is a summer threshing-floor but spiritual understanding? On this floor the grains of truth are beaten out from the [1278D] chaff of figures by the threshing of a vehement examination. On this floor the corn of virtue is separated from the beards of the vices by the winnowing of a strict examination. In the threshing of this floor we labor, and, as it were, separate the grains from the chaff, as often as we sunder true and eternal goods from false and transitory ones. Nor let it suffice us to beat out the chaff, but let us be zealous also to turn the heap of it into ash by setting fire beneath it, and to change the brightness of passing things into blackness, and to transform our affection into contempt or hatred of them. On this floor sweats whoever desires to be spiritual. For the spiritual man judges all things, and he himself is judged by no man. Hear a certain spiritual man laboring on this floor: *I purposed,* he says, *in my heart to seek and to search out wisely concerning all things [1279A] that are done under the sun [n: (Eccle.
