I.)]* [var: Vulg. *in animo meo*, "in my mind"] Behold the floor, behold the threshing; and where is the chaff, where is the beard? *Vanity,* he says, *of vanities, and all is vanity.* Behold the chaff, *and I saw that in all things,* he says, *there was vanity, and affliction of spirit [n: (ibid.)]*. Behold the chaff with the beard. But where is the ash? *What fruit therefore,* says the Apostle, *had you in those things whereof you are now ashamed? [n: (Rom. VI.)]* What is the blackness of the ash but the confusion of shame? See then how they had turned the brightness of the stubble into the blackness of abomination, who were now blushing at the things in which they had once been wont to take delight. Hear him too who had turned the chaff of vanities not only into blackness but even into stench, when he said: *I have counted all things as dung, that I might gain Christ [n: (Philip. III)]* [var: Vulg. *arbitror … ut Christum lucrifaciam*, present, "I count … that I may gain"]. But the sorrow of penitence is [1279B] that fire with which spiritual men are wont to burn up the beards of vanities, and to turn them into the ashes of abominations. These ashes assuredly we endure still on the threshing-floor of our conscience, so long as we are confounded or suspect concerning past faults; but, when the wind blows, the ashes are taken away, when at the inspiration of the Holy Spirit all dread of our guilt and [sic: *suscipio*] is swallowed up, and through the hope of pardon the floor of our conscience is cleansed of all the blackness of confusion, so that we may truly sing to the Lord: thou hast cast behind thy back all my sins. Had it not been reduced to ash, I will not say the other members, the iron or the bronze, but even his golden head, when the Prophet said: *And the confusion of my face hath covered me [n: (Psal. XLIII)]*. Will he not make supplication to the Lord [1279C] for the winnowing away of the ashes, when he cried out to the Lord in prayer: *In thee have I hoped, let me never be confounded [n: (Psal. XXX)]*. Had not those black ashes of his confusions been carried away and taken up by the wind, when, cleansed from the stains of his faults through the presuming upon pardon, he broke forth into the confession of praise, saying: *Bless the Lord, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits, who forgiveth all thy iniquities [n: (Psal. CII)]*. See then that by the riches of corruption it is reduced to ash, and afterward is carried off and taken away by the wind; because, unless the transgressing soul first acknowledge its confusions, and blush at them, and burn them up and consume them with a worthy sorrow of penitence, it does not [1279D] cleanse the floor of its conscience from the stains of its faults, and never raises itself to the full security of pardon. But when they have been carried off by the wind, no place is found for them; because after a pardon long sought and scarcely obtained the mind is made not only more cautious but also stronger against like temptations, nay is rendered insuperable against the declines of like corruptions. No place indeed can be found for them, when neither can the sense be deceived nor the affection corrupted unto a like corruption. But what does that mean, that that stone by which the statue is struck, and being struck is broken small; what, I say, is it that the stone does not grow into a crag but is changed into a mountain, nor the stone into a great stone but rather grows out into a great and eminent mountain? But we know that perfect charity sends fear. [var: Vulg. I Joan. 4:18 *perfecta caritas foras mittit timorem*, "casteth fear out"] For the perfection of charity knows not [1280A] how to increase dread, but changes and magnifies it into a mountain of confidence. They that trust in the Lord, as mount Sion: he shall not be moved for ever that dwelleth in Jerusalem. Dost thou see, I pray, how the prophetic sentences run together with one another, how David agrees with Daniel, truth with figure, the sentence of the Prophet with the prophetic vision? *But the stone,* he says, *that struck the statue became a great mountain, and filled the whole earth.* How great a mountain, I pray, is that which filled the whole earth, which shall not be moved for ever? Will you hear how great, how firm, how vast, how immovable? Hear another who holds this mountain of confidence, and sets forth its greatness and immovability: *I am sure,* he says, *that neither death,* [1280B] etc., as far as, *which is in Christ Jesus our Lord [n: (Rom. VIII)]*.



## CHAPTER XXX. *What kind of liberty we have by nature, and what kind of power we receive from grace, and what belongs to liberty or to power.*

Behold, we have heard the dream. But do we still need an interpretation? As he has already said above, it is one thing to know the secrets of the divine judgments, and to know them by divine revelation, and another to have been able to weigh or to penetrate the reason of the same. It is one thing, I say, to see by clear contemplation what is wont or ought to happen in the universe of things, and another what ought to [1280C] befall to which person, for what cause, and with what profit to him to whom it happens. The one belongs, as it were, to the vision of the dream, the other to the interpretation of the dream; and what was given to king Nabuchodonosor out of divine revelation was to see by a likeness from how great a height of loftiness it may befall a man to fall down into the lowest places, and again to rise up to the state of integrity and to the summit of perfection; but he did not receive equal things, to recognize the quality of the person to whom such a thing ought to happen. But what he could not see through himself he received from another, when he hears through Daniel: Thou art the head of gold, and after thee shall rise up another kingdom less than thee. One grace, therefore, is that by which we know the divine judgments, and another that by which we judge our own merits or those of others. The former belongs to contemplation, [1280D] the latter to meditation, or rather to devotion. For that meditation is indeed rightly ascribed to devotion by which the measure of our life and the quality of our merits are judged. And indeed we never better know the corruption of our weakness, nowhere more fully detect it, than when amid the tears of compunction we pour out our whole heart to the Lord. If, then, devotion is rightly understood by Daniel, deservedly is that grace ascribed to him by which the state or the corruption of our life is detected. But it often happens that one man is perfect in one of those graces which I have named, and another in the other, and that what each cannot do through himself he learns from the other. But sometimes one and the same man will receive the fullness of both graces, and yet in one and the same [1281A] spirit the one, as it were, consults the other, when what he could not attain through one state of mind he learns through another. For many things which we cannot do out of the grace of contemplation we obtain by the merit of devotion. This is why Daniel is consulted by the king, this is why the king is instructed through Daniel: *This is,* he says, *the dream; and its interpretation also we will tell before thee, O king.* Happy is he to whom, while there is yet time, this vision is shown and its interpretation revealed. While he is still a king, he can have dominion over his own passions: *Thou,* he says, *art the King of kings.* We know that bodily sense presides over the motion of the body, appetite over sense, affection over appetite, and rational consent over all these, according to what is written, that another is higher than the high, and over these there are yet [1281B] others more eminent, and moreover the king rules over all the earth that serves him. The king of kings, therefore, is rational consent, which presides over all the motions of the heart and of the body, and restrains them within the rights of its own dominion (the power having nonetheless been received from God). For hear what is said, and understand by whom this power is given: *Thou,* he says, *art king of kings, and the Lord of heaven hath given thee a kingdom, and strength, and empire, and glory.* [var: Vulg. Dan. 2:37 *Deus caeli*, "the God of heaven"; chunk 0025 of this work prints the verse with *Deus*] The free will of man has received and has a kingdom in this, that it ought to preside over all other things that are in man; it has received strength, and has it so long as it is able bravely to resist its own passions; it has received empire, and has it so long as it exercises, or is able to exercise, its actions and wills and thoughts in good. It has received glory, and has it so long as it still rejoices in a good conscience: *Our glory,* he says, [1281C] *is this, the testimony of our conscience [n: (II Cor. I)]*. We know who it is that says: *Without me you can do nothing [n: (Joan. XV)]*. So much, then, can we do as we have received the power to do. For what hast thou that thou hast not received, for to have such power and strength is nothing else than to have cooperating grace. Thy power, cooperating grace. As much grace as thou hast, so much power also hast thou; and as much as the grace received grows, so much also does thy power advance; and as much as grace is diminished, so much also is taken from thy power; and if ever grace is withdrawn, power perishes together with it. It is plain, then, from these things that the power of the will is one thing, and the liberty of the will another. For it is one thing to be able to do great things, and another to be [1281D] free. Thou canst be both free and weak, just as, on the contrary, thou canst be both sound and a slave. If thou art sound and strong, thou canst do both many and great things; but nevertheless, if thou art free, thou canst not, nor oughtest to, be compelled to anything. And if thou losest soundness, thou losest thy former power, yet not thy liberty as well. It belongs, therefore, to power that we can do good so long as we are able to do it. But to liberty, that we cannot be compelled unwilling to anything, whether good or evil. How many err in the definition of free will, because they know not, or dissemble, how to distinguish between power and liberty. See nevertheless what difference there is, since a man often loses power, but can never lose liberty. Likewise no one receives power unto all goods, but every man receives liberty unto all goods or evils. [1282A] For, as has already been said, he can be compelled unwilling to no good or evil. But although he is free for all things, he does not for all that have power over all things, otherwise he would be omnipotent. But it is much in every way when he receives power unto those things which suffice him for salvation. And what when those things also are at hand which suffice for perfection. As it is said here: and all things in which the children of men dwell, and the beasts of the field, and the fowls of the air he hath given into thy hand, and hath set all things under thy dominion? He holds, as it were, in his own hand all things in which the children of men dwell, when he has cooperating grace unto those things which, by his help, are wont to lie subject to human counsels and zeals. He possesses the beasts of the field among the rights of his own power, when he is able bravely to restrain the onsets of worldly desires [1282B] within the bounds of equity. He powerfully commands the fowls of the air, to whom he occupies his own thoughts, as often as he wills, with good meditations and spiritual *theoriae*. In this manner, then, he has deserved that all things be set under his dominion who has received grace from God unto each of these things which we have named.



## CHAPTER XXXI. *On the various steps of corruption, and the properties of those who descend from good into evil.*

But let us ask what this means, that to these things there is subjoined: *Thou art therefore,* he says, *the head of gold, and after thee shall rise up another kingdom less than thee [n: (Dan. II)]*. Give heed, I pray, to what he says, to what he sets out to teach us by his interpretation: Thou art, he says, the head of gold. [1282C] For, to say nothing of the rest, this alone, I think, is the thing in which we have need of an interpreter; and would that we might understand the one interpreting, and know this at least through an interpreter. Does not one statue represent the person of one man, and does it not, as we have expounded, signify the transgression of anyone falling from the highest things into the lowest? If he who is of this sort is one, having a golden head, a silver breast, but the other members of bronze or of iron, why, I pray, if he to whom this is said is himself the golden head, why is he not himself also the silver breast, and the rest in this manner? Or art thou perhaps thyself in that part in which thou art golden, and not thyself in that part in which thou art not golden? Whosoever therefore thou art, when after the golden head thou hast now begun to have a silver breast, see, [1282D] I pray, and diligently give heed, lest perhaps thou thyself be now not thyself. If, after much charity and a great devotion of spirit, thou hast ceased to be devout and left off being golden, wilt thou be the same as thou wast before? *Man,* he says, *when he was in honor did not understand; he hath been compared to senseless beasts, and is become like to them [n: (Psal. XLVIII)]*. To be like to God, a wonderful glory; to be like to cattle, a miserable disgrace. Therefore it is one man and another, he that is like to God and he that is like to cattle. Man was made good, and was created unto goodness: *This only I have found,* says Ecclesiastes, *that God made man upright, and that he himself hath entangled himself with infinite questions [n: (Eccli. VII)]*. If, then, thou glowest with charity and abidest in the love of the good, thou hast a golden head, and thou art thyself, because thou art that which, and unto which, thou wast made and [1283A] oughtest to be. But when charity grows cold in thee, when thou hast now begun to fail from thy former fervor, wilt thou still be thyself, and not rather another less than thee? Thou art, he says, the head of gold, and after thee shall rise up another kingdom less than thee. Art thou not now less than thyself, when thou hast begun to do out of counsel alone what before thou wast doing out of great counsel and much desire? And after thee, he says, shall rise up another kingdom less than thee. Is it not another kingdom when the mind is ruled by counsel alone, than when it is driven also by the desire of the good? Is not counsel alone, without desire, a lesser kingdom than a fervent desire with prudent counsel? Is it not less to do good out of deliberation alone than also out of great love or delight. Rightly, then, is it said: And after thee shall rise up another kingdom [1283B] less than thee. And afterward concerning the third kingdom it is inferred, when it is said: And another third kingdom of bronze, which shall rule over the whole earth. As what is done out of love belongs to the gold, and as what is done out of deliberation alone belongs to the silver, so the good that is done out of simulation belongs to the bronze. In the first charity reigns, in the second truth, in the third reigns pretense. See then, I pray, how rightly it seems to fit this third kingdom that it is described as ruling over the whole earth. For the emperor of this kingdom has no lot in the kingdom of heaven, who exercises his body in good work but neglects to nourish his heart in good will: *The kingdom of heaven,* he says, *is within you [n: (Luc. XVII)]* [var: Vulg. Luc. 17:21 *regnum Dei*, "the kingdom of God"]. Within indeed, within in the heart charity reigns, within truth reigns; yet not content with these [1283C] bounds they break forth outward through good work. See then whether perhaps those two aforesaid kingdoms belong to the kingdom of heaven, if the kingdom of heaven is altogether within us, in that either of them can be found within us. But that king and emperor of the third kingdom, having no part in the kingdom of heaven, driven down from the height and cast forth outside, because he cannot in heaven, claims a kingdom for himself on earth. For he hath cast forth his inmost parts in his own life, and cannot say, our conversation is in heaven. How much more, then, can his dominion not be in heaven? Yet he rules over the whole earth, exercising the flesh in good work, leaving the mind empty of good intention. *And the fourth kingdom,* he says, *shall be as iron. As [1283D] iron breaketh in pieces and tameth all things, so shall it break in pieces and crush all these things.* What is it that he says, all these things, unless that this kingdom crushes the other aforesaid kingdoms. How is iron wont to break in pieces the other metals, namely those, the gold and the silver? As in the gold charity, in the silver truth, in the bronze pretense, so, as has been said above, in the iron cruelty is signified. But who could fail to know how the rigor of cruelty is wont to scatter and to destroy holy desire, which belongs to the gold; true counsel, which belongs to the silver; the pious but simulated service, which belongs to the bronze work? Well, therefore, has it been said: and the fourth kingdom shall be as iron.



## CHAPTER XXXII. *On the diverse steps of corruption, and their properties, in those who descend from evil to evil.*

[1284A]

But we must again return a little to what has gone before, and show how this interpretation also fits the other reading. Now according to that reading, the first kingdom is that of arrogance, the second that of boasting, the third of obstinacy, the fourth of savagery. For arrogance belongs to the golden work, boasting to the silver work, obstinacy to the bronze work, savagery to the iron. Let us see what our interpreter says of the head of gold, or what he understands, or how it fits him: *Thou,* he says, *art king of kings: and the God of heaven hath given thee a kingdom, and strength, and empire, and glory, and all things in which [1284B] the children of men dwell, and the beasts of the field and the birds of heaven he hath given into thy hand, and hath set all things under thy dominion.* Often, when we receive such and so great a grace as we have heard described here or expounded above, it comes about that we grow proud against God from that very thing for which we ought to have been more devout and more beholden to God. But that, I ask, how merciful and how worthy of wonder it is, that when our swollen mind grows proud against God he does not at once strike us with strict punishment, nor withdraw his grace on the spot. But first he approaches us with a devout admonition, now inwardly, now outwardly; within, by divine revelation, without, by human exhortation. Within, by inward inspiration; without, by human reasoning, as here first in secret by a dream, afterwards openly [1284C] by a word. Thou, he says, art king of kings, because, stronger than the strong and than the stronger, thou art strongest and canst rule, because thou still hast grace as thy helper; do penance therefore while thou canst, while thou still hast grace working with thee. Thou art still king of kings, and thou canst still in princely wise be prince over the vices too, and still lord it over thy passions. For although thou art deserting grace, thou art not yet deserted by it. Be not proud, he says, be not high-minded, lay aside the sooner the arrogance of thy heart, and what thou canst do of God's gift, ascribe not to thyself: for the God of heaven hath given thee a kingdom, and strength, and empire, and glory. Still in the motions of thy heart or of thy body thou hast a kingdom, because thou canst dispose the good; thou hast strength, because thou canst resist the evil; [1284D] empire, because thou canst urge the more remissly; glory, because thou canst overcome the rebellious. Yet there is nothing whence thou shouldst be proud, there is nothing thou shouldst ascribe to thyself: for the God of heaven hath given all these things to thee, and all things in which the children of men dwell, and the beasts of the field and the birds of heaven he hath given into thy hand, and hath set all things under thy dominion. That thou presidest over the beasts of the field, that thou presidest over the birds of heaven, that thou canst lord it over the appetites of the flesh and over the thoughts of the mind, that thou art able to work good things and to meditate on useful ones: this thou hast not of thy own virtue, but of the divine gift. For all things in which the children of men dwell, and which obey reason and right counsels, come to be of his gift; by his co-working they come forth into act, they turn out well, they prosper. Whatever therefore thou canst do usefully, [1285A] thou canst do of him and through him, who is incapable of nothing, because he can do all things. And so all thy possibility comes of his gift, who hath set all these things under thy dominion. Thou therefore, he says, art the head of gold, who, grace still accompanying thee, canst both correct evils and practise good things. Press down thy pride, therefore, lest thou lose grace as well: for God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace to the humble. And we know that pride is the beginning of all sin. And he that committeth sin is the servant of sin. What then? Will there not now be another kingdom, when sin has already begun to hold dominion and thou to render service, than there was then, when thou couldst press sin down, so that it did not reign in thy mortal body? I think therefore that when thou hast begun through pride to lose grace, [1285B] without which thou wilt be able to do nothing, and to lose thyself; I think, I say, that another kingdom, less than thou, will now rise up, according to what is written: Thou, he says, art the head of gold, and after thee shall rise another kingdom, less than thou. But since every arrogant man glories in himself, while boasting glories in another's favour, it can rightly be said in some respect of the head of gold, that is, of the arrogant man, that he is still himself, in that he has not yet deserted himself, he who has set his glory in himself. But he withdraws from himself when he places his glory in another. Consider then how much less a thing it is to glory in the hissing of another's mouth and in false praises, than in goods of one's own, and often true ones, though received from another. Rightly therefore is it said: Thou art the head of gold, [1285C] and after thee shall rise another kingdom, less than thou; and there is added, and another third kingdom of bronze, which shall rule over all the earth. Bronze, in that it is exceedingly durable, rightly denotes obstinacy, as we said above. And so a man then has a belly and thighs as it were of bronze, when he clings obstinately even to those things at which he ought rather to blush. See then how aptly it seems to agree with this kingdom that it is said to rule over all the earth. For how does that not rule over all the earth which extends its tyranny even to the commanding of shameful things? And the fourth kingdom, he says, shall be as iron. As iron breaketh in pieces and subdueth all things, so shall it break in pieces all these, and shall crush them. If we ought to understand savagery in the iron, how, [1285D] I ask, can a kingdom of this sort break in pieces and crush the other kingdoms? Without doubt, however shameless the mind may be, yet the glory which it was wont to have in itself through arrogance, or in another through boasting, it altogether (nor is this a wonder) disturbs and confounds. For who, amid so many and so open madnesses of his own savagery, would either believe himself holy, or be confident that this could be believed of him by another? But those violent laws of savagery are wont so to crush and confound the kingdom of obstinacy, that in the time of its fury the mind can persevere in no purpose (however right, however honourable). But whatever in the time of tranquillity the mind deliberates and disposes concerning peace or patience, even with a vow or an oath, in the time of its disturbance an oncoming fury [1286A] scatters and dissolves. Those things which we have thus far said concerning the exposition of this vision we have handled according to a twofold consideration, after the measure of our understanding. But the rest which follow run together, for both readings, into the same sense, and do not require a twofold exposition, as do those that have gone before. For what is savagery but cruelty? So too impatience: what else is it than a pitiable frailty? Thus under diverse names we ought to understand the same thing.



## CHAPTER XXXIII. *How the mind is cleft against itself, torn and confounded, when the extremities of corruption are reached.*

Now therefore let us consider what follows: *Moreover,* he says, [1286B] *whereas thou sawest both of the feet and of the toes a part of the potter's clay and a part of iron, the kingdom shall be divided, which nevertheless shall rise out of the plantation of iron [n: (Dan. I)]*. But if by the foot necessity is understood, and by iron cruelty, what does it mean that a certain part of the feet is described as being of iron? Is anyone found hard and harsh, or even inflexible, towards his own necessities? We know that the covetous man shall not be filled with money, and he that loveth riches shall reap no fruit from them; and yet he does not cease to labour, nor are his eyes satisfied with riches, nor does he consider, saying: For whom do I labour, and defraud my soul of good things? Does he not seem to thee to walk upon an iron sole, who all the days of his life eateth in darkness, and in many cares, and in misery and [1286C] in sorrow? Truly, as it is written, *there is nothing more wicked than the covetous man [n: (Eccle. X)]*, who neither has compassion on his neighbour nor pities himself. Why do we now wonder that a man of this sort has legs of iron, when he already has the soles? Why do we now complain that he is harsh towards his neighbours, who is already hardened towards his own uses? He that is evil to himself, to whom will he be good?

Note however that he who is of this sort is first hardened in iron legs towards his neighbour. Afterwards he is hardened also in iron feet towards himself. See therefore, whoever thou art that readest these things, that thou do not perchance, after the love and zeal of wisdom, turn back to the love and gain of money; this is to bend the head of gold down into feet of iron. The bowels of the covetous are cruel: set now before thine eyes and consider any [1286D] covetous men thou wilt. See, I pray thee, how anxious they are, how laborious, how sparing, how austere towards themselves. Yet what have these same men often been wont to do, or what will they yet do, if at another's cost they are fed, clothed, and sheltered free of charge? Thou wilt surely see them wishing to be clothed in soft raiment, to be soaked with surfeiting and drunkenness, to grow numb with sleep and idleness, to be angry and indignant when they see something of their accustomed comforts wanting to them. Does such a man not seem to thee to walk upon feet in part of iron and in part of clay, when thou seest one and the same man so sparing in his own goods, so prodigal in another's, serving now austerity, now luxury? Moreover, he says, in that thou sawest of the feet and of the toes a part of the potter's clay and a part of iron, the kingdom shall be divided, which nevertheless shall rise out of the plantation of iron. [1287A] The foot is divided into five toes, and the condition of necessity is beyond doubt parted into five, when it is extended to all the senses of the body. But when we studiously seek the delights of the senses or warily shun them, what else do we do than lean upon two feet, on this side and on that, on the right hand and on the left, and walk between prosperity and adversity along the road of our desires? But thou mayest often see these men indulge one sense more vehemently and those another, and for the delights of some one sense willingly endure the troubles of the other senses. How many acquire over much time and great labour what they spend in the surfeiting or drunkenness of a single day or hour? How many fears, how many honours, how many chills, of the enemy, of the night, and of the cold, do adulterers willingly endure, that they may attain to the momentary blandishments [1287B] of foul pleasure? Have not all such men a part of the feet or of the toes of clay and a part of iron, who in the one thing are so patient and almost insensible, and in the other so impatient? Moreover, whereas thou sawest, he says, of the feet and of the toes a part of the potter's clay and a part of iron, the kingdom shall be divided. Truly divided will that be which is of this sort. For, to set down by way of example some few things out of many in one man: since one and the same man is often both covetous and gluttonous, how great, I ask, is the quarrel and contention that is frequently in his heart, when gluttony bids him spend, and avarice bids him keep back, one and the same coin. In this way, then, many times upon a slight occasion the kingdom is divided against itself, disturbed and confounded, until it is utterly laid desolate. For every [1287C] kingdom divided against itself shall be brought to desolation, and house upon house shall fall.

It is surely to be noted what is said of this kingdom, which nevertheless, he says, shall rise out of the plantation of iron. For when the transgressing mind first turns back to worldly desires, the spirit is hardened for the enduring of the world's labours, and at that time, according to the saying of Job, it counts it a delight to be under the briers [n: (Job XXII)], so long as it may in any manner attain the end of its desires. O how happy they would be, if the things they endure for the love of money, or for the gaining of some worldly pomp or glory, they endured patiently for the love of justice! But they who so patiently bear so many troubles, so many injuries, so many contumelies [1287D] for the gain of covetousness, do not hear with an even mind so much as one light word of correction for the love of virtue. This I take to be what follows, when it is at once subjoined: *According as thou sawest the iron mingled with clay of mire, and the toes in part of iron and in part of earthenware, in part it shall be solid, and in part it shall be broken.* For men of this sort are strong and patient, as has been said, in that very part in which their labour might have served virtue as a soldier. But as to what he says, of clay, of mire: what else is clay of this sort than foul habit? For mire is hardened as it were into clay when a foul action is drawn into a habit; but out of the hardening of foul habit a man is cast down into impatience, and after the manner of clay is lightly broken, now by wrath, now [1288A] dissolved into concupiscence. But, as we have shown concerning the covetous, many are seen to satisfy their own pleasures gladly when they can do so without expense of money; but when they cannot do so without loss of gain, to go vehemently against them. Do not these men seem to thee to mingle iron and clay of mire alike? *And whereas thou sawest,* he says, *the iron mingled with clay of mire, they shall indeed be mingled to human seed, but they shall not cleave one to another, even as iron cannot be mingled with clay.* [var: Vulg. *humano semine*, ablative, "mingled with human seed"; Migne's dative governs the gloss that follows] What are human seeds, but the counsels of carnal prudence? The prudence of the flesh teaches us to seek money for the things necessary for use. The same teaches us to withdraw much from the necessaries of life, and to spare money, lest it seem to fail for necessary uses. See how it cleaves to human seed, since [1288B] the one seems as it were by counsel to require the other; yet they are not mingled together, because the one often seems to contradict the other. The love of riches commands one thing, and the love of delights another; the heat of pleasure one thing, the gain of covetousness another. But when in this manner diverse vices hurry a man in diverse directions, or drive him to contrary things, they wretchedly afflict him, they suffer him to rest neither by day nor by night; and in a manner as wonderful as it is wretched, they who are of this sort anticipate the times of their own damnation, while by the inward anxiety of the spirit, or by outward affliction, they rage savagely against themselves; and unless the clemency from above look upon them, they go through temporal torments to eternal ones.



## CHAPTER XXXIV. *How a man is sometimes advanced by God from the depth of iniquity to the highest summit of charity.*

[1288C]

But the divine mercy often comes to the help of salvation in that which, so far as lies in the men themselves, is a heaping up of damnation, according to what is written: where iniquity abounded, grace also did more abound [n: (Matth. XXIV)]. [var: Vulg. Rom. 5:20 reads *delictum*, "offence", where Migne's noun is that of Matt. 24:12, to which his own note points] For often, when the grace from above visits men of this sort amid the straits of their calamities, it sets this very enormity of their own unhappiness before their eyes, and in the consideration of it pricks them to the lamentations of penitence; and having drawn them out of the pit of misery and out of the mire of dregs, by certain steps of advance it carries them from the depth of iniquity to the highest summit of charity. Is not this what Scripture speaks, [1288D] where it is consequently added: *In the days of those kingdoms the God of heaven shall raise up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed, and his kingdom shall not be given to another people. It shall break in pieces and shall consume all these kingdoms, and itself shall stand for ever, according as thou sawest that a stone was cut out of a mountain without hands, and it broke in pieces the clay, and the iron, and the bronze, and the silver, and the gold [n: (Dan. II)]*. [var: Vulg. *non tradetur*, "shall not be delivered over"] And so in the days of those kingdoms, in the time of so great malice and so great misery, an abundance of grace is given, and there is raised up a kingdom of charity which can never perish. For he that abideth in love shall abide for ever. And so this kingdom shall never be destroyed. *Charity* indeed *beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things [n: (I Cor. XIII)]*. And his kingdom shall not be given to another people, [1289A] for this is that fountain (as Augustine says) whereof a stranger doth not partake: *It shall break in pieces,* he says, *and shall consume all these kingdoms.* But would you know how charity breaks in pieces and consumes all these kingdoms: *Charity,* says the Apostle, *is patient, is kind; charity envieth not, dealeth not perversely, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, seeketh not her own, is not provoked to anger, thinketh no evil, rejoiceth not upon iniquity, but rejoiceth with the truth.* Further it is added of this kingdom, that itself shall stand for ever; and *Charity,* says the Apostle, *never falleth away,* according as thou sawest, he says, that a stone was cut out of a mountain without hands, and it broke in pieces the clay, and the iron, and the bronze, and the silver, and the gold. We know that the kingdom of God is begun from fear, but is consummated [1289B] in charity. And so by the stone of fear the work of confusion is cast down, and the kingdom of charity is founded. But the stone by which the kingdom of charity is founded is cut out without hands: for the striking in of fear and the inspiration of charity comes to be in the Holy Spirit, not by human work: *The charity,* he says, *of God is poured forth in our hearts, by the Holy Spirit who is given to us [n: (Rom. V)]*. It shall break in pieces, he says, and shall consume all these kingdoms, according as thou sawest that a stone was cut out without hands, and it crushed the clay, and the iron, and the bronze, and the silver, and the gold. The destruction of the opposing kingdoms is begun from fear and perfected in charity. Through fear they are rooted out of consent, through charity they are plucked out of effect. Charity therefore, which is patient, breaks [1289C] in pieces the fragility of clay; charity, which is kind, breaks in pieces the rigidity of iron. What, I ask, is that in which the bronze of simulation is broken in pieces, but charity which envieth not? And what is it that breaks in pieces the obstinacy of bronze, but charity which dealeth not perversely? If in the silver boasting is understood and in the gold arrogance, what is so contrary to them as charity, which is not puffed up, nor is ambitious, nor seeketh the things that are her own? If either in the silver that work is understood which is done out of deliberation alone and not out of love, it is not done so much out of love as out of truth: what is so agreeable to charity, which rejoiceth with the truth? If in the head of gold the failure of the best work is reproved, in that it is not [1289D] brought through to the heel of its due end, what better convicts or corrects this work than perfect charity, which never falleth away? O happy kingdom of charity, which abideth for ever! O happy kingdom which shall never be destroyed, since to another people it shall for ever be given [cj: *dabitur*; read *non dabitur*, "shall not be given"]! Happy kingdom in which patience endures and kindness perseveres! Happy kingdom, in which no one envies; happy indeed, in which there is no perverse dealing, no one is puffed up; truly happy, in which no ambitious man seeks the things that are his own; no one is burned! Perhaps he hints something to us in this, that whereas above, in the enumeration of the crushing, he set first the iron and afterwards the clay, in this place he plainly sets first the clay and afterwards the iron. But we know that in some men fear rules, and in others shame. For some indeed are more fearful than modest, [1290A] but others more modest than fearful. Those therefore who are the more timid are the more easily pricked by the consideration of their own cruelty than of their own pleasure. But those who are the more modest are the more readily softened to penitence by the recollection of foul pleasure than of iniquity. If therefore by the iron cruelty is understood, and by the clay pleasure rightly so, what wonder if elsewhere the iron and the clay are read as broken in pieces in one order and another, since according to the quality of spirits; or of manners, the order or the occasion of inward compunction and true contrition varies in one man and another?

## CHAPTER XXXV. *What prudence is far too late, and what is useful and sure.*

Daniel still goes on, and adds: *The great God,* [1290B] he says, *hath shown the king what shall be hereafter [n: (Dan. II)]*. [var: Vulg. *ventura*, "what shall come to pass"] God, he says, is great: perhaps he had grown great in the thought and the love of the man to whom he had revealed so great a depth of mysteries, so that not undeservedly he ought to magnify his greatness above all others. The great God hath shown the king: not to any man whatsoever, but to a king the Lord hath shown these things, so that he who pants after the foreknowledge of things to come and after grace of this sort may recognize, with royal liberty and authority, that this realm of his is to be ruled and ordered. The great God hath shown the king what shall be hereafter. O with how great mercy of God is it done, that while it is still to come, while it can still be guarded against, a man's own ruin is revealed to him, that with so great solicitude he may foresee and recognize what he ought to fear, what to beware of, what [1290C] peril he ought to fight against. Slow indeed, and far too late, is that foresight when the peril already imminent cannot be avoided. The great God hath shown the king what shall be hereafter. Happy is he who can foresee the imminent ruin while he is still king, and can still lord it over his passions and turn aside the pressing peril! But let us see what is subjoined after all these things, when it is said: *And the dream is true, and the interpretation faithful.* We often penetrate many deep things of the divine mysteries by the liveliness of the reason implanted in us, and some things concerning what is to come we foresee with the eye of prudence, in wary solicitude, before they arrive. But in these things constancy often totters, and it does not fully grasp what it might hold unshaken through the security of certitude. For the thoughts of mortal men are fearful, [1290D] and our foresights uncertain. But on the contrary, what we discern in the light of God, what we know from his revelation, we hold with such certitude and confidence that we can be shaken by no doubtful ambiguity concerning it. This is what the Psalmist figuratively expresses when he says: *At the brightness that was before him the clouds passed away [n: (Psal. XVII)]*, for the Lord to look upon is to illuminate. For since he is the true light, after the manner of the sun, by that very act by which he looks he lights up, kindles, and illuminates. And so at the divine regard we are often filled with so great a splendour of the divine light, that in that which is divinely revealed every clouding of ambiguity or hesitation is straightway taken out of the midst. And so the clouds pass away, when those doubts which were wont to becloud the spirit withdraw. For the clouds to pass away [1291A] is to hold the clear-sightedness of truth and the serenity of understanding without any questioning. He who confidently asserted it showed that he had certitude of this sort, and the security of certitude, in the assertion of his own judgment. And the dream is true, and the interpretation thereof faithful. But what the king did at these things, Scripture subjoins.



## CHAPTER XXXVI. *That an unstable and indiscreet humbling is indeed worthy of reproof.*

*Then king Nabuchodonosor fell upon his face and adored Daniel, and he commanded that they should sacrifice victims and incense to him [n: (Dan. II)]*. Greatly, and no wonder, did he humble himself, and deservedly ought he to have been humbled after he knew that so great a peril hung over him. [1291B] But who would not justly reprove him in this, that he rendered to a mortal man the honour which is owed to God alone? But perhaps, because he perceived him to be a true temple, he judged him worthy of such honour. But for our own edification we must diligently sift these things, and subtly inquire what is wont to be enacted in us after their likeness: He fell, it says, upon his face: by the face a man is known, and that part in a man is held more comely and more worthy than the rest. What else therefore is it to fall upon one's face, than even to despise, with a lofty longing, that which is chief or best in oneself, and to reckon that very thing whereby one was wont to become known to others and to appear as it were venerable, as something weak and almost [1291C] or utterly nothing? Consider how he fell upon his face, how he humbled himself, or rather how he would have us humbled, who compared all our justices to the cloth of a menstruous woman. But it is neither a very great thing nor much of a wonder if we cast ourselves down at that time in which we already discern that our peril hangs over us. Then, it says, the king fell upon his face. Then he fell, when, at Daniel's teaching, he recognized his own peril. But it must be known that that humbling which is without perseverance cannot fight against the imminent peril.

This also is to be noted, that often the more inconsiderately and immoderately a man casts himself down, the more insanely and enormously does he afterwards break out into pride. Consider in the king a humbling unstable and indiscreet, [1291D] and afterwards a pride more than human. For he who first adored Daniel, that same man afterwards commanded his own statue to be adored.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. *That we ought to trust in no virtue of our own, nor to wish to glory in it.*

Victims, it says, and incense he commanded that they should sacrifice to him. To kill animals for Daniel, or to burn incense, and to expend anything whatever of that kind for his use or profit, would not be blameworthy at all. But it is blameworthy to sacrifice these things to him, and to expend divine honour upon a mortal man. In the immolation of a victim the flesh of brute and irrational creatures is slain; in the burning of incense a sweet odour is spread more widely As therefore living but brute flesh is slain, [1292A] when any irrational appetite or affection in us is mortified by the crushing of the flesh; and then we spread abroad more widely as it were the odour of incense, when we enlarge the repute of any virtue with worthy heralding of praises. And so to slay for our own Daniel some of those things which still live bestially in our appetites or affections, and to practise a mortification of that sort for the use and profit of our devotion, will without any contradiction not be unprofitable. But when we commend Daniel's office with manifold praise, and concerning the virtue of devotion spread abroad on every side the fragrance of good repute by the commendation of our speech, we do indeed a good work, if in all these things we seek not so much the glory of our Daniel as his profit. And, that I may say more openly [1292B] what I think, it is surely good to restrain our life for the sake of the grace of devotion and of instancy in prayer; it is good to commend the virtue of prayer and to extol it with praises, provided that it be done to this end, that our devotion may grow to the better and rise up more fervent, not that it may appear more glorious. How many there are who, when they believe that they have obtained some grace through instancy in prayer, already presuming much upon their own devotion or holiness, wish great things to be thought of it by others also. This is what Nabuchodonosor did, who, after he had come through Daniel to the desire of his vow, heaped upon him an honour as foolish as it was vain. But what we reprove concerning this virtue of which we speak, we ought to beware of in any virtue or [1292C] grace whatever. Hear it openly, mark it diligently, hold it in memory: if in any grace, in any effort, if in any virtue of thine own thou trustest, presumest, gloriest, thou art indeed bestowing divine honour upon it, and shamelessly enough; not to say that thou art making a God for thyself. He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord. Cursed be the man that trusteth in man; therefore also he who trusteth in himself or in any virtue of his own: *My glory,* he says, *I will not give to another, nor my praise to a graven thing [n: (Isa XLII)]*. [var: Vulg. *et laudem meam sculptilibus*, "and my praise to graven images", plural]

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. *How many seek the knowledge of the virtues and the teaching of morals for display, not for profit.*

How many glory, and wish to be glorious in the eyes of men: I will not say over the fact that they have virtues or holiness, but over the fact that they know how to discourse prudently [1292D] about the virtues and to dispute eloquently. O how much better, O how much more profitable it would be for thee not to have the gold of knowledge and the silver of eloquence, than to make thyself an idol out of them! The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the works of the hands of men. To paint out the measure and the mere form of the virtues by understanding and teaching, and to hold them in memory, but to lack their effect: what else is it than to carry certain idols in the heart? The knowledge of holiness without a good intention: what else is it than an image without life? Knowledge alone, without the effect of holiness and the affection of goodness: what else is it than a vain idol without motion and without sense? *A mouth,* he says, *they have, and they shall not speak; eyes they have, and they shall not see; ears they have, and they shall not hear; nostrils they have, and they shall not smell. [1293A] Hands they have, and they shall not feel; feet they have, and they shall not walk; neither shall they cry out in their throat [n: (Psal. CXIII)]*. The mouth, as we all know, is the instrument of speaking; the eyes, the instrument of seeing; the ears, the instrument of hearing; and in this manner it ought to be understood of the rest also. What therefore is it to have a mouth, eyes, ears, or any such things, and to exercise them for no uses at all, but to have the instruments of the offices and to lack the offices of the instruments? Thou readest that with the heart we believe unto justice, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation [n: (Rom. X)]. And so to the mouth belongs confession; to the eyes, circumspection; to the ears, obedient hearing; to the nostrils, discretion; to the hands, working; to the feet, advance; to the throat, supplication. Behold, that empty knowledge of thine perhaps knows exceedingly well what the virtue of confession is. [1293B] It knows that all things are washed away in confession. It knows perhaps how it ought to confess, and yet it does not confess. It has a mouth therefore, and speaks not. It knows perhaps how it ought to look around upon its own life, yet it dissembles to look around upon it as it should. Thou hast in a manner the instrument of seeing, but thou lackest the office of seeing. Thou knowest perhaps what the virtue of obedience is, and of what kind it ought to be, and yet thou wilt not obey. This is to have ears, and not to hear. Through knowledge thou hast perhaps the instrument of discerning spiritual fragrance. But while thou spendest no zeal upon discernment in matters of conduct, thou gloriest emptily in a useless instrument. Thou knowest how thou oughtest to exercise thyself in good work, and yet thou wilt not take the fruit of good work by experience: this is to have hands, [1293C] and not to feel. For what is it to feel with the hands, but to prove the fruits of works by experiencing them? Thou hast received through knowledge the feet of advances, if thou hast learned how one ought to stretch forward to the things that are before. But having feet thou dost not walk at all, if thou tendest not to advance. Thou hast received the teaching of supplication, and thou wilt not supplicate: this is to have a throat, and to be unwilling to cry out.



## CHAPTER XXXIX. *That in the carrying out of any virtue these seven things ought to be observed.*

But if we attend diligently, we ought to observe these seven things in the carrying out of any virtue. The first is that which belongs to the mouth: to condemn and accuse the evils done before. The second, which belongs to the [1293D] eyes: to investigate diligently what is to be done, and through investigation to know it. The third, which belongs to obedient hearing: when counsel has been found, to rest in it by consenting, and to be willing to comply. The fourth, which is as it were a various thing: warily to detect the evils that lie in wait for the good that is to be done, and prudently to discern them. The fifth, which likewise looks as it were to the hands: to fulfil in work the good that has been deliberated. The sixth, as it were by a certain advance of the feet: from a good beginning always to tend to better things. But because we are of ourselves sufficient for none of these, we ought to implore the divine help for them all. But if we know these things and yet do not practise them in work, what else, in acquiring and cultivating idle and useless kinds of knowledge, do we make [1294A] or worship than vain and empty idols, while we are content with the mere acquaintance with the virtues? See how perverse and damnable a thing it is to seek spiritual teaching for display alone, and not for edification. This is assuredly the prudence of the flesh, and one that is utterly an enemy to God? What, I ask, does it profit; nay, how much does it hurt, to seek with great labour and the utmost zeal, and to investigate, and anxiously to wish to know, the things which thou art in no way willing to practise in work? For it stands clearer than the light that the servant who knows his lord's will and does it not, but rather does things unworthy, shall be beaten with many stripes. O what a counsel, and how useless, to seek the counsels of life for this alone, that thou mayest have wherewith thou canst appear wiser than the rest, and obtain the name of master! How sharp a prudence, how cunning a foresight, [1294B] to press vehemently after the searching out of those counsels in which, once obtained, thou art in no way willing to rest! But we often see it happen to minds of this sort, by the just judgment of God, that such as their spiritual foresights were before towards spiritual things, such afterwards do their carnal foresights become towards carnal things. Of what kind, I say, their spiritual counsels stood before towards heavenly and divine things, of that kind after a little are their carnal counsels found to be towards worldly and human things. For just as in spiritual things and in the gains of the soul they first see what they might healthfully do, and yet are unwilling to do it; may it be [cj: *sit*; read *sic*, "so"] that afterwards in advantageous fleshes and in temporal gains they see what ought usefully to be done, and yet, conquered by concupiscence or bound fast by sloth, are wholly unable to do it. But this very thing is wont to happen to some men [1294C] even profitably, so that from that very fact they now begin to detest and abhor their own vices, and over this very thing to implore the divine help, when they see that not even amid the greatest perils can they restrain themselves from their own excesses; whence comes that prophetic imprecation, or petition: *Let them that make them become like unto them, and all such as trust in them [n: (Psal. CXIII)]*. But that we may return to that from which we digressed, let us at least gather from this how foolish and empty a thing it is to wish to glory in the mere empty knowledges of the virtues, and in certain idols as it were of the virtues themselves, since with God it is detestable that a man should presume upon any virtue of his own. Behold, we reprove Nabuchodonosor, and deservedly ought we to reprove him, in that he had commanded Daniel, though [1294D] a faithful man, to be presented with divine honour; how much the more if he had wished the same thing to be rendered to Daniel's image.

## CHAPTER XL. *That desire is often corrupted from the very source by which the understanding is illuminated.*

But let us see amid these things how truly he thought and spoke concerning God, who willed such empty things to be done. The king therefore, speaking, says to Daniel: *Verily your God is the God of gods, and the Lord of kings, revealing mysteries, since thou couldst open this sacrament. [n: (Dan. II)]*. Behold how soundly he thinks even concerning divine things, and yet what he practised in deed was like to idolatry. Thus, thus, at one and the same time both Moses on the mountain is lifted up to the contemplation of the highest and divine things, and [1295A] the people committed to him is cast down in the valley to the crime of idolatry and to the worship of the calf; and often indeed it comes to pass in one and the same spirit, in a manner as wonderful as it is pitiable, that from the very source by which human understanding is illuminated on high toward divine things, from that same source the crowd of desires is the less corrupted. For who does not know how the greatness of revelations lifts an incautious mind into pride, since the Apostle himself says of himself: *Lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, there was given me a sting of my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me [n: (I Cor. XII)]*. For often certain men, while still set amid the very sights of divine revelations, grow proud within themselves with a silent mind; already thinking great things of themselves, they count it worthy to be esteemed great by others; already they search out with shrewd solicitude how they may become known [1295B] to others also; already they catch at the breeze of empty favour, and change into a vain glory that true glory which they were wont to have with God. Of such the Psalmist says: *And they changed the glory into the likeness of a calf that eateth hay [n: (Psal. CV)]*. Since indeed it is written: *All flesh is hay, and all the glory thereof as the flower of hay [n: (Isa. XL)]*. [var: Vulg. *flos agri*, "the flower of the field"] What else will the calf that eateth hay be, but the appetite for human favour, courting a carnal and temporal glory? What else therefore will it be to worship a calf, an animal wanton indeed and brute, than in the courting of temporal glory to serve an irrational appetite, and to set one's own glory in a temporal and empty glory? And Nabuchodonosor indeed, [1295C] whom nevertheless we justly reprove, did something more tolerable, in that he presented with divine honour a man, an animal to be sure, but a rational one. For beyond doubt it will be more irrational to worship an irrational animal than a rational one. Some trust and glory in their own virtue, but others in the mere estimation of virtue. Those, over what they have or believe themselves to have; these, over what they are esteemed by others to be. Those, over the testimony of conscience, yet not as before God; these, over the testimony of report, as before their neighbour only. And so the former is as it were an irrational animal, the latter as it were a rational animal. Happy is he who glories over the testimony of conscience, yet so as in the Lord. Otherwise it is a very thankless thing to glory over the gift, but not in the giver of the gift. How much better, how much more rightly [1295D] would the said king have adored God rather than Daniel, and sacrificed to him who had indeed taught him (though by Daniel's office) what he was seeking.



## CHAPTER XLI. *That some things we know from divine revelation, and others we gather from reason.*

But since he did things to be reproved, as we have already said, let us see how rightly he thought concerning God in that which he said: Verily your God is the God of gods, and the Lord of kings. Since the royal power is chief and highest, what is it for the king to say this, but from the inmost sense of the soul to hold it firmly and unmovably? What is it for Daniel to hear this from the king, but that the inmost sense of the soul neither ought nor is able to lie hidden from the true devotion of the spirit? Or perhaps in this, that some things Daniel [1296A] learns from God and others he heard also from the king, Holy Scripture mystically hints that, for the use of our devotion, some things are those which we learn from divine revelation, others those which we weigh out from the liveliness of reason implanted in us. But in that, speaking of God, he says "your" and "our", he attends to the regard of grace, not to the condition of nature. For in a certain special way he belonged properly to those who, out of the gift of his own grace and by the prerogative of merits, had obtained with him a singular place of familiarity beyond the rest, and the boldness of confidence. And without doubt it is devotion which both renders God propitious and makes him familiar. God, he says, of gods, and Lord of kings. For although there be some that are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth, according to that word: *I have said: You are gods [n: (Psal. LXXXI)]*, by name [1296B] indeed they can be so called: for what God is naturally and substantially, that they can in no wise be. He is therefore the God of gods, and the Lord of kings. Because, as the Apostle testifies: *There is no power but from God [n: (Rom. XIII)]*. For that some are set over others, that men of virtues are able to have dominion over their own vices and passions, they receive assuredly from the gift of the highest King. He says therefore: Verily your God is the God of gods, and the Lord of kings, revealing mysteries; but whence he gathers and conjectures these things he at once subjoins, when he says: Since thou couldst open this sacrament. For from this, that he revealed to him the secrets of his own heart, and from this likewise, that he revealed to him the hidden things of the divine counsel, the one concerning the past, the other concerning the future, at one and the same time, [1296C] he weighed, with a wonderful liveliness of wit, the revelation of the highest Godhead. And from this, that he heard concerning the secret of his own heart and proved it true, he gathered that that also was true which meanwhile he could not prove by experience concerning the counsel or the purpose of the Godhead. Prudently therefore he observed that it was the highest wisdom which was able to open to Daniel, in so dark an abyss of the human heart, the secrets of another's conscience. For, according to Solomon's sentence, God alone it is who knows the heart of all the sons of men. Shrewdly none the less he perceived that it was the highest power which was able to reveal to Daniel, according to its good pleasure, the order and disposition of things to come and of things to be done. For who else than God could manifest to him the divine counsel? According to that word [1296D] which Isaiah said: *Who hath known the sense of the Lord, or who hath been his counsellor? [n: (Isai. XL.)]* [var: Vulg. Isa. XL:13 opens *Quis adjuvit spiritum Domini*, "Who hath helped the spirit of the Lord"; the wording printed here is that of Rom. XI:34, *Quis enim cognovit sensum Domini*] For, as the Apostle witnesses, just as no one knows the things that are of man save the spirit of man which is in him, so no one knows the things that are of God, save the Spirit of God. Rightly therefore is it said: Verily your God is the God of gods, and the Lord of kings, revealing mysteries, since thou couldst open this sacrament.

## CHAPTER XLII. *That it is best that our devotion advance so far that no occupation can interrupt its office.*

Then the king raised Daniel on high, and gave him great and many gifts. If by Daniel we rightly understand devotion, what else will it be to lift Daniel on [1297A] high than to reckon the office of devotion, among all other offices whatsoever, as chief and principal, and to hold it as it were in the highest place? And it is wont to come to pass, after the mind proves by experience how great the virtue of true devotion is, that it stretches out more vehemently toward its pursuits and diligently presses upon its advancements, that by investigating it may seek, by seeking may find, whence it may advance in the selfsame thing toward better things. What else therefore than great and many gifts does the Daniel of our devotion receive, when out of zeal eagerly bestowed he easily finds, as it were, certain talents of understanding and gains of prudence, whereby he may grow toward greater things and be enlarged to very many? *And he set him,* he says, *prince over all the provinces of Babylon, and chief of the magistrates over all the wise men of Babylon.* [1297B] O would that our devotion might advance so far that it should appear higher than all the princes of Babylon, wiser than all the prudent of Babylonia, and stand out more precious, by the judgment of our mind, than everything that pleases in the world or seems precious, and by the decree of the will obtain the higher gain! This will be, as I judge, for Daniel to receive from the king the citadel of princedom and of mastery. Would that it might at length at some time befall our devotion to attain that measure of perfection wherein no affection, however vehement, no occupation, no solicitude, no suggestion or persuasion could in us, I will not say scatter, but not even interrupt its zeal, and that unmoved apostolic word be fulfilled: *Without ceasing [1297C] pray! [n: (I Thess. V.)]* Would that all other offices whatsoever were so disposed or ordered that they might be proved to serve as soldiers, or even to be subservient, to the uses and advantages of our devotion!

## CHAPTER XLIII. *That even in the uses of our necessity we ought to do nothing improvidently, nothing inconsiderately.*

*But Daniel requested of the king, and he appointed over the works of the province of Babylon, Sidrac, Misach and Abdenago [n: (Dan. II)]*. The king without doubt consents to Daniel asking, when the will of the mind readily accepts and receives whatever conscience suggests to it in the time of inmost devotion. But what, I ask, is that province of Babylon that is spoken of, or what are the works of that province? Certainly God made the province lying round about Babylon: [1297D] for the walls indeed and the buildings human effort completed. If therefore Babylon is rightly interpreted *confusion*, if whatsoever things are hers seem to lie subject to confusion, how, I ask, could that which God made and instituted belong to Babylon, or be under confusion? But we know that God has subjected man to a manifold necessity: for the necessity of eating, of drinking, and of any things of that kind, he received from the very right of his own condition. But if he had persisted in that first state of his condition, man would in no way blush at these things, because he could have practised them without any sin. [1298A] But now we justly blush at those same offices of necessity, because, overcome by the vice of our corruption, we have not strength to practise them without fault. Rightly therefore is that broad, and truly much widened, corruption of our infirmity assigned to the Babylonian possession, which is not doubted to lie subject to confusion. In a province of this kind, therefore, and in the office or the works of our necessity, it will be altogether most useful to have set those aforesaid men in charge, and to have brought all things under their disposition. As we have already said above, by those three men we ought to understand circumspection, discretion, deliberation. We ought therefore, not only in spiritual pursuits and exercises, but also in secular business and in the uses of necessity, to do nothing incircumspectly, nothing [1298B] indiscreetly, nothing improvidently. And this will be to have appointed Sidrach, Misach and Abdenago over all the works of the province of Babylon. And so in these things also, in which we take counsel for human necessity, or serve the common infirmity, let us do nothing without modesty, nothing without measure, nothing without good intention, nothing beside order, nothing beside reason, and we obtain such mastery as Daniel willed us to have in the Babylonian province. Finally, according to the sentence of the Wise Man, do all things with counsel, and thou hast such mastery as the prophet designates for thee out of the mystery. For there is altogether need of circumspection and of discretion, if we wish to do nothing improvidently, nothing inconsiderately.

## CHAPTER XLIV. *That whatever strikes the spirit through thought ought to arouse the devotion of the mind.*

[1298C]

But at the last, in the conclusion of the discourse, it is brought in: *But Daniel himself was in the doors of the king [n: (Dan. II)]*. Now we know that through the doors [sic: *perfores*] the entrance to the inner parts lies open. Daniel, finally, keeps watch as it were in the doors of the king, when our devotion warily keeps vigil over all suggestions whatsoever, and in the very entrance of temptation fights back with prayer against all the machinations of the evil one, lest any infestation or violence oppress the incautious mind, or circumvent it by fraud. Happy the state of the spirit, and to be sought after with all zeal, when everything that strikes the spirit through thought also at once, without any delay, arouses the devotion of the mind. The devotion [1298D] of the mind ought therefore studiously to forestall every consent of the will, and to fortify it beforehand with prayer. And this will be for Daniel to preside over the doors of the king. At every suggestion, at every emerging thought, let us ask of the Lord that he lead us not into temptation, and let us have Daniel presiding over the doors of our city. Hear what the Wise Man admonishes according to these things, when he says: *At all times bless God, and ask of him that he direct thy ways [n: (Tob. IV)]*. And may he direct our ways to the true life, who without end lives and reigns. Amen.

## BOOK TWO.





## CHAPTER ONE. *Of the security of conscience, or the renewal of advancements.*

[1299A]

*I Nabuchodonosor was at rest in my house, and flourishing in my palace [n: (Dan. IV)]*. What do we understand by the house, but conscience, and what by the palace, but the security of conscience and the confidence of security? For a palace also is a house, yet not any house whatsoever can be called a palace. For a palace is a certain house that is strong, lofty and royal. If by the house we ought to understand conscience, rightly by the palace is understood the security of conscience. And so he sits at rest in his own house whom his own conscience does not bite back. A quiet conscience is made by a worthy satisfaction for past [1299B] evils, and by a wary and provident turning aside from present evils. And so he remains at rest in the house whom his own conscience bites back neither for past nor for present fault. He was at rest in the house who truly said: *For neither hath my heart reproved me in all my life [n: (Job XXVII)]*. He stood at rest in his own house who could truly say: *For I am conscious to myself of nothing [n: (I Cor. IV)]*. He was assuredly at rest in the house at that time, and was flourishing in his own palace, when he said: *Our glory, this is the testimony of our conscience [n: (II Cor. I)]*. Because in the flower fruit is hoped for, rightly by the flower is figured the certain expectation of the goods to come. Because the flower is the beginning of the fruits to come, rightly none the less [1299C] by the flower is understood the renewal of advancements. In the flower therefore is figured either the certain expectation of rewards, or the new promotion of merits. And so he truly flourishes in his own palace who, under the testimony of his own good conscience, securely awaits the crown of glory. Hear one resting in his own house and flourishing in his own palace: *But I shall appear before thy sight in justice; I shall be satisfied when thy glory shall appear [n: (Psal. XVI)]*. That he says, I shall appear in justice, pertains to the rest of the house. That he says, I shall be satisfied when thy glory shall appear, pertains to the flowering. He was none the less flourishing in his own palace who with the conscience of a great security said: *I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; for the rest there is laid up for me a crown of justice, which the Lord [1299D] will render to me in that day, the just judge [n: (II Tim. VI)]*. Does not he also seem to thee to flourish in his own palace, whose sense is renewed from day to day? He sits and flourishes in his own palace who, amid his own great works which he gladly does, purposes in his heart yet greater and better ones.

## CHAPTER II. *Of the illumination of the intellectual sense, or how the sights of our contemplation are wont to strike a useful fear into the mind.*

*I saw a dream,* he says, *which terrified me, and my thoughts [1300A] upon my bed, and the visions of my head troubled me [n: (Dan. IV)]*. We sleep before we see a dream. Because through the dream the bodily sense of the body is lulled, rightly by the dream is understood that alienation of the mind through which the memory of all outward things is utterly cut off. But to see a dream is to pass over in mind into the secret place of divine contemplation. And so he sleeps and sees a dream who through excess of mind ascends into the contemplation of sublime things: I saw a dream, he says, which terrified me. Of dreams of this kind, some deter, others soothe, others sadden, others gladden. The contemplation of eternal joys assuredly gladdens (nor is it a wonder), but the beholding of the divine judgments terrifies. For who could worthily express how [1300B] glad, how joyful his own vision or revelation makes him to whom God has revealed through his Spirit that which eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, nor hath ascended into the heart of man? But how, on the contrary, does his own vision terrify him who by the lifting up of the mind sees through contemplation by how wonderful, by how hidden a judgment of God it is that one man sometimes goes forth even from prison and from chains unto a kingdom, and another born in a kingdom is consumed in want? Whom, I ask, would the abyss of the divine judgments not terrify, when, touched by the divine light, the understanding of the mind perceives clearly that the course is not the swift men's, nor the war the strong men's, nor bread the wise men's, nor riches the learned men's, nor favour the craftsmen's, but time and chance in all things? The Prophet had [1300C] certainly seen that the judgments of the Lord are a great abyss, and the visions of his head had terrified him, when he said to the Lord: *For I have feared thy judgments [n: (Psal. CXVIII)]*. Yet visions of this kind are wont to terrify, not so much at that time in which they are seen through excess of mind, as at that time when, after sleep has been shaken off, they are recalled to memory, when with subtle examination they are gone over again with oneself in a silent mind. Hence is that which follows, when it is said: And my thoughts upon my bed, and the visions of my head troubled me. For indeed he asserts that he is troubled by two things: by his own thoughts, and by the visions of his own head. For when the mind considers out of divine revelation something to be wondered at, nay rather to be dreaded, and afterwards, returning to itself and going over it with itself, judges itself [1300D] with a strong examination, lest perchance it be worthy that some such thing should befall it, it is dealt with by its very own thoughts, so that its own vision terrifies it. My thoughts, he says, upon my bed. What is here understood by the bed, but the leisure of inmost quiet; and the vision of the head, but the illumination of the intellectual sense. And the visions, he says, of my head troubled me. And so his own thoughts upon his own bed, and the visions of his own head, then terrify each man and by terrifying trouble him, when out of that which, after the secret of divine revelation, he handles with himself [1301A] in the busy leisure of his own meditation, he wakes up unto a wholesome solicitude and a useful dread. For when a man knows out of divine revelation how one is wont to advance from good to better, another to sink from evil into worse things, or how it befalls that some fall down from the highest goods into the lowest evils, or climb up from the lowest evils to the heights of the virtues; what wonder, I ask, if his own vision compels him to dread? *Man knoweth not* indeed *his own end; but, as fishes are taken with the hook, and birds are caught with the snare, so are men taken in the evil time, when it shall suddenly come upon them [n: (Eccle. IX)]*.

## CHAPTER III. *That the grace by which we know the divine judgments is one, and that by which we discern our own merits another.*

[1301B]

But see how astonishing a thing it is, and how dreadful, that often the mind, irradiated by the divine light, sees through contemplation what ought worthily to befall such a man as it is itself, and yet knows not that it is at that time such a one, upon whom by the divine sentence such a judgment deservedly presses. Did not this same thing befall king Nabuchodonosor, who knew from God's revelation the divine sentence concerning the cutting down of the tree, and yet knew not how to draw to himself the likeness of the tree that was shown? He saw what by the divine sentence would press upon such a man as should bear in himself the image or the likeness of a tree of that kind, [1301C] and yet that he himself stood forth such a one, because he could not through himself, he knew through another. See therefore that the grace is one by which we know the divine judgments, and that other by which we discern our own merits. For those we find by contemplating, these by meditating. And so that power we have received from the grace of contemplation, but this from the zeal of meditation and the grace of discretion. And often one and the same man receives both graces together, although he cannot exercise both together at one and the same time. And so it is as though one consulted another, when what he could not fully do through one and the same state of mind, he learns from another state and at another time, which meanwhile may suffice for the full knowledge of himself. Hence it is that Nabuchodonosor is instructed through Daniel [1301D] concerning those things about which he himself seems to doubt in his own vision. And in a wonderful manner, while the king narrates his own vision to the prophet, not knowing it he teaches another what he may learn from him, and Daniel learns from the questioner who does not know, what he ought to teach the learner. Thus indeed, thus often the mind, prudently unknowing, brings back from the light of contemplation that which afterwards it may find through meditation, and may more fully know. And meditation receives from the foreknown light of revelation that whereby it may loose the knots of doubt. As we have already said above, by the king we understand free will, by Daniel devotion. And so to a king of this kind belongs that contemplation which lies subject to the will of the mind, when the spirit already has it at hand, and exercises it as it were out of its own power. So also that meditation [1302A] seems to belong to Daniel which, out of the zeal of devotion, a religious mind is wont to exercise about the circumspection of its own morals. The king thus designated therefore seeks, as it were, the interpretation of his own dreams from Daniel, and finds it, when the spirit afterwards, by meditating and by looking about, reads in its own morals the things which it descried amid the free flights of its own contemplation, and understands them more deeply. But let us now see how urgently Nabuchodonosor sought what he knew not.



## CHAPTER IV. *How we ought to lay aside secular pursuits, and to turn them to the investigation of spiritual things.*

But amid these things, let those whom the visions of the head and the thoughts that follow trouble learn from the example of king Nabuchodonosor [1302B] what they ought to do: *And by me,* he says, *a decree was set forth, that all the wise men of Babylon should be brought in before me, and that they should show me the solution of the dream [n: (Dan. IV)]*. Behold how diligently, behold how urgently he seeks what he knows not, unless [cj: *nisi*; read *nec*, "nor does he first desist"] he first desists, until he finds the solution of his dream which he seeks. Hence it is that Job says of himself: *The cause which I knew not, I diligently investigated [n: (Job XXIX)]*.
