[var: Vulg. *diligentissime*, "most diligently"] To set forth a decree is to establish something firmly, and such as it may in no wise be lawful to violate. See therefore how vehemently he willed that to be done concerning which he sets forth a decree. To the wise men of Babylon belongs the wisdom of this world, which is foolishness with God. To the wise men [1302C] of Babylon belongs the prudence of the flesh, which is an enemy to God. And so the wise men of Babylon are the exceedingly sharp searchings of worldly philosophy. The wise men of Babylon are the exceedingly sharp counsels of the prudence of the flesh. What therefore will it be to bring in wise men of this kind, and to call them back to the inner parts, but to turn to spiritual pursuits those exceedingly sharp searchings of our investigation which we were wont to bestow upon secular business? For those things are as it were outside which can be perceived by the outward sense. But those things are as it were within which cannot at all be comprehended save by the inward sense. Within, therefore, are spiritual things; without, bodily things. And so we bring in the wise men of Babylon when we turn secular pursuits, and all outward pursuits whatsoever, to spiritual understanding and to the investigation [1302D] of spiritual things. To bring in the wise men of Babylon is to postpone the care of outward things, and to bestow zeal upon spiritual exercises alone. He was keeping his own wise men in the inmost parts who said: *I thought upon the days of old, and I had the eternal years in mind. I meditated in the night with my own heart, and I was exercised, and I swept my spirit [n: (Psal. LXXVI)]*.

But it is to be noted that our wise men are now within, now without, and yet are not in our sight. That is held as it were in the sight of our will which is done through intention and out of deliberation. But it often befalls, out of the great accustomedness of our pursuits, that the spirit runs back incidentally to its ingrained searchings, and, before it notices what it intends, weaves in [sic: *invectere*] much delay there; that is, not to have its own wise men [1303A] before its own sight. But he without doubt makes his own wise men stand before his own sight who restrains his own pursuits from all wandering, and, according to the purpose of his own deliberation, bestows them upon useful and necessary things alone. The mind holds and watches its own wise men as it were in its own sight, when it keeps vigil with so great care over its own zealous meditations that it may nowhere be allowed to turn aside the foot of its investigation, save whither it had directed them out of deliberation, insomuch that no wandering of its own searchings can escape past the effort of its own shrewdness even for a little.

## CHAPTER V. *How he ought to press on who pants after the unravelling of the divine mysteries.*

[1303B]But let us now see why he gathers his own wise men into one, or drives them to the inner parts: that they should show me, he says, the solution of the dream. As we have already said in the exposition of the other vision, it is one thing to discern the divine judgments with the eye of contemplation and as it were through a dream, and another to weigh the reason of the same, and by the liveliness of one's own discretion to judge with what equity or with what usefulness they come to pass. That belongs to the seeing of the dream, this to the interpretation of the dream. We therefore see a dream in a certain manner, when we bring the hidden judgments of God into contemplation and admiration. We seek the interpretation of our dream when, after the sights of our contemplation, we investigate the reason, [1303C] the manner and the order of those things which we have seen through the lifting up of the mind. Does it not belong to the seeing of the dream to bring into consideration those astonishing great works of the divine judgments which we read in the Scriptures, and to cleave longer and more diligently to the admiration of them? Does it not belong to the interpretation of the dream to seek their mystical understanding, and to be able to explain it through exposition? Was he not panting after dreams of this kind who said in prayer: *Enlighten mine eyes, and I will consider the wondrous things of thy law [n: (Psal. CXVIII)]*. [var: Vulg. Ps. CXVIII:18 *Revela oculos meos*, "Uncover mine eyes"; this work prints *Revela* at 1253A and at 1262C] But how great a thing he would count it to receive grace divinely for the interpretation of dreams of this kind, you can weigh from that saying of his. For when he has premised concerning the Lord: *Who declareth his word unto Jacob, his justices and his judgments unto Israel,* he at once subjoins: [1303D] *He hath not done in like manner to every nation, and his judgments he hath not made manifest unto them [n: (Psal. CXLVII)]*. He had already seen as a dream the things which he had caught out of the light of his own contemplation: that all things happen alike to the just and to the wicked, to the good and to the evil, to the clean and to the unclean, to him that immolates victims and to him that despises sacrifices. He had sought the interpretation of the dream, but had not yet found it, when in another place he said: *Behold this I have found,* said Ecclesiastes, *one and another, that I might find out the reason which my soul still seeketh, and I have not found it [n: (Eccle. VII)]*. He must therefore gather his own wise men into one, and call them back to the inner parts, who desires to obtain grace for the interpretation of dreams of that kind which we have already determined. *Then came in the soothsayers, the magicians, the Chaldeans and the diviners. Then,* he says, [1304A] they came in. What is then, but after the decree, after the purpose of deliberation? For many often set forth many things, yet by no means do them, because as easily as they establish something, so easily do they again reject what was established.

First therefore it is to be observed by us that we establish useful things. But secondly, that we firmly hold what has been usefully established. Mark how firmly he established that which that best deliberator weighed to be best: *I have sworn,* he says, *and I have determined to keep the judgments of thy justice [n: (Psal. CXXVIII)]*. Thou hast heard of the establishing of the vow; hear also of the performing of the vow: *I will render my vows in the sight of all his people [n: (Psal. CXV)]*. [var: Vulg. Ps. CXV:14 *Vota mea Domino reddam coram omni populo ejus*, "I will pay my vows to the Lord before all his people"] Then came in the soothsayers, the magicians, the Chaldeans and the diviners. Above he set forth generally concerning the wise men of Babylon; [1304B] here he expressed certain of them specially. The soothsayers, he says, the magicians, the Chaldeans and the diviners. But because it truly stands that wise men of this kind are not truly wise, Holy Scripture almost nowhere calls them wise save with a determination, but now of Babylon, now the king calls them the wise men of his own kingdom, or something of this sort. If therefore by the soothsayers, the magicians, the Chaldeans and the diviners we understand depraved pursuits, frivolous, foolish and empty pursuits, see how manfully, see how wholesomely we turn pursuits of this kind to spiritual exercises. And so we drive the wise men of Babylon to the inner parts, when the care and the solicitude which we were wont to bestow upon superfluous things we bestow upon spiritual things alone. We occupy the wise men of Babylon as it were [1304C] in the interpretation of dreams, when, superfluous pursuits being wholly set aside, we press singularly upon the unravelling of the divine mysteries or judgments.

## CHAPTER VI. *How empty a thing it is to search into the deep things of the mysteries without the mastery of the Holy Spirit.*

But when the wise men had been brought in, the king still adds and says: *And I told the dream in their sight, and they showed me not the solution thereof [n: (Dan. IV)]*. What, I ask, is it to tell our dreams in the sight of our wise men, but, after contemplation, to recall to memory the sights of our contemplation, to go over them with shrewd meditation, to discuss them with zealous thoughts, and out of the comparison of those things which we know [1304D] to loose the knots of our questions, and to wish to shape the investigation of spiritual things according to the accustomed manner of our searchings? Do we not tell our dreams in the sight of our wise men and seek the solution, when we bring together in a mutual comparison the things which we know of human matters and the things which we desire to know of divine ones, when, according to the learned manner and order of the disciplines handed down, we presume to discuss and to penetrate the perplexed things of the divine mysteries or judgments? But whatsoever in the divine secrets is presumed out of human effort is attempted in vain, and so long as it is sought in this manner, the labour is spent for nothing. According to that which is read of this dream: and they showed me not the solution thereof. Assuredly our wise men by no means find the solution [1305A] of dreams divinely shown, because the disciplines of our learning, or any human traditions whatsoever, cannot suffice for the discussion and the investigation of the divine secrets. For who would presume to search out that height of the divine counsel out of his own sense, when he hears the Lord's prophet crying and crying again: *Who hath known the sense of the Lord, or who hath been his counsellor? [n: (Isai. XL)]*. [var: Vulg. Isa. XL:13 opens *Quis adjuvit spiritum Domini*, "Who hath helped the spirit of the Lord"; the wording printed here is that of Rom. XI:34, and this work prints the same verse with *Quis novit* at 1296D] Who would trust to penetrate that depth of the mysteries and of the divine Scriptures out of his own shrewdness, when he reads the apostle Peter, how he equally restrains all men from presumption of this kind? *This,* he says, *first understanding, that prophecy of Scripture is not made by private interpretation [n: (II Petr. I)]*. [var: Vulg. *quod omnis prophetia Scripturae*, "that no prophecy of Scripture"] Without doubt the interpretation of the holy Scriptures [1305B] is never properly made without the mastery of him who inspired them.



## CHAPTER VII. *That toward the unravelling of the mysteries we advance better by devotion than by investigation, and that it belongs to true devotion to discuss all things, that it may be able to judge all things.*

If therefore we wish to be instructed unto the mystical understanding of the divine Scriptures, unto the learning of the divine judgments, we advance better toward this same thing by praying than by investigating, and we are illuminated more deeply by devout compunction than by profound searching. Whence it is that to those things which we have premised there is at once subjoined: *Until my colleague Daniel came in before me, whose name is Balthassar according to [1305C] the name of my God, who hath the spirit of the holy ones in himself [n: (Dan. IV)]*. [var: Vulg. Dan. IV:5 has *deorum* before *sanctorum*, "the spirit of the holy gods"; Richard restores the word in both of his own re-quotations below] Behold, he is said to have the spirit of the holy gods who is found fit for the interpretation of the dream. In this indeed, that these gods are called holy gods, those are assuredly excluded of whom it is sung in the psalm: *All the gods of the Gentiles are devils [n: (Psal. CXIII)]*. But assuredly they who are designated in this place. They are believed to have the Holy Spirit; because, if they had not the Holy Spirit, they would not be holy gods. He is perceived to be of the number of these gods to whom by the Lord's voice it is said: *Behold I have appointed thee the god of Pharao [n: (Exod. VII)]*. And so the Psalmist expressed gods of this kind, when in another place he said: *I have said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High [n: (Psal. LXXXI)]*. Every [1305D] holy man receives the spirit of gods of this kind, that he may be able to be holy. For all our justification, all our sanctification, is without any doubt from that spirit. Without this spirit we know not what we should pray, as we ought; for we have learned, by the Apostle's teaching, that it is he who maketh intercession for us with unspeakable groanings [n: (Rom. VIII)]. [var: Vulg. Rom. VIII:26 reads *postulat*, "asketh"; *interpellat*, "maketh intercession", is the verb of Rom. VIII:34] That our devotion therefore may be able to be true, it must have this spirit. If therefore by Daniel true devotion is understood, rightly is it said of him through Nabuchodonosor: Who hath the spirit of the holy gods in himself. But since he expressed above certain wise men, and such as it truly stands are not truly wise, it is a wonder how Daniel is in this place said to be their colleague. For unless he has something in common with them, [1306A] I know not how he should stand as their colleague. But this I know, that that spirit which Daniel, according to the testimony of Scripture, had received, makes men spiritual. But the spiritual man judgeth all things, and he himself is judged of no man. For the Spirit is wont to search all things, even the deep things of God. If the spiritual man judgeth all things, if the spirit searcheth all things, then those same things also which worldly philosophy searches; then those same things also which carnal prudence searches. If all things, then those also which any perverse doctrine whatsoever searches. For he who is spiritual is wont to discuss all things, that he may be able to judge all things. Hear finally how that spiritual man tried all things in his own wisdom, that he might be able to judge all things: *I gave,* he says, *my heart, that I might know prudence and doctrine, and errors and folly [n: (Eccle. I)]*. Thou seest [1306B] how this man searches out, how he searches, not only good morals, but also errors, not only prudence, but also folly. And so it belongs to true devotion to bring both good things and evil into contemplation, to investigate all things, to discuss all things, that thereafter it may also be able to judge all things. And so true devotion has, out of investigation and searching, something in common with the wise men of Babylon, so that it is deservedly said on that account to be their colleague. Yet they differ in intention. For true devotion investigates empty and perverse doctrines not for this, that it may cleave to them or place any confidence in them, but that by judging it may convict, confute and condemn them. And so our Daniel and the wise men of the world run by the same way through investigation, although [1306C] through intention they do not reach the same issue. Rightly therefore is Daniel called their colleague, with whom in the courses of his own pursuits he seems in some part to share.

## CHAPTER VIII. *With what pursuits of devotion he ought to press on who awaits from God the revelation of hidden things.*

Until my colleague Daniel came in before me. Thou weighest from these things, as I judge, how this Daniel now enters from outward things to inward, now goes forth from inward things to outward. He is outside when our devotion, by meditating, by judging, by praying, is solicitous concerning outward things. He is within when it is occupied with the same exercises or [1306D] pursuits, and solicitous for inward things. For it must needs provide good things before God and before men. Before men in speech and in work, before God in thought and in will. And so to call our deeds and our words back to judgment, and to make supplication to the Lord for them, this is for Daniel to be outside. To search out thoughts, affections, wills, intentions with deep searching, and to be pricked with compunction in prayer for such things, this is for Daniel to abide within. Or this is for Daniel to be outside: to weigh both our inward and our outward things according to human judgment; and this is for Daniel to be within: to esteem both these and those according to the divine judgment. When, even amid the good works which we do, when amid the useful things [1307A] which we say, we weigh with subtle examination what men would think of us, what they ought to think, if they saw our intentions, if they saw our sordid thoughts, if they saw our depraved affections; when, I say, we do this, we hold Daniel as it were outside. But when it is sought with zealous discussion how our works or our words are judged in the sight of God, even then when according to human judgment they seem good, when such a pursuit is pressed with great devotion, our Daniel is found within. What therefore is it for Daniel to enter to the inner parts, but out of inmost devotion, in those things which are to be discussed or to be sought concerning outward things as well as inward, to have recourse to the divine judgment? And it often comes to pass, while our wise men fail in the interpretation [1307B] of dreams, while zealous meditations, while inmost searchings presume to penetrate the hidden things of the divine judgments, the deep things of the divine mysteries, and cannot; it comes to pass, I say, often, that the mind, after a failure of this kind, admonished by that very failure of its own, returns to itself, attends more diligently to its own infirmity, and more fully acknowledges that without God's help it can do nothing. Then it begins, out of the consideration of its own infirmity, to groan, to sigh, to reprove its own presumptions, and now to hope from the Lord's revelation alone for the things it had before emptily presumed upon out of its own pursuits, and to press wholly upon the zeal of devotion. And this is for Daniel to enter after the wise men.



## CHAPTER IX. *How great the virtue of true devotion is, which makes a Son of God, which joins the human spirit to God.*

[1307C]

Until my colleague, he says, Daniel came in before me, whose name is Balthassar. Balthassar is interpreted *hair of the head*. Rightly therefore is Daniel called Balthassar, because our mind is adorned out of true devotion, and out of true devotion is made subtle unto every depth. But in this place, when Daniel is called Balthassar, something is added that still lies hidden, whereby, as I judge, we are called forth to a deeper understanding. Daniel, he says, whose name is Balthassar, according to the name of my God. But this we now wish to forewarn in this place, that many places of the Scriptures sound something foolish or perverse according to the history, [1307D] which nevertheless, when mystically discussed, speak something right according to the spiritual understanding. For that Daniel is called Balthassar by the king according to the name of his god, what else does it seem to sound, according to the letter, than idolatry? But as blessed Gregory says: « Often any thing whatsoever is, through the history, a virtue, and through the signification a fault, just as sometimes a deed done is, in the fact, a cause of damnation, but in the writing, a prophecy of virtue. » For when he was treating of king David's fault, while he was treating of Urias's innocence, when he had wished to interpret Christ by the adulterous David, and by the innocent Urias the Jewish people: what, he says, through this effect can be said more wicked than David, what more clean than Urias? But again, through the mystery, what is found more sacred than David, what more faithless than Urias, when the one by [1308A] the fault of his life signifies the innocence of prophecy, and the other by the innocence of his life expresses in prophecy a fault? For the virtue of the sacred discourse so narrates things past that it may express things to come. So it approves a thing in the fact, that it may contradict it in the mystery. So it condemns things done, that it may persuade that these same things are to be done mystically. So also in this place assuredly, that which according to the history is reprehensible can, according to the mystery, express something commendable. Whose name, he says, is Balthassar according to the name of my God. If by the royal person we rightly understand the royal spirit, whom, I ask, does he call his God but Christ? For although the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit is truly one and the same God, yet every religious man rightly says, according to a certain manner of speaking, that Christ is his own: by whose name [1308B] he remembers that he was marked, by whose grace he was prevented, and to whose person, finally, he acknowledges that he cleaves more familiarly through the mystery of the Incarnation, out of the communion of nature. But if Balthassar is interpreted *hair of the head*, let us now see how this name may seem to agree with Christ, or how according to this name of his God the mystical Daniel is deservedly named. But we know that the head of the man is Christ, and the head of Christ, God. We know without doubt that God the Trinity is the beginning of all creatures; we know none the less that the person of the Father is the beginning of the other persons in the Trinity. And although it is called a beginning here and there according to one manner and another, yet in both places it can be called a beginning as fittingly [1308C] as truly. Since therefore the person of the Father is the beginning of all things, he can by right be designated by the head. If therefore the Holy Spirit is called by a likeness the finger of God, why should not Christ likewise be called by a likeness the hair of this head? The hair arises from the head, and Christ is begotten of the Father. The Lord said to me: *Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee [n: (Hebr. I)]*. The head is adorned with hair, and the Father is glorified through Christ: *Father,* he says, *glorify thy Son, that thy Son may glorify thee [n: (Joan. XVII)]*. Thou seest certainly how justly Christ is called Balthassar, that is, the hair of the head, whom the Catholic faith truly confesses to be the true Son of God the Father. Do not we also receive this name, when from Christ [1308D] and through Christ we obtain that we ought deservedly to be called sons of God? *Brethren,* says John the apostle, *we are the sons of God, and it doth not yet appear what we shall be [n: (I Joan. III)]*. [var: Vulg. I John III:2 opens *Carissimi, nunc*, "Dearly beloved, now"; and it reads *apparuit*, "hath appeared", for the present *apparet*] Hence it is that to him who of his own will begot us by the word of his power we say in our daily prayer: *Our Father who art in heaven [n: (Matth. VI)]*. If therefore Christ can fittingly enough be called Balthassar, because he is the Son of the highest Father, why should not the true Christian also be called Balthassar according to the said reason of the name, who according to the grace of adoption is reckoned among the sons of the same God the Father? Yet not every Christian is worthy of this name or of this honour. Devotion alone it is that distinguishes them; devotion alone makes sons of God. If therefore devotion is understood in Daniel, see how rightly he is called Balthassar in effect. Through whom [1309A] any man whatsoever is adopted into the liberty of the sons. But what else is devotion, but the fervent love of the mind toward God? *But the charity of God is poured forth in our hearts by the Holy Spirit, who is given to us [n: (Rom. V)]*. Rightly therefore is devotion called the hair of the head, which seems as it were to flow forth from the highest head of all, while it is begotten out of the inspiration of the highest Father. Rightly is he called Balthassar who after the manner of hair seems to cleave to the highest head of all. Thou weighest, as I judge, from these things how great is the virtue of true devotion, which makes a son of God, which joins the human spirit to God, and makes it with him as it were one spirit. *He who* indeed *cleaveth to God, is one spirit [n: (I Cor. VI)]*. [var: Vulg. I Cor. VI:17 reads *Domino*, "to the Lord", where the plate prints *Deo*]

## CHAPTER X *That most of all in the time of praying the intellectual sense is wont to be opened to certain men.*

[1309B]

Daniel having entered, the king speaks the dream before him, as is shown by the words that follow: *And the dream,* he says, *I spoke before him [n: (Dan. IV)]*. To speak a dream of this kind before Daniel is, in the time of praying, to be touched by the memory of the mysteries concerning which we desire to be divinely instructed, and while praying to be affected with the desire of divine revelation. For as those recognize by experience who have deserved to be divinely relieved and gladdened by frequent relievings, in the time of praying most of all are they wont to receive the light of illuminating grace, and out of its inspiration to penetrate the deep things of the mysteries. For out of inmost compunction [1309C] the spirit is washed and cleansed, and beyond doubt the purer it is rendered, the more easily, the more deeply is it illuminated. Hence it is that Balaam testifies of himself: *He hath said, the hearer of the words of God, who hath beheld the vision of God almighty, who falleth, and so his eyes shall be opened [n: (Num. XXIV)]*. [var: Vulg. Num. XXIV:4 has no *Dei* after *omnipotentis*, and reads *aperiuntur*, "are opened", for the future *aperientur*] What is it that is said, that by falling the eyes are opened, but that while praying the intellectual sense is often opened. We are indeed wont often to prostrate ourselves upon the earth with the whole body, when we wish to pray more attentively. So far therefore as it seems to look to the exposition of the letter, his eyes are opened as it were by falling who receives the light of revealing grace while he prostrates himself in prayer. But if the same letter is mystically discussed, it seems to run together into the same meaning. For what is it to fall, [1309D] but to humble oneself out of the remembrance of one's own sins, and out of true contrition to lay aside the rigidity of the heart? But the spirit often, while it casts itself down in this manner, rises again in a greater grace, because by falling it recovers the light of its own eyes, which, being ill upraised, it was holding closed. Yet we can say that this without doubt is to fall: to consent to a flattering fault. But we know that there are some who lift themselves up out of the multitude of their own revelations. But those who are of this kind are permitted, by the worthy judgment of God, to fall, that they may cease to be proud. While therefore they slip into fault, they are confounded, they are pricked with compunction; being pricked they are purged, being purged they are illuminated. But if, being illuminated, they are again proud, by being proud they lose the light which they had received. And so, being illuminated [1310A] and lifted up, they are cast down again and again; having fallen and been humbled, they are illuminated again and again. This vicissitude of falling and of rising again they often alternate, and many long and much frequent these manners of alternating. But many at length conclude this custom of alternating with a most evil end, of whom it stands that they received the grace of spiritual charisms not so much for their own advantage as for that of others. Of these without doubt Balaam bore the type by his own works, and expressed their property in his own words, when he says: He hath said, the hearer of the words of God, who seeth the vision of the Almighty, who falleth, and so his eyes are opened. [var: Vulg. Num. XXIV:4 has the perfect, "hath beheld", where this second printing prints the present *videt*, "seeth"; the printing at 1309C keeps the perfect]



## CHAPTER XI. *That the secular kinds of learning ought to be subservient to spiritual studies, and to serve as soldiers for the gains of true devotion.*

[1310B]

But that we may return to that from which we digressed, we hold this for certain: that many often, in the time of their prayer, receive the light of revealing grace, and that many advance to grace of this kind out of the virtue of devotion. Hence it is that the king with all confidence demands of Daniel the interpretation of his dream, when he says: *Balthassar, prince of the soothsayers, whom I know that thou hast the spirit of the holy gods in thee, and every sacrament is not impossible to thee. Tell the visions of my dreams which I saw, and the solution of them [n: (Dan. IV)]*. [var: Vulg. *quoniam ego scio*, "forasmuch as I know"; the relative printed here leaves the clause without a governing verb] In these words this first is to be noted, that he is here called prince of the soothsayers who above was called their colleague, and not theirs only, [1310C] but of the other wise men of Babylon also. Among the secular kinds of learning we assuredly know some to be useful and necessary for use, but others (such as the art of soothsaying is) altogether perverse. If therefore true devotion can turn those which are without doubt perverse to some use of virtue, and can constrain within them a certain princedom of the spiritual soldiery, even as here we can gather from the art of soothsaying, what then is to be thought of those which can be useful and good? For, to say nothing of the rest, does not Daniel then hold the princedom, is not any perverse learning whatsoever compelled to be subservient to devotion, when from the consideration of it human error is more fully recognized, when from the going over of it again the spirit is humbled, confounded, pricked with compunction, and stirred up to the [1310D] zeals of devotion? Does not any perverse learning whatsoever serve devotion, when the spirit exacts of itself the times which it was wont to waste in useless studies of this kind, when from the comparison it gathers how much he ought to watch over spiritual studies who goes over again in his mind that he once sweated at follies so great? And so let Daniel be understood as the colleague of the said wise men in such wise, that he be believed to hold among them, by the right of equity, a certain princedom of the spiritual soldiery. All secular kinds of learning, therefore, ought to be subservient to spiritual studies, and to presume nothing in their exercises which does not serve as a soldier for the gains of true devotion. When therefore we press importunately upon the secular kinds of learning, when by the importunity of our studies we interrupt the exercises of our devotion, we assuredly compel him who ought to hold the princedom, [1311A] Daniel namely, to serve. But it must be attended to how great an evil it is to abuse even good kinds of learning, and by the abuse of them to have better studies hindered, when out of the office of devotion any perverse learning whatsoever ought, and is wont, to be bent to good uses.

## CHAPTER XII. *That it is useful to bestow the highest care upon the highest devotion.*

Now rightly is devotion set before good studies, rightly does it hold the princedom over evil ones, rightly is the primacy among all the wise men of Babylon granted to Daniel, if that stands truly which is said through Nabuchodonosor: I know that thou hast the spirit of the holy gods in thee, and every sacrament is not impossible to thee. Does not [1311B] this seem to agree with that sentence, if it be rightly weighed, which is heard from the mouth of Truth: *Amen I say to you, whatsoever you shall have asked in praying, believe that you shall receive, and it shall be done unto you [n: (Marc. VI)]*. [var: Vulg. Mark 11:24 *Propterea dico vobis, omnia quaecumque orantes petitis … et evenient vobis*, "Therefore I say to you, all things whatsoever you ask … and they shall come unto you"] But that devotion is not true and full which cannot believe the attestation of Truth. But if it can believe, it can by asking and believing obtain. And so to the highest devotion no sacrament becomes impossible, if it can be obtained out of faith. Rightly therefore does the judgment of the spirit strive to obtain, out of the virtue of devotion, that which is proved by the testimony of Truth not to be impossible to it. Tell, he says, the visions of my dreams which I saw, and the solutions of them. [var: Vulg. and the lemma at 1310B print the singular, *solutionem*] The best kind of zeal, therefore, is to bestow the highest care upon the highest devotion, in that no sacrament, according to the reason demonstrated, [1311C] is impossible to it. According to the example, then, of king Nabuchodonosor, let us set our Daniel before any wise men of ours whatsoever; let us compel all our studies, all our exercises, to be subservient to the gains of true devotion; and then beyond doubt we shall not attempt in vain whatsoever we usefully presume, with God's help, concerning the divine mysteries out of his office. But now let us pursue the order of the vision, and let us search out the sense of the spiritual understanding, at least according to moral edification, leaving greater things to greater wits.

## CHAPTER XIII. *Of the manner, or the quality, of contemplating; and that things are seen otherwise in their own being, and otherwise in reason alone, or in the highest truth.*

[1311D] *The vision,* he says, *of my head in my bed. I was seeing, and behold a tree in the midst of the earth, and the height thereof excessive. A great tree, and strong, and the tallness thereof reaching unto heaven; the sight of it was even unto the ends of all the earth. The leaves thereof most beautiful, and the fruit thereof excessive, and in it the food of all. Under it dwelt the animals and the beasts, and in the branches thereof abode the birds of heaven, and of it all flesh did eat [n: (Dan. IV)]*. As is plain from the things above, the vision of the head is the understanding of the mind. The bed, moreover, is the tranquillity of the heart and the leisure of a zealous quiet. The vision of the head in the bed is divinely perceived when, amid the secret leisures of its zeal, the human mind is lifted up by divine inbreathing to the contemplation of truth. I was seeing, he says, and [1312A] behold a tree in the midst of the earth. It is one thing to see the things themselves in their own being, and another to see them in reason alone, or in the highest truth. It is one thing to see each of them in its own proper essence, and far another to see them in wisdom alone. It is one thing to see the substances of things in their genera and species, and another to see them singly in their individuals. The latter belongs to sense or to imagination, but that first one belongs to reason and to contemplation. When therefore the mind is caught up to a certain universal consideration of things, and is divinely lifted up to behold the beauty of the universe, and is delightfully fixed and wonderfully refreshed in a contemplation of this kind and in the sweetness of contemplation, it often sees in the divine light how many and of what sort the kinds of things must needs be, [1312B] and holds it unshaken that nothing of all those which the order of the highest disposition and the beauty of the universe require can be utterly lacking. For example, it sees that there must needs be good men and likewise evil, and among the good some better than others, and some best of all; and so among the evil, some worse than others, and some worst of all. It sees none the less that some must needs be evil and persevere in evil, others be evil and forsake malice for ever, and others forsake it for a time and return again to malice. So, conversely, it sees that some are good and persevere in good, that others fall irrecoverably, that others after a lapse return to goodness. Of this sixth kind of things he seems to be whom Nabuchodonosor contemplates in the light of God, who is shown to him by a likeness, at whom also, after [1312C] he had returned to himself, he wondered within himself, or even had pity. He was seeing that the beauty of the universe required such a one, and that such a one could by no means be lacking; and yet he knew not that he himself was such a one, or that he bore in himself the image of such a man as should fall suddenly from so great a sublimity, and lie long in the lowest places, and yet at last return to his former state. This is what it is that the great tree is first raised up on high, is afterward cut away, and yet its roots are kept in the earth, whence it may be repaired again. Let us therefore see, we also, and let us learn from him what kind of tree it is that he sees, or how it fell, or how that could fall which was so great and of such a kind.



## CHAPTER XIV. *Of the greatness of grace in a mind that is afterward to fall, and what is wont to be the cause of ruin amid so great a fullness of grace.*

[1312D]

I was seeing, he says, and behold a great tree in the midst of the earth, and the height thereof excessive. [var: Vulg. Dan. 4:7, and the lemma printed at 1311D, have *ecce arbor in medio terrae*, without "great"] What shall we understand by the greatness of the tree, but the immense strength of virtue? Was not that also a great tree which received the fullness of grace and of fortitude? *Stephen,* he says, *full of grace and fortitude [n: (Act. VI)]*. Behold a great tree in the midst of the earth, and the height thereof excessive. This tree, therefore, was great, was high, and was in the midst of the earth. It spread itself out to many and great things by virtue, it raised itself to high things by subtlety, and it stood in the inmost things by intention. It stretched itself out to strong things, it raised itself to the highest things, and it remained fixed in the inmost things. [1313A] It was in great things by exercise, in the highest by zeal, in the inmost by desire. Because therefore it did strong things, it was a great tree; because it desired inmost goods, it was in the midst of the earth; because it thought subtly of sublime things, its height was great. A great tree, he says, and strong, and the tallness thereof reaching unto heaven. Behold a great tree, a robust tree, a tall tree. Great for doing good things, strong for enduring evil things, tall for contemplating sublime things. Great in actions, strong in temptations, sublime in investigations. Consider how high it was, whose tallness even touched heaven. Its tallness touched heaven, because the sublimity of its investigation penetrated the heavenly things. And so its tallness was high, and its height was tall. Truly it was a great height [1313B] which plunged itself into the highest and heavenly things. Choose therefore, in the consideration of this tree, what thou mayest wonder at the more: its greatness, its strength, or its tallness. A great tree, he says, and strong, and the tallness thereof reaching unto heaven, A great tree it was, which could truly say: *Everywhere and in all things I am instructed. I know how to be humbled, I know also how to abound, and to suffer want. I can do all things in him who strengtheneth me [n: (Philipp. IV)]*. [var: Vulg. Phil. 4:12 *Scio et humiliari, scio et abundare (ubique et in omnibus institutus sum) et satiari, et esurire, et abundare, et penuriam pati*: the received text has *institutus*, "taught," for *instructus*, and sets the "everywhere and in all things" clause after the two verbs, not before them] A strong tree it was, which could confidently say: *I will not fear what man can do unto me. If armies in camp should stand together against me, my heart shall not fear [n: (Psal. LV)]*. *If a battle should rise up against me, in this will I hope [n: (Psal. XXVI)]*. Beyond the other trees it was tall, which doubted not to say of itself: *And I went beyond in wisdom all that were before me in Hierusalem, and [1313C] my mind hath contemplated many things wisely, and hath learned [n: (Eccle. I)]*. [var: Vulg. Eccl. 1:16 *et didici*, "and I have learned," in the first person; Migne's third person makes "my mind" the subject] Its tallness touched heaven, who could truly say: *We speak wisdom among the perfect, yet not the wisdom of this world, nor of the princes of this world that are brought to nought. But we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, which is hidden, which he predestined before the worlds, which none of the princes of this world hath known [n: (II Cor. XXIX)]*. But see, whosoever thou art that hearest or readest these things, if perchance thy height is great; see, I say, and diligently attend, lest perchance it be also excessive. This perhaps was blameworthy in the tree here described, this perhaps stood as the cause of its cutting down, that its height was excessive. And the height thereof, he says, excessive. Perhaps Nabuchodonosor was walking in great things and in things wonderful [1313D] above himself, and this perhaps stood to him as the cause of his ruin. Perhaps Nabuchodonosor was minded of high things, and therefore his height was excessive: *Be not,* says the Apostle, *high-minded, but fear [n: (Rom. XI)]*. For as for him who eats much honey it is not good for him, so he who is a searcher of majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory. Seek not therefore the things that are higher than thee, lest perchance thy tallness be too high. The searcher of majesty is overwhelmed by glory, and that tree deserves the sentence of cutting down whose height is excessive. Were not trees of this kind high, and did they not justly deserve to be cut down, which, when they had known God, glorified him not as God, or gave thanks: *But they became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened [n: (Rom. I)]*.

## CHAPTER XV. *Of the greatness of authority in a mind that is afterward to fall into ruin.*

[1314A]

But let us hear what is further said of this tree in that which follows: The sight of it was even unto the ends of all the earth. The sight of a tree of this kind reaches unto the ends of all the earth, when the dignity of his name who is of this kind is alike revered by those near him through likeness of morals and by those far off through unlikeness of morals, and his authorities are alike loved by the good and feared by the evil. Did not his sight stand forth even unto the ends of all the earth, of whom the truth of that sentence stood firm: *We are the good odour of Christ unto God in them that are saved, and in them that perish. To some indeed the odour of death unto [1314B] death, but to others the odour of life unto life [n: (II Cor. II)]*. Was not the sight of those trees also spread abroad even unto the ends of all the earth, of which it is truly said: *Their sound hath gone forth into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world [n: (Psal. LXXXI)]*. But according to a certain other sense also the sight of our tree in our own selves lies open even unto the ends of all the earth, when now the experience of his own virtue is hidden from no one of us, neither in great things nor in the least. For if by the tree we take virtue, and by the sight of the tree the cognizance of virtue, when we have now learned with much zeal and much exercise what we can do in each several matter, what else have we done than publish the sight of our tree even unto the ends of all the earth? Had he not published the sight of his tree [1314C] even unto the ends of all the earth, and had he not already begun the experience of his own virtue through all things, who truly affirms of himself that which we have already set down above. For I have learned in what things I am sufficient. *I know how to be humbled, I know also how to abound everywhere, and in all things I am instructed [n: (Philipp. VI)]*. [var: Vulg. Phil. 4:12 *Scio et humiliari, scio et abundare (ubique et in omnibus institutus sum)*; this second printing also reverses the order of the two members against the printing at 1313B]



## CHAPTER XVI. *Of the multitude of learning in a mind that is to fall into ruin, and what is wont to be the cause of ruin amid so great a fullness of learning.*

There is further added concerning this tree: The leaves thereof most beautiful, and the fruit thereof excessive, and in it the food of all. In the leaves, words; in the fruit, learning; in the food, teaching. By the leaves the fruit is clothed, and by well-composed words [1314D] the sentence is adorned: *For the mouth of the wise adorneth learning [n: (Prov. XV)]*. [var: Vulg. Prov. 15:2 *Lingua sapientium*, "the tongue of the wise"] Good fruit has savour and feeds; and spiritual learning sweetly refreshes spiritual hunger by holy admonition. And so the most beautiful leaves are eloquent words; the copious fruit is an instructed sense, a manifold intellect. The food of all is the full instruction of all, the discreet admonition of each. Beautiful leaves of words, as I judge, that tree had, and it abounded in the fruits of good senses and of useful counsels, which could truly say: *They that heard me waited for my sentence, and being attentive held their peace at my counsel. To my words they durst add nothing, and my speech dropped upon them [n: (Job XXIX)]*. Copious fruit that tree had, which could say in truth: *But to me [1315A] God hath given to speak according to my mind, for he himself hath given me the true learning of those things which are: that I may know the disposition of the whole world, and the virtues of the elements; the beginning and the ending, and the midst of the times; the alterations of their courses, and the endings of the times; the changes of manners, and the divisions of times; the courses of the year, and the dispositions of the stars; the natures of animals, and the rages of beasts; the force of winds, and the thoughts of men; the differences of shrubs, and the virtues of roots; and whatsoever things are hidden and unforeseen, I have learned [n: (Sap. VII)]*. Was not the food of all in him who acknowledged himself a debtor unto this very thing, when he said: *To the Greeks and to the barbarians, to the wise and to the unwise, I am a debtor [n: (Rom. I)]*. Is not the food of all in him who by his teaching can edify [1315B] all? Has he not the food of all in himself, who by the spirit of counsel which presides over his mind, and by the grace of discretion in which he is strong, is sufficiently able to instruct with wholesome counsel and to raise up with kindly admonition those beset by any temptation whatsoever, those oppressed by any tribulation whatsoever? Does not he likewise, so far as pertains to himself, find the food of all in himself, who knows how by his own meditations and spiritual theories to nourish any holy desires whatsoever, and to inflame his own spirit to any good works whatsoever, as often and as much as he has willed? But, as we hinted above concerning the height of the tree, let us see whether perchance this also be blameworthy in it, that it is said to have excessive fruit. For it is not [1315C] said that its fruit was much, or its fruit copious, but its fruit, he says, excessive. He reproves excessive fruit who says, In superfluous matters search not manifoldly. It is one thing importunately to seek things impossible, though perchance they be useful, and another curiously to investigate things useless, though these also be possible. The former pertains to the excess of height, the latter pertains to the superfluity of fruits. The presumption of things incomprehensible is forbidden when it is said: *Seek not the things that are too high for thee, and search not out things stronger than thee, but the things which God hath commanded thee,* etc. [n: (Eccle. III.)] The curiosity of superfluous things is reproved in that it is said, In superfluous matters search not manifoldly, and in many of his works be not curious. Will you hear of trees [1315D] which are of this kind, which will not temper the boldness of presumption and of curiosity, how often they incur the sentence of cutting down: *For the suspicion of them,* he says, *hath supplanted many, and hath held their sense in vanity [n: (Eccli. III)]*.

## CHAPTER XVII. *Of the rigor of discipline which a mind that is to fall into ruin is often wont to exercise toward others.*

We have heard from what precedes of what learning he was who is designated by this tree; let us hear yet from what follows of what discipline he was. We have heard how by teaching he could either instruct the untaught or inform the ill-advised; let us hear how by discipline he is wont both to press down the carnal and to raise up the spiritual. [1316A] Under it dwelt the animals and the beasts, and in the branches thereof abode the birds of heaven, and of it all flesh did eat. By the animals and the beasts understand animal men, carnal and secular minds; by the birds take the spiritual, flying to heavenly things on the wings of good zeals and of holy desires. Now we are wont to see two kinds of carnal men. One indeed which serves concupiscence, the other which yields to wrathfulness. And so by the animals we understand minds given over to pleasure; by the beasts, wrathful minds. If by beasts we can fitly understand none but wild animals, it remains that under the name of animals we ought here to understand tame ones only. Rightly therefore are voluptuous minds designated by the animals, which serve the belly alone. [1316B] Rightly none the less are wrathful minds designated by the beasts, which rage with tooth and claw. Of such, therefore, it is rightly said: Under it dwelt the animals and the beasts, in that minds of this kind, dissolute through concupiscence or wrathfulness, ought indeed justly to be pressed down by the rigor of discipline. Rightly did the birds of heaven abide in the branches, and as it were in the higher places, in that spiritual men, kindled with heavenly desires, ought deservedly both to be raised into authority and to be exalted with worthy honor: Under it, he says, dwelt the animals and the beasts, and in the branches thereof abode the birds of heaven. Therefore it confined the bestial in the lowest places, but lifted the spiritual into the high places. Let our prelates learn, let them learn here what they ought to do; [1316C] let them learn, I say, to press down undisciplined morals, to lift up and to honor the good. What, I ask, is this kind of monstrous thing, that the trees of our time bear in their branches bears and lions, or any other bestial minds whatsoever of this sort, but press down in the lowest places the birds of heaven and any feathered flying creatures whatsoever, against the laws of their condition and the ordinances of the Creator? How often have I myself seen, and seeing have groaned over, the wicked man exalted above measure and lifted up above the cedars of Lebanon. What, I ask, is it that you do, who lift up on high brute and bestial hearts of this kind, and suspend them as it were in the air? If you truly love them, why do you not spare them? What, I ask, do you prepare for them but ruin, while you suspend them on high and bear them as it were in your branches? What else shall each man say to him who exalted him, or rather [1316D] to him who subverted him, at the end, in the very border of ruin, but that lifting me up thou hast dashed me down? Let the birds of heaven abide in the branches, and let those whom the wing of sanctity lifts up hold their place in the highest. Let the beasts hold their place beneath the branches in the lowest, and let those who have downward-bent faces through the appetite of the flesh feel the strictness of a devout severity and of a just humiliation. Under it dwelt the animals and the beasts, and in the branches thereof abode the birds of heaven, and of it all flesh did eat. Of that tree assuredly does all flesh eat, by whose examples of virtues all are edified, by whose consolations all are cherished, by whose benefits all are strengthened and are refreshed with teaching. O what a tree, O of how great a sublimity, to which so great a proclamation of praise belongs!



## CHAPTER XVIII. *Of the rigor of discipline which a mind that is to fall into ruin is wont to exercise upon itself.*

[1317A]

But this very thing also which is said of this tree we fulfil in our own selves, if we restrain carnal affections under the rigor of discipline, and occupy our thoughts in the circumspection of our morals, and through spiritual meditations nourish all our senses in good desires. For what do we understand by the flying creatures but subtle thoughts, and what by the fourfooted and earthly creatures but carnal affections? By the animals, those desires which arise beside reason; by the beasts, those which strive against reason: beside reason, the vain and frivolous; against reason, the perverse and hurtful. By the tree, as has been [1317B] said, we take the strength of fortitude, and rightly by the branches of the tree we understand the works and the exercises of virtue. And from branches of this kind we gather in their own season the fruits of good merits, according as we have heard through the Prophet: *Thou shalt eat the labours of thy hands, blessed art thou, and it shall be well with thee [n: (Psal. CXXVII)]*. From branches of this kind come forth the fruits of wholesome counsels and of subtle understandings, when through many trials the exercises of the virtues instruct a man unto the perfection of discretion and of learning. For many things which we cannot attain by investigation we learn more fully and more certainly by experience; hence that saying of the Psalmist: *By thy commandments I have understood [n: (Psal. CXVIII)]*. He understands from the commandments who, from that [1317C] which he does, advances to a greater understanding. Hence it is that elsewhere it is written: *In the understandings of his hands he led them [n: (Psal. LXVII)]*. He leads another in the understandings of his hands who directs him by sure steps of advancement to the way of truth which he has learned through the trials of works. Small and of little certainty is that learning which the experience of things does not help and confirm: hence it is that it is said through the Wise Man: *He that is not experienced knoweth few things [n: (Eccle. XXXIV)]*. But not only from the good things which we do, but also from the evils which we endure, are we instructed unto discretion, and from the very temptations we are made more prudent. Of this that voice of the Wise Man admonishes us, which says: *He that hath not been tempted, what doth he know? [n: (Ibid.)]* [var: Vulg. Sir. 34:11 *Qui tentatus non est, qualia scit?*, "what manner of things doth he know?"] A man experienced in many things hath thought many things, and he who [1317D] hath learned many things shall declare understanding. [var: Vulg. Sir. 34:9 *cogitabit*, future, "shall think many things"] And so from the branches of the tree fruit is gathered, because from much exercise of the virtues learning shall be multiplied. And the more perfect and the more approved each man is, the more abundant fruits he begets, and the more delightfully he refreshes. *But for the perfect,* says the Apostle, *is solid food, for them who by custom have their senses exercised unto the discerning of good and evil [n: (Hebr. V)]*. Good indeed, and branches of a good tree, are those which bear such fruit and beget the food of souls; which receive the flying creatures of heaven and suspend sublime thoughts on high; which cover the beasts and press down the assaults of the flesh. I think that the Apostle too was pressing down the animals beneath branches of this kind, when he said: *I chastise my body, and bring it into subjection [n: (I Cor. IX)]*. But he who [1318A] would accustom the birds of heaven to the branches of a tree of this kind, let his will be in the law of the Lord, and in his law let him meditate day and night.

Let us beware, therefore, of making our nest in the earth after the manner of certain birds, or of living in watery places, and of forsaking the branches of the tree; and let us be ashamed to cleave to worldly cares and to the desires of the flesh by the importunity of unremitting thoughts: *Mind the things that are above,* says the Apostle, *not the things that are upon the earth [n: (Coloss. III)]*. And so our birds ought for a season to be lifted up to heavenly things, and to be suspended in the contemplation of eternal things, and again, after their sublime flights, to return to the branches of their own tree, and there to tarry, nay even to dwell. For what else is it for the birds of heaven always to return to the branches of their own tree, and to inhabit there, [1318B] but for the thoughts of one's own heart frequently to be called back to the consideration of one's own morals and works, and to press the more often upon the circumspection of them, and to lean upon it the more vehemently? Hence it is that it is said through Solomon: *The sun riseth and setteth, and returneth to his own place [n: (Eccle. I)]*; for the sun of the understanding, after its rising and after the ascent of sublime contemplation, returns again to its own place, and the eye of the heart is called back to the circumspection of itself, that it may again be lifted up to higher things. For the heart which sleeps as to the keeping of itself quickly loses the grace of contemplation which it had received. Rightly therefore is it said of this tree, and in the branches thereof abode the birds of heaven, in that the circumspections of the mind ought chiefly to be watchful about the custody of themselves. Behold, we have now [1318C] heard what we ought to think concerning a tree of this kind. Yet let no one suppose that I believe king Nabuchodonosor to have been such as he hears me describe out of the mystical signification: for neither was he such in his own person, but out of his own person he prefigured such a man, and in the tree he saw he designated such a one. But let us meanwhile pursue the mystical description, and we shall find perhaps in it what we may justly wonder at; and not only what we ought to admire, but rather what we may worthily bewail, and what we ought deservedly to fear concerning ourselves.

## CHAPTER XIX. *That upon any summit of the virtues whatsoever one ought always to fear the ruin of morals.*

Let us hear therefore what he further says of this tree, and let each man learn and groan at what he ought to fear: [1318D] *I was seeing in the vision of my head upon my bed, and behold a watcher, and a holy one came down from heaven, and cried out mightily, and said thus: Cut down the tree and cut off its branches; shake off its leaves and scatter its fruit. Let the beasts flee which are under it, and the birds from its branches [n: (Dan. IV)]*. [var: Vulg. Dan. 4:11 *dispergite fructus ejus*, plural, "scatter its fruits"; the exposition at 1321C–D follows the singular printed here] Woe to the sons of Adam, woe to the human condition. What, I ask, how much soever he shall have advanced, how much soever he shall have ascended, will he be able to be secure for the rest, if so great a man and one so perfect could fall from so great a sublimity, and that as it were within the moment of a single hour? Let us call to mind, therefore, of what sort he is described above out of the mystical tree who here is bidden to be cut off, and then we shall the better recognize how justly the ruin of morals [1319A] is feared by those who are set upon any height of virtue whatsoever. In the greatness of the tree we wonder at the measure of fortitude; in its height, at the profundity of subtlety; in the spreading of its sight, at the greatness of authority. In the beauty of its leaves, at the eloquence of speech; in the excess of its fruits, at the multitude of instruction; in the food of all, at the teaching of edification; in the subjection of the beasts, at the rigor of severity; in the cohabitation of the birds, at the providence of circumspection. Who therefore, unless he be mad, promises himself security amid so great a hazard of mutability, if he was truly once such a one who afterward was cut down and fell? Truly, as the Scripture says: *Blessed is the man who is always fearful. For he knoweth not what the day to come may bring forth [n: (Prov. XXVIII)]*. [var: Vulg. Prov. 27:1 *ignoras enim quid superventura pariat dies*, "for thou knowest not what the day to come may bring forth"; the second clause is not part of Prov. 28:14, to which the note points]



## CHAPTER XX. *That whatsoever is done concerning us is dispensed by God's disposition and by angelic administration.*

[1319B]

Yet let no one think that God has no care for human things, let no one dare rashly to reprehend his judgments, when he sees or hears that something has happened beside expectation, or against reason, as it seems to him. Behold, he by whom the sentence of cutting down is given or dispensed is said to have come down from heaven and to have been holy. Behold, he says, a holy watcher came down from heaven. [var: Vulg. Dan. 4:10 and the lemma at 1318D read *vigil, et sanctus*, two subjects, "a watcher, and a holy one"] When therefore thou hearest that the minister of this work comes from heaven, understand that this is done by God's disposition; and when thou readest that he is holy, believe that he justly executes that which is just. Behold, a watcher and a holy one came down from heaven. About the care of men both the good angels and the evil expend a perpetual solicitude, and neither by night nor by day do they withdraw themselves even for a little from this [1319C] solicitude; but the evil are watchful for assailing, the good for protecting, so that both may rightly enough be called watchers. But that it is a good angel who either learned this sentence from heaven or disposed it on earth is sufficiently shown from this, that he is reported to be holy and to have come down from heaven. O how rightly does this name befit the good angels, upon whom the sleep of error or of forgetfulness never creeps as touching the business of our salvation! O height of angelic devotion! They who are secure concerning themselves yet bear solicitude for us. Of this watch of the angels about our salvation, and of their watchful custody, is that apostolic sentence: *Are they not all ministering spirits, sent in ministry [1319D] for them who receive the inheritance of salvation? [n: (Hebr. I.)]* [var: Vulg. Heb. 1:14 *qui haereditatem capient salutis*, future, "who shall receive the inheritance of salvation"; the received text also runs *Nonne omnes sunt administratorii spiritus*] What else, therefore, is it for watchers of this kind to come down from heaven, but for the ministers of our salvation to have a care of earthly things, and, according to what they divinely learn in the highest things, to dispose human affairs also in the lowest? Rightly therefore is it said: Behold, a watcher and a holy one came down from heaven, and cried out mightily; and said thus: Cut off the tree. [var: Vulg. Dan. 4:11 and the lemma at 1318D read *Succidite arborem*, "Cut down the tree"] And so some things there are which the good angels do by themselves, others which they permit to be done, nothing at all is anywhere done without their disposition. Good things therefore are done by their cooperation, but evil things by their permission. Good things therefore are administered through the good angels, evil things through the evil. Since he knew that to overthrow, as regards the state of rectitude, was an evil, the good angel was unwilling to cut off the tree; nevertheless, because he knew that the merit of this one man, [1320A] or the good of the universe, required it, he permitted it to be done. For in that he says, Cut off the tree, understand a permission and not a precept. For herein obedience is not enjoined upon the malignant spirits, but licence is granted. This at length he permitted them at some time to do, which he was not ignorant that they had long and much desired. Hence it is that it is said by the Lord to Judas the betrayer: *That which thou dost, do quickly [n: (Joan. XIII)]*. For herein a precept is not enjoined upon him, but the faculty of acting is conceded.

Now it is known to all that we are wont to use the outcry of a great voice as often as we would make something known to those set far off. But what stands farther apart one from another than an angelic spirit and a malignant spirit, not so much by the distance of place as by the [1320B] diversity of will? Hence it is that that prodigal son, who is read to have wasted all his substance in living riotously with harlots, is reported in the Gospel to have gone away into a far country [n: (Luc. XV)], in that, made distant by the depravation of his will, he is estranged from the good pleasure of the supreme Father. According to this manner, therefore, they are assuredly far distant from one another, distinguished and disjoined by a lot so various and so contrary: an angel confirmed in good, an angel confirmed in evil; an angel deputed to glory, and an angel consigned to Gehenna. Rightly therefore is that watcher and holy one reported to have cried out mightily, that from this it might be openly given to understand of what kind those angels were, and how far removed from a good angel they might be seen to be, to whom a sentence of the watchers, dictated from heaven, is made known not without a mighty outcry. [1320C] Yet there is among certain of the good angels also a great distance, a difference not of contrary will but of supereminent dignity, becomingly ordained of God. Whence neither does it seem incongruous if some outcry is described among them, whereby the difference of their dignity may be denoted. Rightly therefore is the angel who is here brought in as having conceded to the malignant spirits the licence of tempting reported not only to have cried out, but to have cried out mightily. Behold, he says, a watcher, and a holy one came down from heaven and cried out mightily, and thus said: Cut down the tree.

## CHAPTER XXI. *That the malignant spirits can do nothing against us save by God's permission.*

[1320D]There are two things which from the present passage we can plainly gather. The first, that the malignant spirits cannot tempt us save so far as they are permitted. The second, that if they were let loose for our assailing according to all their power, no one could endure their onset. For since they who can and will cut down the tree yet do not cut it down unless permitted, it plainly appears that without God's permission they presume nothing in their persecution of us. But what would they presume upon men without God's permission, who, as the Gospel attests, dared not invade even the herd of swine without divine licence? [n: (Matth. VIII; Marc. V; Luc. VIII.)] So much licence, therefore, is let loose to them in the assailing of the elect as their profit [1321A] requires, or as justice deserves. For what human virtue could sustain their onset, if, having received licence from God, they were able straightway to overthrow a tree so great and of such a kind? But in this the apostle Paul consoles us: *Faithful,* he says, *is the Lord, who suffereth you not to be tempted above that which you are able, but will make also with the temptation issue, that you may be able to sustain it [n: (I Cor. X)]*. [var: Vulg. 1 Cor. 10:13 *Fidelis autem Deus est, qui non patietur vos tentari*, "God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted"] Unless therefore that tree had been too high, and had swollen concerning its own virtue, and presumed too much, it would not have received from God the sentence of cutting down. Consider now a great tree, and one presuming too much upon the abundance of its own fortitude: *I said,* he says, *in my abundance, I shall never be moved [n: (Psal. XXIX)]*. But straightway, from the withdrawal of grace and the temptation that came upon it, it learned [1321B] what, or how much, it could of itself: *Thou hast turned away,* he says, *thy face from me, and I became troubled [n: (ibid.)]*. And so the tree is cut down when the virtue of constancy is little by little worn away by temptations, and at last is utterly taken away. Was not the strength of that tree cut down which said: *My virtue hath forsaken me, and the light of my eyes, even that is not with me [n: (Psal. XXXVII)]*. Was not its virtue withdrawn, and the tree, being cut down, fallen to the lowest, when at the regard of a single concupiscence it fell into adultery, and from adultery into homicide?

## CHAPTER XXII. *How, or in what order, the human mind is wont to fall to ruin upon the withdrawal of grace.*

[1321C]When the tree is cut down, the branches also are cut off; because, as the virtue of the spirit fails, good works are little by little withdrawn. The tree is cut down and the branch is cut off, when virtue fails in secret and the work of virtue in the open. First therefore the virtue of the spirit is withdrawn, afterward the faculty also and the occasion of doing well is taken away; and, the strength of the tree being cut down and the branches cut off, the leaves are shaken off and the fruit is scattered; because, as the purpose of the virtues and the exercise of the virtues fail, first the grace of speaking well is taken away, and at last the grace of understanding rightly also is withdrawn. Rightly indeed, after the zeal of good working fails, is the eloquence of speech withdrawn, because every chastisement or exhortation of a depraved preacher can scandalize his hearers rather than edify them, since to him as he speaks [1321D] anyone may silently answer: Why then dost thou not thyself do these things? But to the sinner God hath said: Why dost thou declare my justices, and take my testament in thy mouth? The grace of the leaves is shaken off when, from an infamous suspicion first entertained, the confidence or the authority of speaking is lost. The fruit is scattered when his teaching is despised, which, although through its sense or its counsel it may perchance seem useful, yet on account of the depraved example of his life is easily trodden underfoot. The fruit is scattered when, by the importunate incursion of various concupiscences, the zeal of meditation is dissipated, and the subtlety of investigating and the facility of understanding are confounded by the wandering of thoughts. Behold how easily, behold in what order that mind is cast down from on high which, its merits requiring it, is deserted by divine grace, [1322A] which by divine permission is exposed to the malignant exactors. Rightly therefore is it said of this tree: Shake off its leaves, and scatter its fruit.



## CHAPTER XXIII. *How the mind, after a foul casting down of itself, is wont afterwards both to be despised by others, and to be dissolved into itself.*

But when a man has begun to lose the branches of the virtues and the fruit of counsel, and to have not at all either uprightness of life or the authority of teaching, who now among carnal men would deign to obey him, or who among spiritual men to cleave to him through familiarity? Rightly, therefore, is that added which is still said of this tree: Let the beasts flee which are under it, and the birds from its branches. For the beasts which before were under it [1322B] flee away, when his own subjects refuse obedience to him, and all carnal men despise his mastery. For the birds of heaven to flee from its branches is for all spiritual men to shudder at the infamy of that life, and to shun its fellowships. Did not the younger men abominate the shady coverts of that great tree to which, according to the Lord's testimony, there was none like upon the earth, in that he was truly a great man among all the men of the east, and the first among the chief; did not, I say, the younger men abominate the shady coverts of that great tree, and did not the beasts now disdain to be under it, when he truly protested of himself: *But now they that are younger in time deride me, whose fathers I did not deign to set with the dogs of my flock. The strength of whose hands was [1322C] to me as nothing, and they were thought unworthy of life itself (Job XXX)*. What, I ask, were the elders doing, if the younger, and men so vile, derided him, in that so great a tree had been cut down by the Lord's permission, and smitten with a most grievous ulcer from the sole of the foot even to the crown? How great also was that tree to which the Lord bore testimony, that he had found a man according to his own heart. Did not the birds of heaven dwell in its branches, when he truly protests of himself: *that the innocent and the upright have cleaved to me? [n: (Psal. XXIV.)]* [var: Vulg. Ps. 24:21 begins *Innocentes et recti adhaeserunt mihi*; the *quia* Migne prints inside the quotation is the conjunction binding it to *protestetur*] Had they not also at that time fled away from its branches, when again in prayer he cried out: *Thou hast put my acquaintance far from me, they have made me an abomination to themselves [n: (Psal. LXXXVII)]*; and again: *Thou hast removed far from me friend and neighbour, and my acquaintance because of misery [n: (ibid.)]*. [1322D] But then in any man of virtue is fulfilled what is written of this tree, that, the strength of the wood being cut down, the beasts dwelling beneath flee away, when, the vigour of the spirit being broken and drained by temptations, the mind is no longer strong enough to check carnal onsets, or to coerce any irrational desires under the mastery of reason. We lose the dwelling together of the birds of heaven, when, disturbed by the onrush of so many phantasms, we are not strong enough to practise the pleasant spectacles of sublime investigations. The tree loses the birds that dwell in its branches, when it can no longer practise its meditations about the accustomed circumspection of its own morals. We often grieve that we have lost the companionship of such birds, when we are not strong enough to restrain our thoughts from unfitting wandering, so that each one [1323A] of us may rightly say within himself that word of blessed Job, when he now sees his own birds to have flown away, not without grief of his own: *My thoughts are dissipated, tormenting my heart [n: (Job VII)]*.

## CHAPTER XXIV. *That the divine mercy often both reserves unto repentance those who have basely fallen and been cast down from on high, and waits for their correction.*

But how merciful a thing is this, and how worthy of great wonder, that the divine mercy often neither utterly forsakes such men, nor after such a fall and so great a ruin wholly abandons them, but still often waits for such men unto correction, and reserves them unto repentance. Woe to thee, whosoever thou art that dost catch thyself to be such a one, if thou despisest the riches of his goodness, and of his patience, and of his longsuffering. [1323B] Or knowest thou not that the kindness of God leadeth thee to repentance, who has not yet cut away the roots of thy hope, but has hidden them in the secret place of his judgments, and as it were in the bosom of the earth? Let us hear, therefore, how that height of the divine mercy tempers the sentence of its own severity, when after the waste of so great a scattering it still adds something concerning this tree for our consolation: *Nevertheless,* he says, *leave the shoot of its roots in the earth.* This is that which we neither can nor ought to pass by without wonder at the divine kindness, in him who bids the shoot of its roots be left in the earth, whence it may again be repaired, and reformed to its former fullness. Nevertheless, he says, leave the shoot of its roots in the earth. Then is the tree as it were plucked up by the roots, when [1323C] after evils have been perpetrated it is hurled headlong even into despair. For the tree loses as it were its own roots, when it loses all hope of correction, and falls into despair. That tree had been plucked up by the roots, and had remained in its falling without any shoot of repair, which, speaking to the Lord and despairing of pardon, said: *My iniquity is greater than that I may deserve pardon [n: (Gen. IV)]*. For what else are the shoot, or the root, of a tree of this kind, but the purpose of correction and the hope of the divine propitiation? For every good work germinates out of a good purpose, that it may break forth into effect and grow strong unto the sturdiness of good habit; and in vain does the tree of virtue strive after other things, which is not rooted in the hope of the divine propitiation: *For [1323D] it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy [n: (Rom. IX)]*. What else, then, is it for the shoot of the roots to remain to a tree of this kind after its ruin, than for anyone after the fall of sin to have a purpose of repentance and to hope for the fruit of repentance from the divine mercy, so far that, feeling concerning the Lord in goodness, he may dare, and say: *He will not be angry unto eternity, neither will he threaten unto eternity? [n: (Psal. CII.)] For when he shall have been angry, he will remember mercy [n: (Habac. III)]*. [var: Vulg. Ps. 101:9 *Non in perpetuum irascetur*, "not for ever", and the clause is a statement; chunk 0014 prints the same verse at 1262B with *in perpetuum* and no question mark] [var: Vulg. Hab. 3:2 *cum iratus fueris, misericordiae recordaberis*, second person, "when thou shalt be angry, thou wilt remember mercy"] How many do we daily see who, amid the outrages which they assiduously commit, do not lose the hope and the purpose of coming to their senses, and who purpose not only to put away their sins, nay rather to leave all things that are of the world, and to come to an order and to religion. What else do these retain than the roots of a good shoot? Whence, [1324A] when the time of showing mercy shall have come according to the divine good pleasure, they sprout forth unto good zeal. But others, when they are admonished concerning conversion, affirm even with an oath that they will never come to an order or to religion, and when they are rebuked concerning their sins, asseverate under solemn oath that they cannot restrain themselves from their own pleasures. They therefore who are of this kind, who have lost the hope and the purpose of correction, have they not, together with the tree of virtue, lost also the shoot of the roots? Against which it is said of this tree: Nevertheless leave the shoot of its roots in the earth.



## CHAPTER XXV. *To how great depravity the mind is sometimes hardened, which nevertheless is divinely reserved unto pardon.*

It is truly a wonder how at a single outrage [1324B] many often fall at once into despair. Others do not, even after many and very great and long-continued evils, lose the hope or the purpose of coming to their senses. And of this is rightly understood that also which is here still brought in concerning this tree, namely, that *it be bound with a bond of iron and of bronze among the grasses which are without, and let it be dipped in the dew of heaven, and let its portion be with the wild beasts in the grass of the earth. Let his heart be changed from man's, and let the heart of a beast be given him [n: (Dan. IV)]*. From these things assuredly, as I judge, thou weighest how great the evils are; but hear yet how long-continued they are: *And let seven,* he says, *times be changed over him.* For what is more rightly understood in the bond of iron and of bronze, than the habit of untameable perversity? In the iron, audacity; in the bronze, obstinacy; in the grasses of the earth, the lowest goods, earthly goods.
