For what are these earthly [1324C] goods, which are common to us with the beasts, but certain grasses of the earth. Of which it is rightly said: which are without. For by that very thing they exist without, in that they are bodily and carnal, and not spiritual. For the inward goods are spiritual, but the outward are bodily. Those belong to the inner man, these to the outer man. Those, then, are invisible, but these visible; those eternal, these temporal: *For the things which are seen,* says the Apostle, *are temporal, but the things which are not seen, eternal [n: (II Cor. IV)]*. [var: Vulg. closes *quae autem non videntur, aeterna sunt*; Migne's printing drops the second *sunt*] But those belong to the mind, and these to the flesh. But all flesh is hay, and all the glory thereof as the flower of hay. When therefore the depraved mind has begun to incline itself to lowest goods of this kind, and as it were in the grass of the earth to sate its carnal desires, [1324D] and to bring delights of this kind into habitual use, then, as the crooked habit little by little grows strong, it often comes to pass at last that it can no longer temper its own appetite away from the love or the use of them. The depraved mind, therefore, is bound as it were with a bond of iron in the grass of the earth, when out of a crooked habit it is hardened in the love of carnal pleasures. Because iron tames all other metals, it rightly, as has been said, designates audacity, which reveres no one, dreads no one. And since bronze is more durable than all the rest, we have already said that obstinacy is rightly designated by it. The crooked habit, therefore, grows hard as it were in the rigidity of iron, or also of bronze, when the depraved mind presses upon its accustomed desires as obstinately as audaciously. Is not that mind bound with a bond of iron and of bronze which is turned away [1325A] from its accustomed concupiscences by the terror of no man ever, by the admonition of no man ever? Does it not already feel bonds of iron or of bronze, which neither yields to threats, nor acquiesces in counsels? It stands firm, therefore, that minds of this kind can in no wise be corrected, save assuredly in the power of him who, as often as he willed, has ground down the gates of bronze and shattered the bars of iron. With gates, surely, we block the passage of those going forth, but with bars we fortify and make fast the closure itself. What, then, do we understand by the gate but contradiction, and what by the bar but rebellion? And we know indeed that for certain men it is not enough to contradict the admonitions or the mandates of their prelates, but when they cannot refute or turn aside their ordinances by words, they strive also to withstand them by deeds, and to rebel against them by works, [1325B] and as it were to fortify the gates of their contradiction with the bars of rebellions. If therefore, as has already been said above, by bronze is rightly understood obstinacy, and by iron audacity, what else will the gate of bronze be, but obstinate contradiction, and what the bar of iron, but audacious rebellion? What else, then, is it for the Lord to shatter the gates of bronze and the bars of iron, than to coerce obstinate contradiction and audacious rebellion by an inward inbreathing and by compunction of heart? It belongs, therefore, to God alone, as has been said, to grind down this so great hardness of heart, and to soften it unto repentance and humiliation. When therefore anyone, according to the aforesaid manner, is bound with a bond of iron and of bronze among the grasses which are without, let the loosing of so great a hardening [1325C] and binding be looked for from the mercy of God alone.

## CHAPTER XXVI. *How the mind, which is depraved in its morals, is afterwards imbued with errors or deceits.*

But there is still added, to the increase of the evil, that which is joined on: And let it be dipped in the dew of heaven. What do we understand by the dew of heaven, but the subtle and scarcely intelligible suggestions of the devil? For if by the earth the body is fittingly enough designated, why should not the spirit be equally rightly designated by heaven? In comparison with bodies, therefore, those spiritual substances in the demons can be called heavens. And in the Gospel they have been called birds of heaven, not on account of justice, not on account of glory, but on account of their angelic and spiritual nature. [1325D] The depraved mind, therefore, is dipped in the dew of heaven, when through the suggestions of the devil it is imbued with divers errors. For out of the exultation of its own concupiscences it often runs into so great a darkness of errors, that it calls evil good, and good evil, putting darkness light and light darkness, putting bitter for sweet and sweet for bitter. He therefore who is bound without among the grasses of the earth must needs be dipped in the dew: for after the depravation of morals, the sense also is depraved and is easily entangled in many errors. Hence it is that in the overthrow of Jerusalem the king first lost his sons, and afterwards his eyes [n: (IV Reg. XXV)]. He assuredly loses spiritual sons, who loses the offspring of the virtues which he had long nourished. But when the sons have been lost, the light of the eyes is plucked out, because often from the depravation of the wills the keenness of understanding [1326A] is overdrawn and beclouded. He therefore who loses the desires of the heavenly, who wraps himself in the love of earthly things, whom the bond of cupidity binds fast as it were by a pasturing upon grasses, must needs at some time run into the darkness of errors, and, as the clouds of heaven drop down, infect himself with a certain dew of seduction. Does not he also seem to thee to be dipped in the dew of heaven, who by the suggestion of malignant spirits is trained unto every deceit, so that after their likeness he may willingly will, and easily be able, to deceive his neighbours and to circumvent them by frauds? For without doubt, when an excessive love of earthly things begins to reign, it little by little brings in fraudulence, but at the last it drives on to violence and rapine. Whence it is that he subjoins, and let its portion be with the wild beasts in the grass of the earth.

## CHAPTER XXVII. *How the mind is sometimes let loose unto every cruelty, though it be nevertheless divinely reserved unto repentance.*

[1326B]

And it is a wonder indeed, yet none the less true, that the divine disposition permits some to be let loose unto the highest cruelty, whom nevertheless it disposes to reserve unto repentance, inasmuch as it has preordained them unto eternal life. It is said, therefore, of a man of this kind: And let his portion be with the wild beasts in the grass of the earth. By the wild beasts, which rage with tooth and claw (whence also from their fierceness they are called ferocious), all cruel men can rightly enough be understood. Of such the Psalmist: *The sons of men,* he says, *their teeth are weapons and arrows, [1326C] and their tongue a sharp sword [n: (Psal. LVI)]*. By the grass of the earth we understand the delights of a flesh that is to die and the glory of a life that passes. For all flesh is hay, and all the glory thereof as the flower of hay. They therefore seem to have a portion with the cruel, and as it were with the wild beasts in the grass of the earth, who for the sake of avarice and ambition are let loose unto rapine and deceit and unto every cruelty. For what is it to have a portion with the ministers of cruelty, and with wild planks, but to receive a lot with such companions in the due of retributions, even as in the likeness of morals? But on the contrary the Prophet utterly shunned to have the fellowships of such men, or to receive a portion with them, when he said: *I have hated the church of the malignant, and with the wicked I will not sit [n: (Psal. C)]*. Whence also [1326D] elsewhere: *The crooked heart hath not cleaved to me [n: (ibid.)]*. Let his heart be changed from man's. The heart of a soul that prevaricates and rushes into the depths is changed from man's, when all affection of humanity and of mercy is utterly lost, when out of the love of temporal things and out of the vice of avarice it is hardened to the marrow against the works of mercy, according to that word. The bowels of the covetous man are cruel [n: (Prov. XII)]. [var: Vulg. Prov. 12:10 *viscera autem impiorum crudelia*, "the bowels of the wicked"; Migne prints *avari*] But after so many steps of corruption, that also is still added to the increase of the evil which is brought in below, and let the heart of a beast be given him. The heart of a beast is given and received, when a neighbour pursues his neighbour without regard to any advantage of his own, by the mere instinct of malignity, as emptily as cruelly. Hear what the Prophet feels concerning such men: *The bloody and deceitful man,* he says, *the Lord will abhor [n: (Psal. V)]*.



## CHAPTER XXVIII. *How evil goes rioting on in those who ever slip into worse things.*

[1327A]

Attend, I beseech thee, how evil goes rioting on. First goods are lost, afterwards evils also are committed. In the shaking off of the leaves, and the scattering of the fruits, understand the declines of goods. In the binding among the grasses and the hardening of the heart, understand the increases of evils.

But this is to be noted, by what steps the accumulation of vices grows: first one is cast down into avarice, but at last through manifold steps of corruption is let loose unto every cruelty. First, then, the prevaricating soul is bound with a bond of iron and of bronze, when with strong labour and obstinate solicitude it is untiringly occupied about the acquisition of earthly things. [1327B] It is dipped in the dew of heaven, when by a malignant suggestion it is imbued unto deceit, so that at the instigation of avarice it may acquire by fraudulence what it cannot acquire by effort. But at last its portion comes to be with the wild beasts in the grasses of the earth, when that which it can acquire neither by effort nor by deceit, it desires and busies itself to obtain by violence and rapine. Behold how the disease of avarice grows, and brings in the evil of cruelty. Now the first step of savagery is when for some advantage of his own a man presumes, or endures (yet not without remorse of conscience), to rage against his neighbour. The heart is changed from man's, when it is moved by no compassion, softened by no humanity, when in the practising of rapines it is stung by no [1327C] regard of the divine fear, by no goading of punishment or of conscience whatsoever. He receives the heart of a beast who rages even gratuitously, who without any cause breaks out into open malice. The first step of malice, then, is when without any cause at all a man is hardened toward his neighbour. The second, when in his neighbour's miseries he is touched by no compassion. The third and worst, when he now feeds and delights himself in that neighbour's evils.

## CHAPTER XXIX. *That it often happens that the mind is corrupted in every form, which nevertheless is agreed to be reserved unto repentance out of the divine mercy.*

But one thing more is added, and as it were in the last place, in which the sentence of severity seems to be consummated. [1327D] And let seven, he says, times be changed over him. Seven times are changed, when by the various steps of corruption the quality of our infirmity is varied, while it is ever turned unto worse things. Do we not then run into another time, and one as it were contrary to the former, when against a vice which we were before able to resist we now begin to be wholly unable to prevail? The time, then, is manifoldly changed about anyone, when the manner of his corruption is multiformly varied. For the domination of the vices little by little softens the spirit, and renders it ever more and more feeble, and step by step drives it on to worse things. But in seven days, as we commonly know, all time is unrolled, and therefore universality is often figured by that same sevenfold number. Likewise the capital vices are read to be seven. Hence it is [1328A] that in the Gospel we read that the unclean spirit brings in seven spirits with him, and inhabits his house which he had left for a time, because any one vice, when it has already begun to have dominion, is wont step by step to bring in after it that whole detestable college of vices. Hence on the contrary the sinful woman is described as purged of seven demons, who is freed from every tyranny of the vices by the sevenfold grace. The sevenfold change of times, then, is a multiform, nay rather a universal depravation of morals. For seven times are as it were changed over him who is corrupted in every form, and who at last at some time nervelessly bends to every servitude of the vices. But see now how wonderful it is that the divine mercy is sometimes wont to reserve a man of this kind [1328B] unto repentance.

## CHAPTER XXX. *How it is wont to serve the profit of many that some men happen to fall from a height.*

*In the sentence of the watchers it is decreed, and the word of the holy ones, and the petition, until the living know that the Most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and to whomsoever he will he shall give it, and he shall set the lowliest man over it [n: (Dan. IV)]*. [var: Vulg. Dan. 4:14 *donec cognoscant viventes quod dominetur Excelsus in regno hominum … constituet super eum*; Migne prints the indicative *dominatur* and *super eo*] As we have already said above, by the watchers in this place we understand the holy angels. But by the Apostle's teaching we have learned that all ministering spirits are sent for the sake of those who receive the inheritance of salvation. The angels, therefore, fellow-workers of our salvation and ministers of the divine [1328C] ordination, dispose human affairs according as they know, by God's revealing, that it agrees with the common profit of men. But it is often wont to serve the profit of many that some men happen to fall from a great summit of loftiness, that the rest may learn not to be high-minded, but always to think humble things concerning themselves, and upon any summit of the virtues to fear the ruin of their morals, and may truly acknowledge that it is the Lord alone who works in us to will and to accomplish according to good will. [var: Vulg. Phil. 2:13 *qui operatur in vobis et velle et perficere*, "in you"; Migne prints *in nobis* and drops the first *et*] This profit of such a ruin the prophetic word intimates, saying: *Until the living know that the Most High ruleth in the kingdom of men.* [var: Vulg. *dominetur*, subjunctive] By the divine dispensation, therefore, when the common profit demands this, men of great authority are permitted to fall, at that time only [1328D] in which they are found to grow proud over their own greatness. And so about one and the same person there comes one and the same judgment, as just as it is merciful: just indeed as regards that person, but merciful inasmuch as it profits toward the wariness of others. For it is exceedingly just that he who insolently swells up over the divine gifts should learn from his own ruin how much he is nothing, and how much he can do nothing by himself. But the same decree is said to be also the word of the holy ones, for this reason, that what is foreseen by certain of them in the light of God as to come is brought into common. But it is the petition of the holy ones, because they not only will it to be done, but even with desire seek after that which they foreknow to be useful to many and to serve the divine glory. A judgment of this kind, then, will be the decree of the holy ones, because it is mercifully just; [1329A] the word of the holy ones, because it is truly to come. A petition, because it is justly merciful.



## CHAPTER XXXI. *How some men learn from their own fall, and some from another's, that they ought to attribute nothing to their own powers.*

Until the living know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men. Behold the profit: that the living may know. The affections in us surely live according to God, while they are strong in good, and grow strong unto the works of the virtues, while they have cooperating grace, and are able to exercise themselves in spiritual zeals. Then without doubt they die, when the cooperating grace is withdrawn in them. But it is withdrawn when the wicked mind grows proud over its own goods and over the divine gifts, and ascribes its own merits to itself. When grace has been withdrawn, the good affections [1329B] fail and languish toward every good, and thus from living they become dead. For what else is the failure of the virtues, than as it were a certain perishing of them? They therefore who first attend to their own infirmity and to the divine grace only when they are already failing in good, these men learn and acknowledge the mastery, or the benefit, of the divine dominion and moderation after death, and as it were through death. What, then, is it for the living to acknowledge the dominion and princedom of the supernal majesty in the kingdom of men, but for each one, even at that time while he still lives in good works, to attend to his own infirmity, and to ascribe nothing to himself, nothing to his own merits, and amid any exercises whatever of the virtues not to desert the guard of humility, [1329C] but truly and without simulation to ascribe whatever of evil to himself, whatever of good to the divine grace? And the supernal mercy is indeed wont to humble even men of virtues in certain things, and to withdraw grace, until they learn amid any distinctions of morals to be in nothing high-minded, to presume nothing concerning their own virtue. Happy are they who learn the weak things of human frailty from another's fall rather than from their own, and advance in the grace of humility. But it goes well indeed even with those who from their own ruin wake up to the guard of humility, since at last at some time after the fall of their infirmity they rise again the stronger. The type of both things is expressed in the ruin, or the repair, of king Nabuchodonosor, because he himself also is repaired after his ruin unto greater glory, and many through his ruin are instructed unto the [1329D] wariness of circumspection. Until the living know, he says, that the Most High ruleth in the kingdom of men. It belongs, then, to the living to have knowledge of this kind: for one leading a just life of whatsoever sort, and a heavenly one, to persevere in good zeal, and to attribute nothing to himself out of his own goods. The living assuredly have knowledge of this kind, when they both endure in a good intention, and presume nothing concerning their own virtue, but ascribe to the Lord all that they usefully can, in that he it is who alone ruleth in the kingdom of men, since the kingdom is the Lord's, and he shall rule over the nations. Surely both that outward kingdom by which men are wont to be set over men, and likewise that inward one by which they ought to have princedom over their own vices and passions, are disposed by him and dispensed, and both are possessed out of his [1330A] gift. But the former we must assuredly avoid and flee altogether, even as the mistress Truth teaches us by her own example. But the latter we ought to desire, and to seek, and with the highest desire to ask for, and with the Prophet to entreat: *Give rule to thy servant [n: (Psal. LXXXV)]*. [var: Vulg. Ps. 85:16 *Da imperium tuum puero tuo*, "thy command"; Migne drops *tuum*] Must we, I ask, believe the prophetic soul to be of so great ambition that he would seek the kingdom of Israel from the Lord, and that not even shame would restrain him from a petition of that kind? But if he could not restrain his tongue from seeking this, why did he not at least forbid his hand to write any such thing? But far be it to suspect any such thing of a soul so holy, and a soul prophetic. But he was assuredly asking of the Lord's mercy such a kingdom, or rule, whence he hoped for the outcome, or the advancement, of his own salvation. [1330B] *Give rule,* he says, *to thy servant, and save the son of thy handmaid.* [var: Vulg. *Da imperium tuum puero tuo*; Migne again drops *tuum*] Ask thou also, therefore, such rule, or kingdom, from the Lord thy God, that on this behalf thou mayest be able to sing: *But I am appointed king by him [n: (Psal. II)]*. For it is a saying true enough: to whomsoever he will he shall give it. For it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy. [var: Vulg. Rom. 9:16 *Igitur non volentis, neque currentis, sed miserentis **est** Dei*; Migne prints *enim* and moves the copula forward, where chunk 0040 prints the same verse at 1323D as *Non enim volentis neque currentis, sed miserentis est Dei*] For if thou hast nothing which thou hast not received, how much more a kingdom?

## CHAPTER XXXII. *That the measure of greatness hangs upon the manner of humility.*

And he shall set, he says, the lowliest man over it. For he resisteth the proud, but to the humble he giveth grace, and assuredly the humbler a man is, the more sublime. [1330C] Without doubt, if we think upon that inward kingdom, thou wilt be in this kingdom the more sublime the humbler thou art, and without ambiguity the greater, the less thou shalt have been in thine own eyes. To whom, I ask, can it be doubtful that in that outward kingdom it often happens far otherwise, or rather contrariwise? But in that inward kingdom the measure of greatness ever hangs upon the measure of humility. Because he will set the humble man in it, and the lowliest over it. He is humble who truly despises himself in his own sight, but he is humbler who does not shrink from being despised also by others. But he is the lowliest who not only despises his own contempt, but even greatly covets it. What, then, I ask, can pride do against him, to whom his own contempt has come into contempt? Since therefore, as [1330D] Scripture testifies, pride is the beginning of all sin [n: (Eccle. X)], what, I ask, can sin do against him, from whom, by the victory over pride, the beginning of all sin is far off? See therefore how strong and how powerful he who is of this kind is found in that kingdom, which is established against sin, which is destroyed or scattered by sin alone. Behold, now from the end of the vision we manifestly gather what we spoke of far above, that the common good and the profit of the universe demanded such a man, perhaps such as is designated in the tree; such a man, I say, who according to the likeness of the tree should fall from a certain sublime state and rise again, so that out of his own ruin he might strike into those who stand a fear of falling, and out of his own repair might reform those who lie prostrate unto the hope of rising again.



## CHAPTER XXXIII. *That it is one thing to discern the divine judgments through contemplation, and another to weigh the reason of them.*

[1331A]

Behold the dream which Nabuchodonosor saw; but he still requires its interpretation, whence also he says: *This dream I, king Nabuchodonosor, saw. Do thou therefore, Balthassar, tell the interpretation in haste, because all the wise men of my kingdom are unable to declare the solution to me. But thou art able, because the spirit of the holy gods is in thee [n: (Dan. IV)]*. [var: Vulg. Dan. 4:15 *Hoc somnium vidi ego Nabuchodonosor rex*; Migne inverts the title to *rex Nabuchodonosor*, and prints *nequeunt* where the Vulgate has *non queunt*] As I have already said in what went before, it is one thing to discern the divine judgments with the eye of perspicacity or of foresight, and another to penetrate and know the reason of them by the judgment of discretion and the liveliness of understanding. The former belongs to the vision of the dream, the latter to the interpretation of the dream. [1331B] To the vision of the dream it belongs to know from divine revelation what must come to pass; but to the interpretation of the dream it belongs to understand the quality of the person to whom this must happen, namely, to weigh the cause which is wont to drive a person of whatever kind to a fall of this sort. This is what Daniel found out by investigating, and opened to the king by interpreting, when he says: Thou art that tree which thou sawest. For what is it to say, thou art, but: I weigh thee to be such a one, I find such a cause in thee, whence I doubt not that some such thing must happen to thee? But wilt thou know yet more openly how, after a vision has been divinely shown, we are wont, nay rather ought, to seek its interpretation? Behold, perhaps someone sees through the light of contemplation how the common profit requires the fall [1331C] and the repair of certain sublime men. He sees how this very thing commends the grace of God, how this very thing forms those who still stand unto wariness, how it repairs the fallen unto hope, how from this the beauty of the universe appears more wonderful; and he holds it certain that it must come to pass, in that the omnipotent goodness neither wills nor ought to hinder the common good. But again he begins to wonder how it can agree with the highest justice, or how it can be just, that some should be permitted to fall even for the profit of the universe. For as he who made all things is debtor to the universe, so he who established each several thing is debtor also to each. And as it is merciful not to hinder the common good, so it must also be [1331D] just that there be always in him who is about to fall some cause on account of which he deservedly ought to lie open to the impending ruin. He therefore who covets to know a cause of this kind, and utterly seeks the reason of the divine judgments, what else does he inquire after than the interpretation of the vision that has been shown? But then he demands an interpretation of this kind as it were from Daniel, when what he cannot obtain by investigation he ceases not to wrest from the Lord by a chief zeal, and one of the highest devotion. This dream, he says, I Nabuchodonosor saw. Do thou therefore, Balthasar, tell the interpretation of it in haste. Thou weighest, as I judge, that the king sees some things by himself, and wrests others from Daniel, because some things are such as occur to the spirit freely and easily, others such as cannot be known without great labour and huge solicitude. In the former [1332A] the spirit is provoked to rise up to greater things; in the latter it is exercised and humbled, lest it presume. But it is intimated that in those things which the king had seen he was not without fear, who requires the interpretation with haste. And we too are admonished to seek with all haste the resolution of that matter wherein a suspicion of danger can strike in fear.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. *That we often acquire by the merit of devotion the cognizance of those things which by no sagacity of ours, by no zeal of ours, are we able to penetrate.*

It is surely to be noted that Daniel is called *Balthassar*, that is, hair of the head, where he is invited to the subtle resolution of sublime things. For among human members, what is more sublime than the head, what more subtle than the hair? [1332B] Rightly, therefore, is he called hair of the head, from whom the subtlety of a sublime understanding is demanded. And the true devotion of the mind is rightly called, from its effect, unless I am mistaken, the hair of the head, because through it the mind is without doubt sharpened unto every subtlety. Through its effect, then, it is itself the hair of the head, it is itself the subtlety of the mind. Let us hear yet what he subjoins to these things: Because all the wise men of my kingdom are unable to declare the solution to me. Who are, I ask, the wise men of that inward kingdom, but the keenest points and the most piercing senses of the human heart? Attend, therefore, what the virtue of devotion is, how rightly it is called the hair of the head, if through it the mind can do what it cannot do through all the wise men of its own kingdom. When therefore the mind seeks in manifold ways what is above its own understanding, and by seeking presses on, by pressing on [1332C] fails, by failing distrusts, what else, I ask, does it now say within itself, silent through distrust, but this which king Nabuchodonosor openly professes? Because all the wise men of my kingdom are unable to declare the solution to me. But since Truth says: *Amen I say to you, whatsoever you ask when praying, believe that you shall receive, and it shall be done unto you [n: (Marc. XI)]*. [var: Vulg. Mark 11:24 *Propterea dico vobis, omnia quaecumque orantes petitis, credite quia accipietis, et evenient vobis*; chunk 0035 prints this same verse at 1311B with *petieritis* where Migne prints *petitis* here] If therefore the mind believes what it hears, if it turns itself to prayer, if through true and inmost devotion it does not distrust that it can obtain what it could not obtain by investigation, what else, I ask, does it assert within itself, through the confidence of hope and the constancy of faith, but that very same thing which the king said to Daniel: But thou art able, he says? And he adds the cause also: Because the spirit of the holy gods is in thee. We know [1332D] that in the Holy Scriptures holy men have been called gods, and by the same reason this can be said of the angels also. Who, then, is the spirit of those gods, but the Holy Spirit? He assuredly it is who intercedes for us with unspeakable groanings. He it is who suggests to us what we should pray. He who teaches how we ought to pray. Without this Spirit our devotion cannot be true; and what it shall have attempted with him and through him cannot go for nothing: But thou, he says, art able, because the spirit of the holy gods is in thee.

But it is to be noted that king Nabuchodonosor did not seek useless and superfluous things through Daniel's office, but such things as it behoved to be known for the wariness of avoiding danger. And that which we ask shall be given to us also, if after his example we seek with faith and out of true devotion [1333A] that which we cannot without danger be ignorant of.



## CHAPTER XXXV. *That the spirit, while it is humbled by much consideration of its own weakness, is often divinely enlightened unto a sublime understanding.*

*Then Daniel, whose name is Balthasar, began to think silently within himself for about one hour, and his thoughts troubled him [n: (Dan. IV)]*. I think that it belongs to Daniel, and that it is the office of true devotion, to return to oneself, to forget outward things and to think upon inward ones, and this chiefly at that time when one must take counsel for his own salvation or another's. One is the time for investigating the things that are above oneself, and another the time for examining the things that are within [1333B] oneself. For all things have their time. There is therefore a time for contemplating the mighty works of God, and there is a time for considering our own weaknesses. The latter is the time of laughing. For in the evening weeping shall abide, and in the morning gladness. Why should there not be a time of laughing in the morning of divine revelation and in the contemplation of the eternal light? Why should there not be a time of weeping in the evening of a dreadful vision, in considering the darkness of the human conscience? It is evening time when before the eyes of the contemplative the light of revealing grace comes forth and turns him into admiration of itself, and often snatches him beyond himself through the height of the mind: *The goings out,* he says, *of the morning, and at evening thou shalt delight [n: (Psal. LXIV)]*. What are those goings out of the morning, but the excesses of the human mind toward the irradiation of the true sun? He says [1333C] therefore that the goings out of the morning delight; why not the evening also, or the goings in of the evening? For in the morning we are wont to go out from inward things to outward, and in the evening to return from outward things to inward. But who may we worthily wonder how sweet it is, or how delightful, when charity is now fervent and as it were under the summer season, to shake oneself out of sleep at the morning light of the radiant Godhead, and to break out beyond the straits of the human mind into the air of liberty, and to pass over by an alienation of the mind into that broad field of the divine spectacles? And so the goings out of the morning delight, but the goings in of the evening sadden, at that time without doubt when the spirit turns back to the consideration of itself: *Unto myself,* he says, *my soul is troubled* [1333D] [n: (Psal. XLI)]. But in the horror of the nightly vision, in the consideration of a dreadful conscience, there is one sure relief of the spirit, namely the memory of one's God; and this is what is added there: Unto myself my soul is troubled, *therefore will I be mindful of thee.* This is what he says elsewhere: *I was mindful of God, and was delighted [n: (Psal. LXXVI)]*. And in this place: *The goings out of the morning, and at evening thou shalt delight.* Thou, he says, shalt delight; not the hour itself, not the goings in themselves of the evening time. For what delight, I ask, could there be in considering that dark abyss of the human heart? For the heart of man is perverse and unsearchable, and who shall know it? This is why, with Daniel, while he thinks long, his own thoughts trouble him within himself. But he who willingly considers his own weaknesses, diligently goes over them again, [1334A] and humbles himself in the consideration of them, while he zealously examines that which he was able to detect in himself by himself, is often enlightened by God even unto that which he could not know by himself. This is why Daniel, while he meditates long and silently within himself, is divinely instructed to foreknow the ruin of the royal power and the cause of that same ruin.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. *On the true devotion of the mind, how it ought to examine itself.*

But he ought to meditate upon his inward things not slightly and as it were in passing, who wishes to be instructed unto a deep and full knowledge of himself, who desires that the things necessary for his own salvation or another's be revealed to him. So Daniel thought within himself for about one hour, and [1334B] obtained the cause which he sought. The hour of investigation is then at last closed with its due end, when that which is sought is now found. And we too, therefore, when the moment of necessity presses, let us be earnest to pray, to seek, to knock, as much as necessity compels, or opportunity allows and the continuance of our zeal has filled up the present hour. But if by Daniel devotion is to be understood, perhaps this will be for Daniel to think within himself: for our devotion to examine itself, to try itself, to inquire within itself how fervent, how frequent, how suppliant it is. It thinks within itself when it weighs the quality, the measure and the intention of its own zeal and exercise. It thinks within itself while it diligently inquires whether this very thing which it rightly intends it presumes not upon [1334C] its own powers, but upon the piety of the Lord alone. And so our devotion, when it often deals with this within itself, detects the vice of arrogance which before lay hidden within it. But without doubt the vice of arrogance, when it has begun to prevail over the mind, is always wont to be the cause of ruin. When therefore devotion has found that this vice has grown to such enormity, it gathers that a coming ruin of the spirit is at hand, and greatly fears it. For it knows that before ruin the heart shall be exalted, and that God resisteth the proud.



## CHAPTER XXXVII. *How devotion sometimes detects the whole state of the inner man, and as much discerns it present as it foresees it future.*

[1334D] *The king answering said: Balthasar, let not the dream and the interpretations thereof trouble thee [n: (Dan. IV)]* [var: Vulg. *interpretatio ejus*, singular, "the interpretation thereof"; the next lemma prints the singular]. That the king forbade Daniel to be troubled, what else is it but that the mind deludes itself, and by an empty hope often takes away a profitable fear? But behold, Daniel does what he willed to be done by us when danger is at hand, and what belongs to true devotion: he turns himself to prayer *Balthasar answered and said: My lord, the dream be to them which hate thee, and the interpretation thereof be to thine enemies.* [var: Vulg. *his qui te oderunt*, masculine, "to them that hate thee", and without *sit*; the re-quotation three lines below prints the masculine] They are malignant spirits who have blazed out against us with an inextinguishable hatred. The vices are the true enemies of the soul, which drive it to eternal destruction. We are taught to imprecate their ruin in that which is said: The dream be to them who hate thee, and the interpretation thereof to thine enemies. When therefore the mind is assailed by the spirit of pride and [1335A] by such kindlers of vices, when it is oppressed by arrogance and vainglory, it ought to flee to prayer, and after Daniel's example to demand their ruin. But when the devotion of the spirit cannot prevail by prayer against arrogance and vainglory, often from that very thing it understands more deeply, and gathers more surely, that the swelling of the spirit could not be healed save by a foul and shameful casting down of itself. And this is what Daniel speaks through a mystery, when he says: *They shall cast thee out from among men, and thy dwelling shall be with beasts and wild beasts.* Let us now hear what he says, and from it let us gather how devotion often detects the whole state of the inner man, and as much describes it present as it foresees it future. Let it say, then, when ruin is now at hand, what [1335B] the spirit meanwhile is by grace, what manner of thing it will be by fault, and let it add last of all the cause of that ruin, or of its own repair. This order, unless I am mistaken, thou wilt find in Daniel's words to the king, if thou examine rightly: *The tree,* he says, *which thou sawest lofty and strong, whose height reacheth unto heaven, and the sight thereof unto all the earth, and its branches most fair, and its fruit exceeding great, and food for all in it, the beasts of the field dwelling under it, and the birds of the air abiding in its branches: thou art the king, who art magnified, and hast grown strong; and thy greatness hath increased, and hath reached unto heaven, and thy power unto the ends of all the earth.* How in these words a certain state of great perfection is described, we have already said above, [1335C] and we ought not to repeat it here.

But note that which is said: The tree which thou sawest, thou art. If by such a tree we must understand a certain great strength of admirable virtue, if by the vision divinely shown we ought to take the revelation of contemplation, what, I ask, will it be to say, thou art the tree which thou sawest, but that thou hast received such grace as thou first sawest through contemplation; and that, having understood through the grace of contemplation what manner of man a man of great perfection ought to be, thou hast deserved of the divine gift to be such and so great a one. In the tree, therefore, is mystically described grace received from God; but in the words that follow is expressed the ruin that comes upon an arrogant soul: *But whereas,* he says, *the king saw a watcher and a holy one [1335D] come down from heaven, and say: Cut down the tree, and scatter it, yet leave the shoot of its roots in the earth, and let it be bound with iron and bronze among the grass without, and let it be sprinkled with the dew of heaven, and let its fodder be with the wild beasts, until seven times be changed over it. This is the interpretation of the sentence of the Most High, which is come upon my lord the king. They shall cast thee out from among men, and thy dwelling shall be with beasts and wild beasts, and thou shalt eat hay like an ox, and shalt be drenched with the dew of heaven. Seven times also shall be changed over thee.* How in these words is expressed the type of a soul falling from a certain lofty state into the depths, is held in what has gone before.

Note that here also, just as above, a thing is first shown by God through contemplation, and afterward to be fulfilled in deed. That the [1336A] king saw belongs to contemplation; that which is added in what follows, they shall cast thee out from among men, belongs to the carrying out of the vision, as if he should say: According to this, that thou hast seen through contemplation that such a ruin from so lofty a state can and is wont to happen, I see a like danger threatening thee, because in thee I find the cause of ruin. But the cause of ruin is hinted in that which is brought in last: Until thou know that the Most High ruleth over the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will. In that he says until thou know, he marks that he had not yet acknowledged this very thing as he ought. But in the words that follow is expressed what manner of man he will at length one day be by grace, and why, or how, he is to be repaired after his ruin. *But whereas he commanded,* he says, *that the shoot of its roots [1336B] should be left, that is, of the tree: thy kingdom shall remain to thee after thou shalt have known that the power is heavenly.* But to hear all these things through Daniel is, through the zeal of our devotion, to detect the enormity of our own arrogance, which is always wont to be the cause of ruin; and, the cause of ruin found and looked through, to incur a most violent fear of falling, yet to hold unshaken a most firm hope of coming to oneself again and of rising again. But how all these things ought to be more fully understood can easily be known from the exposition above.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. *How one ought to fight back against an imminent danger, and how much alms avails, if it be done with a simple intention.*

[1336C] The imminent danger being now known and brought into the midst, Daniel adds in the last place what ought to be done under the moment of so great a necessity, or how the pressing danger ought to be resisted: *Wherefore,* he says, *O king, let my counsel be pleasing to thee, and redeem thou thy sins with alms, and thine iniquities with mercies to the poor; perhaps God will pardon thy beloved ones [n: (Dan. IV)]* [var: Vulg. *delictis tuis*, "thy sins"; Migne prints *dilectis* here and *delictis* at 1337B below]. What, I ask, is more prudent, or what more profitable, than, when danger presses, to flee to the divine protection, and to seek the propitiation of him to whom nothing is impossible? But it is very just that he who in his own necessity seeks support from his superior should show to his inferior the aid he can and ought, so that he who desires mercy for himself may [1336D] willingly spend mercy, that what is written may come to pass: *Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy [n: (Matth. V)]*. Rightly therefore is it said, redeem thy sins with alms, and thine iniquities with mercies to the poor. Perhaps in this twofold clause the sentence is repeated, so that to redeem iniquities and sins is one and the same. Yet we can understand in sins the transgressions of work, and in iniquities the perversities of the will. For that word of the psalm admonishes us that some distinction in these ought, or can, be made: *Thou hast forgiven,* he says, *the impiety of my sin [n: (Psal. XXXI)]*. In alms nonetheless the act of piety is rightly understood, in mercies the affection of piety. And see how rightly a work is expiated by a work, an act by an affection. Redeem thy sins, he says, with alms, [1337A] and thine iniquities with mercies to the poor. Indulgence in outward goods makes men poor, but far more does the want of inward goods render them poor. He is poor who lacks discretion, who has no counsel, who lacks the riches of virtues. But where poverty is, there alms too can be. And by how much the poverty is truer, by so much is the alms greater. It is a great alms to refresh with one's own food flesh that will one day die, but a greater to fatten with the nourishment of its own kind a soul that will live forever. It is an alms to clothe the naked, but a greater to adorn the undisciplined with the discipline of morals. The best kind of alms is to rebuke the restless, to comfort the fainthearted, to be patient toward all. It is a great mercy to suffer together with another's affliction, but a greater to be pricked with compunction for [1337B] another's straying; a noble kind of mercy, to weep for the delinquent, to pardon the penitent, to blot out another's offenses with one's own tears. In these works of mercy we ought to exercise ourselves, who have no outward riches. Perhaps, he says, he will pardon thy offenses. What is it that he says perhaps, and sets it as it were under a doubt, but that not even in these works of mercy can the spirit have full confidence, when, corrupted by the wasting of pride and vainglory, it cannot practice them with a pure and simple intention?



## CHAPTER XXXIX. *How patiently, or mercifully, the long-suffering of God awaits our correction, or how a perverse mind is wont to abuse his patience.*

[1337C] *All these things came upon king Nabuchodonosor [n: (Dan. IV)]*. All things, he says, came upon the king, and upon such a king. All things came, all things can come upon a kingly spirit, and upon such a one as the royal person designates through a mystery: *After the end of twelve months he was walking about in the hall of Babylon. The king answered and said: Is not this the great Babylon, which I have built to be the house of the kingdom, in the strength of my fortitude, and in the glory of my comeliness?* Who, I ask, may suffice worthily to weigh the bowels of the divine pity, in that he does not at once avenge the contempt shown him, but awaits the satisfaction of our correction, and prolongs the times of his propitiation. After the end, he says, of twelve months: in the number twelve the number six is doubled, and in [1337D] six, because of its own perfection, perfection is figured. What then is it, that the divine moderation doubles the six in the delay of its waiting, but that it dispenses the postponement of its vengeance according to the fullness of its justice and of its mercy? For it is a small thing to him to await our correction as much as justice demands, unless he add over and above that which mercy requires, so that his waiting may be as just as it is pious, and as perfect in equity as it is full of piety. But many abuse the kindness of God, and are made worse by that whereby they ought to have been corrected. Behold, while Nabuchodonosor receives the times of making satisfaction given him by God, he swelled the higher by that whereby he ought to have corrected himself. He was walking about in the hall of Babylon. Perhaps true humility, the guardian [1338A] of virtues, is a palace and a most firm dwelling. But such a dwelling belongs to Jerusalem: *Jerusalem,* he says, *which is built as a city, whose participation thereof is in itself [n: (Psal. CXXI)]*. But as true humility belongs to Jerusalem, so feigned humility to Babylon. For what else does feigned humility prepare but disgrace, what else does it look for but confusion? The hall of Babylon, therefore, is feigned humility. The hall of Babylon is a discipline of humiliation without humility. In the hall of Babylon he does not sit, does not lie down, but walks about, whom his own conscience, while it gnaws him, disquiets. He walks about in the hall of Babylon whom his own conscience wearies by accusing him concerning his feigned humility. But to walk about is not to go in one direction, but to wander here and there at random. He therefore walks about whom the goad of conscience drives on from every side.

## CHAPTER XL. *On the type of an arrogant soul, or how it is wont to magnify itself.*

[1338B]

And the king answered and said: What, I ask, is this answering, where no questioning goes before? Was he perhaps answering another's thought, and perhaps a thought which was not at all, but which he believed to be? Perhaps he was answering the thought of those whom he reckoned to be admiring his greatness and authority. But an arrogant spirit has this as its own, that it believes all men to admire its loftiness, which it magnifies within itself at every hour: whence it comes about that before others too it confidently breaks out into words of boasting, and expresses the same thing as Nabuchodonosor, though in other words. [1338C] Let us now consider how high he swelled who broke out into those words which we set down above. Is not this the great Babylon which I have built? Behold ostentation. To be the house of the kingdom; behold ambition. In the strength of my fortitude; behold arrogance. And in the glory of my comeliness; behold vainglory. This is the great Babylon which I have built. We say that Babylon sounds the same as confusion. For a soul that is proud and enters in doubly, to build Babylon is to bend itself to every humility, and, as it were under the pretext of religion, to expose itself to every service and abjection, and to whatsoever things men are wont to blush at, such as mean apparel, lowly bearing, thin food, voluntary servitude. Let him say then: This is the great Babylon, [1338D] a deep humiliation; this is a voluntary casting down, this is a confusion taken by vow, which I have built, which I have resolved to observe. But to what end, to what profit? To be the house, he says, of the kingdom. Does he not seem to thee to build as it were for a house, who acts to obtain authority and the art of mastery, that he may appear to all such and so great a man as ought worthily to be promoted, and preferred to others, and exalted in dignity or even in power? In the strength, he says, of my fortitude. Behold with how great arrogance he has attributed to himself that which wholly hangs upon divine grace. He does not say, in the gift of the divine compassion, but, in the strength of my fortitude. O how otherwise the Truth itself both thought and taught, when it says: *Without me you can do nothing [n: (Joan. XV)]*. But what the wicked mind reckons that it accomplishes by its own fortitude, it consequently twists back [1339A] to its own glory: In the strength, he says, of my fortitude, and in the glory of my comeliness. O how otherwise such a boaster acts than the Apostle enjoined, how otherwise than the Truth our mistress appointed: *He that glorieth,* he says, *let him glory in the Lord [n: (I Cor. II)]*; and that other word: *So let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven [n: (Matth. V)]*. But this man says, in the glory of my comeliness.

## CHAPTER XLI. *How suddenly, often, and how deeply they fall who abuse the patience of God.*

*While the word was yet in the king's mouth, a voice rushed down from heaven: To thee it is said, king Nabuchodonosor: The kingdom has passed [1339B] from thee [n: (Dan. IV)]*. The voice rushed down while the word was yet in his mouth, that is, still under the very time of his glorying. For often a shameless spirit, while it glories beyond measure, in the very act of glorying, its conscience gnawing it, is suddenly dismayed, and by a certain divine nod is shaken with a sudden horror, and by the fear of falling is hurled headlong into the despair of not escaping. A voice rushes down from heaven when that which he perceives with the ear of the heart comes from the inmost senses of the soul. He hears as it were the earth, whatever he draws in through bodily sense. That comes from heaven which he acknowledges through the Spirit. He learns from heaven that which he comprehends intellectually. To thee it is said, Nabuchodonosor: to thee so emptily proud, to thee so emptily glorying. The kingdom has passed from thee, *and they shall cast thee out from among men, and thy dwelling [1339C] shall be with beasts and with wild beasts.* The kingdom passes from any man whatsoever when he loses the grace divinely conferred upon him, by which he was wont to rule over his own desires and passions. They shall cast thee out from among men. By as much as thou hast raised thyself above men through arrogance, by so much shalt thou be cast down beneath men through fault, and thy dwelling shall be with beasts and wild beasts. Cast out from among men, he goes down to beasts and wild beasts and lives there, who, forsaking rational manners, lives thenceforth irrationally, so that, living like a beast and acting like a wild beast, he is with those who live like beasts dissolved into every carnality, and with those who act like wild beasts unbridled into every cruelty. He adds further: *Thou shalt eat hay like an ox.* The ox, when it receives hay, counts it for the highest delights, and seeks nothing [1339D] more sumptuous. Since therefore all flesh is hay, and all its glory as the flower of hay, he eats hay like an ox who places all his joy in temporal glory and in carnal delights, and seeks spiritual delights not at all, neither by zeal nor by desire. Behold into how deep a place he falls who abuses the patience of God. Behold to what end he comes who has received in vain the times for coming to himself again.

## CHAPTER XLII. *That one and the same sentence is foreknown through contemplation, threatened through fear, confirmed through despair.*

*And seven times shall be changed over thee, until thou know that the Most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will [n: (Dan. IV)]*. These things we have already [1340A] expounded above, and we ought not to repeat the same again.

This surely is to be noted, that one and the same thing is repeated rather often, and one and the same sentence of the divine severity is rehearsed a third time. And that I may distinguish it for thee by its own differences: first the spirit, through contemplation and as it were through a vision, acknowledges what is wont to happen; second, through devotion and as it were through Daniel's office, it finds what it must now fear concerning itself; last, broken already by despair at the withdrawal of grace, it plainly detects what it is now unable to avoid. And so one and the same sentence is foreknown through contemplation, threatened through fear, confirmed through despair.



## CHAPTER XLIII. *That without divine protection no one is able to resist his own passions, or malignant suggestions.*

[1340B]

*In the same hour the word was fulfilled upon Nabuchodonosor, he was cast out from among men [n: (Dan. IV)]*. What is in the same hour, but at once, upon the withdrawal of grace, to yield to temptations, and to be unable to resist the malignant spirits that tempt? In the same hour: not that the wickedness conceived goes forth at once into act, since it does not always have the occasion of sinning at hand; but the mind is cast down, and falls, from the moment it consents to sin. It is cast down, and falls, from the moment it seeks an occasion. From this place, as I judge, we can plainly gather that without divine protection no one could resist his own passions, or malignant suggestions, [1340C] even for a little. And so in the same hour he was cast out from among men, *and he ate hay like an ox, and his body was stained with the dew of heaven.* All these things we have already expounded above. But something is added further which we did not read in what went before: *Until his hairs grew after the likeness of eagles', and his claws like the claws of birds.* [var: Vulg. *et ungues eius quasi avium*, "and his nails as birds'"; Migne sets *ungues* twice and drops *ejus*, which the exposition at 1341B restores]

## CHAPTER XLIV. *From how great a summit of virtues it may happen that a man falls into the depths of vices.*

Now hairs are fine and long, and in them deep and exceedingly sharp counsels can rightly be understood. But the body of eagles is covered with a great thickness of feathers. And eagles are wont to see more keenly and to fly more loftily than all other living creatures. [1340D] He therefore has hairs as it were after the likeness of eagles' who is skilled in much prudence, in exceeding great cunning, who in finding out frauds, in weaving deceits, is found now slower than none, inferior to none. But birds of prey, as we all know, rage with their claws; and all birds in common tear and hurt what they seize with their claws. What then is it to have claws like birds', but to hurt whomsoever thou canst prevail against. But if under the type of claws the office of cruelty is rightly understood, is not this very thing expressed above under another figure, where it is said: And thy dwelling shall be with wild beasts. But wild beasts do not go fowling, nor have they anything at all that they may do to birds. Those, therefore, who willingly oppress all worldly and carnal men, and such as brood as it were upon the earth, [1341A] what else do they do but rage against animals after the manner of wild beasts? Are not they rightly to be called animals who serve the belly alone, whose God is the belly, and whose glory is in their confusion? But those who persecute spiritual men, what else do they do but lie in wait for birds after the manner of birds, and rave as it were with their claws? Do they not seem to thee to be birds of heaven who can truly say: But our conversation is in heaven? Are not they to be called birds of heaven who hang themselves aloft on the wing of contemplation? In the former sentence, therefore, we have how they are hostile to carnal men; but in this we have how at length one day they utterly do not spare even spiritual men themselves. Let him say then of such a man, let him say: Until his hairs grew after the likeness of eagles', and his claws [1341B] like the claws of birds, so that he is as ready to circumvent even the circumspect as he is without doubt prone to crush men even conspicuous in virtue. This man is effective in deceiving, this man forward and shameless in persecuting: *Thy mouth,* says the Psalmist, *hath abounded with malice, and thy tongue framed deceits [n: (Psal. XLIX)]*. Behold how he convicts the deceiver. Hear also how he confounds the forward: *They shall hunt after the soul of the just, and shall condemn innocent blood [n: (Psal. XCIII)]*. Do they not rage against the fowls of heaven, and as it were with claws, who hunt after the soul of the just, and condemn the innocent? Or by birds demons can be understood, as we have from the reading of the Gospel [n: (Luc. VIII)]. What then will it be to have claws after [1341C] the likeness of such birds, but to harass any good men whatever by the mere instinct of malignity? Behold, we now have from how high a summit of perfection it may happen that a man of virtues falls into the depths of vices, that a man may learn, in whatever loftiness of sanctity, always to fear the ruin of morals. Call to mind what manner of man he described above from the mystical tree, and at the same time mark to what end he came at length. And of the tree indeed thou readest that the birds of heaven dwelt in its branches, and that all flesh fed upon it. And so it was for the protection of the good, and for the consolation of all. Because the birds of heaven dwelt in it, and all flesh fed upon it. Behold, this same man after all things rages against all with tooth and claw, because his portion also was with the wild beasts, and [1341D] he received claws like birds'.

## CHAPTER XLV. *How meanwhile he who before fell from on high sometimes rises again even to a greater glory.*

What follows gladdens greatly, when after these things it is subjoined: *Therefore after the end of the days I Nabuchodonosor lifted up my eyes to heaven, and my sense was restored to me, and I blessed the Most High, and I praised and glorified him that liveth for ever; for his power is an everlasting power, and his kingdom in generation and unto generation. And all the inhabitants of the earth are reputed as nothing before him [n: (Dan. IV)]*. Behold, he rises again; behold, he returns to his former glory, nay rather to a better, who fell from so lofty a place into so deep a one. Who would not wonder, who would not be astonished? [1342A] Who may suffice worthily to weigh the bowels of the divine piety? Who, I ask, however great a sinner, would not presume upon the divine compassion, and revive unto the hope of pardon? After the end, he says, of the days I lifted up my eyes to heaven. The end of the days is the completion of the divine judgments. If justice, or human judgments, is a light, why not much more the divine judgments? *And he shall bring forth,* he says, *thy justice as the light, and thy judgment as the noonday [n: (Psal. XXXVII)]*. If thy judgment can be a day (nay rather a noonday), how much more the divine judgment? The judgments of God are days, because they are made in the light of truth, in the light of rectitude. For indeed the judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves. The number of such days is ended over any afflicted man when the severity of the divine [1342B] judgments is completed in the striking of him? The end of such days is completed when the punishment of the divine severity is changed into mercy. Nabuchodonosor received the end of these days in his own crushing, when the divine compassion now looked upon him. For if it had not looked upon him, neither indeed would he have lifted his own eyes to heaven. To lift the eyes to heaven is to think upon heavenly and eternal things, and, the care and solicitude of worldly things put away, to have spiritual things alone before the eyes. To look back to heaven, and to have the region of light before the eyes, and to fix the eyes of understanding with the whole intention upon that light of eternity. He had already fixed his eyes there who said: *I thought upon the days of old, and I had the eternal years in mind* [1342C] [n: (Psal. LXXVIII)]. But behold, he who lifted his eyes to heaven received back the sense which he had lost. Mark therefore how profitable it is to lift the eyes to heaven in this manner. I, says Nabuchodonosor, lifted up my eyes to heaven, and my sense was restored to me. And so the sense of the flesh is the animal's own. But the sense of the mind is man's own. The animal's sense is that by which it perceives white and black; but man's own sense is that which discerns between good and evil, true and false. This sense, along with Nabuchodonosor, they have lost, or never had, who call good evil and evil good, putting bitter sweet and sweet bitter, putting darkness light and light darkness. This sense they receive in great part who judge between day and [1342D] day, but more fully they who judge every day. *One,* says the Apostle, *judgeth between day and day, but another judgeth every day [n: (Rom. XIV)]* [var: Vulg. *alius iudicat diem plus inter diem*, "one esteemeth one day above another"; the exposition here and above turns on Migne's *inter diem et diem*]. And so he recovers his own sense who at some time awakens to the judgment of discretion. But his sense is not said to be given, but restored; whence also it is plain that it was first had, but lost. And so the lost sense is then restored to a man when that grace of discretion which he had been wont to have is repaired in him. But he receives his sense while he lifts his eyes, because the spirit, while it thinks upon eternal and heavenly things, awakens to the judgment of discretion. For while it strains vehemently toward heavenly things, it sees how nothing is whatever earthly and transitory thing it loved. He therefore who pants after the grace of discretion, let him strain toward heavenly things, that he may receive the light of his own [1343A] eyes, and, when he has received it, may cry out to his Lord and say: For what have I in heaven, and besides thee what have I desired upon earth? But how not in vain Nabuchodonosor received his own sense, he shows in the words that follow.



## CHAPTER XLVI. *How he glorifies God alone, who was so shamelessly magnifying himself.*

And I blessed, he says, the Most High. Behold, he who above so shamelessly magnified himself now glorifies him alone who, according as the Apostle says, is over all things blessed forever: *And I praised and glorified him that liveth for ever [n: (Rom. IX)]*. Him that liveth for ever: that life, surely, which is himself, for whom to be is nothing other than to live, nor to live [1343B] than to be. For his power is an everlasting power, because what he can do once, he who is almighty can always do. And his kingdom in generation and unto generation, because to him nothing accrues from time, nothing departs, with whom there is no change, nor shadow of alteration. And all the inhabitants of the earth are reputed as nothing before him. By the inhabitants of the earth understand the lovers of earthly things, who know not how to seek the things that are above, nor can say with the Apostle: *But our conversation is in heaven [n: (Philipp. III)]*. But they are truly reputed as nothing who have lost true being, for whom assuredly it were better not to be at all than to be thus, unless someone think it better to be always wretched than not to be at all. For he does according to his own will as much among the powers of heaven as among [1343C] the inhabitants of the earth, and there is none that can resist his hand and say to him: Why hast thou done it? To the same sentence agrees what the Psalmist says: *Whatsoever he would he hath done, in heaven and in earth, in the sea, and in all the deeps [n: (Psal. CXXXIV)]*. Since in what follows the same Nabuchodonosor says in the praise of God that all his works are true and his ways judgments: what is it that here he says that he does all things according to his own will? Surely if all his works are true, all things are done in truth; surely if all his ways are judgments, all things are done in equity: how then according to will? Or is it perhaps that to be done according to equity is to be done according to will, and by the very fact that it is done in equity, by that very fact, I say, it is done according to his will? But if it is [1343D] altogether the same to be done according to equity and to be done according to his will, then his will is the same as equity, and equity the same as will. And there is none that can resist his hand and say, Why hast thou done it? Who should resist him? who gainsay him? since he does all things as powerfully as wisely, since there is no one who could either restrain omnipotence or convict the highest wisdom.

## CHAPTER XLVII. *What proud glorying does, or what devout glorification effects.*

*At that very time my sense returned to me, and I came unto the honor of my kingdom and unto my comeliness, and my figure returned to me [n: (Dan. IV)]*. At that very, he says, time. At that very time in which I blessed God, in that very one in which I [1344A] praised and glorified him. Surely, if we well recall the things said above, he fell there, when he was magnifying himself proudly enough. Behold, this same man rises again when he devoutly glorifies God, and his Lord. Surely thou seest what proud glorying does, surely thou seest what devout glorification effects. Proud glorying deserves a casting down, devout glorification an exaltation. Behold, when he now glories not in himself but in the Lord, his sense returns to himself. What above he called his sense restored to him, he now calls his sense returned to himself; or perhaps a man's sense returns to itself when the eye of discretion is called back to the consideration of itself. The sense returns to itself when it is divinely [1344B] enlightened unto the consideration and knowledge of its own merits. While therefore the human spirit glorifies its God, its sense returns to itself; because while it opens its eyes to that light of the Godhead, and strains vehemently toward it, it more fully acknowledges the darkness of its own weakness: *Come ye to him,* he says, *and be enlightened [n: (Psal. XXXIII)]*. What wonder if by drawing near to the light we are enlightened? what wonder if from light a light is kindled? *And in thy light,* he says, *we shall see light [n: (Psal. XXXV)]*. Light is seen in light when, from the knowledge and working of the divine brightness, the spirit is more fully enlightened unto the knowledge of human weakness. Yet this twofold knowledge is wont to minister alternate increases to itself, and each assuredly to grow out of the other. For from the knowledge of God the spirit advances to the thought of itself, and in the same way [1344C] from much knowledge of itself it grows to the knowledge of God. But behold, while the sense which had been lost returns, he received back his kingdom which he had lost. Without doubt, unless the grace of discretion be repaired in him, the spirit is never brought through to the full integrity of virtue.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. *How through the discretion of judgment, or through circumspection of oneself, the discipline of morals is wont to be reformed.*

I came, he says, unto the honor of my kingdom and unto my comeliness. It is assuredly plain that man's free will receives and holds a kingdom from God, when it can now restrain the evil motions of the heart from evil. But this kingdom is then made honorable when, by [1344D] God's gift, it can now exercise the good motions of the heart in good. And that same kingdom is overlaid with a worthy comeliness when whatever good is done in it is ordered with the highest moderation and with great discretion. And so he receives and obtains a kingdom who bravely tames and manfully restrains the rebellious motions of the spirit. And at that time he who is such shall judge among the nations, shall fill up ruins, shall crush the heads in the land of many. And he has then an honorable kingdom too, when he is now made Lord of hosts in so great a multitude of virtues so innumerable, and, having soldiers under him, says to this one, Go, and he goes, and to another, Come, and he comes, and to his servant, Do this, and he does it. This kingdom is made comely thereby, and most of all when, bearing himself modestly, he moderates all things with meekness [1345A] and tranquillity: *Son,* he says, *do thy works in meekness, and thou shalt be loved above the glory of men [n: (Eccle. XIII)]* [var: Vulg. *in mansuetudine opera tua perfice*, "perfect thy works in meekness"]. And so the honor of the kingdom is to act powerfully, the comeliness of the kingdom to act wisely, so that in that his kingdom he who is the possessor of the kingdom may reach from end to end mightily and order all things sweetly. And my figure returned to me. Figure is an outward quality, namely the exterior form of the body. But bodily discipline belongs to the outward quality, as the composure of the mind to the inward quality. In the figure, therefore, which consists in bodily lineaments, there is rightly understood the discipline of the body, the form of religion, the habit and composure of the outer man. And so the figure returns when, according to the former custom, the form of religion lost for a time [1345B] is reformed. The sense having returned, the figure returns, because through the discretion of judgment and through circumspection of oneself the discipline of morals is either newly established or the old renewed.



## CHAPTER XLIX. *How a cast-down mind ought to examine itself, and to renew itself unto its former fervour.*

Nabuchodonosor still adds and says: *And my nobles, and my magistrates sought me, and I was restored unto my kingdom, and a greater magnificence was added to me [n: (Dan. IV)]*. Behold by whom he is sought, and into his kingdom restored. And my nobles and my magistrates. What is best in a man but good intentions? And who ought to exercise mastery, [1345C] or to dispose that inward kingdom, but discreet deliberations? In the nobles, therefore, the mind's intentions. But in the magistrates we understand the mind's deliberations. And what is it for nobles and magistrates of this sort to seek the lost head of the kingdom, and to restore him unto his own place, but with the utmost intention and deliberation to investigate how, after the ruin, even late, one may be able to reform the lost vigour of the spirit unto its first integrity? But the soul ought sometimes diligently to inquire what sort of thing of this kind it was, how constantly it acted, how much of perfection it obtained. And it ought consequently to deliberate how it may be restored unto its former state; and this will be, as I judge, to seek that royal dignity of the spirit by intention, and to be willing to restore it [1345D] unto its own step. They were seeking this royal dignity in another's heart, and desiring it to be restored unto its own place, because they thought it cast down, who said: *Where is thy fear, and thy fortitude, thy patience, and the perfection of ways? [n: (Job IV.)]* [var: Vulg. *timor tuus, fortitudo tua … perfectio viarum tuarum*, "the perfection of thy ways"] But not only they who fall headlong into evil, but also they who grow lukewarm from good, ought to examine themselves, and to renew in themselves that former fervour of religion. Hence it is that it is written to the angel of Ephesus in the Apocalypse: *I have somewhat against thee, that thou hast left the first charity. Remember from whence thou art fallen, and do penance, and do the first works [n: (Apoc. II)]*. [var: Vulg. *Sed habeo adversum te, quod caritatem tuam primam reliquisti. Memor esto itaque unde excideris*, "But I have against thee, that thou hast left thy first charity. Be mindful therefore"]

Yet it is soundly to be noted that this king is said to have been sought by his own men, but not to have been restored by the same. But who, I ask, restored him, save he unto whom he lifted up his eyes, [1346A] whom he blessed, whom he glorified? For even if it now perhaps lies within our power to seek by deliberation the state of our mind, of what sort it now is, or once was, yet it does not equally lie within our power to repair at will the declines of our virtue. But if we zealously carry out that which we have already received of the divine gift the power to do, perhaps that also will be added over which we have not yet been able to do. And I was restored, he says, unto my kingdom, and a greater magnificence was added to me.

## CHAPTER L. *How from the virtue of humility the spirit is strengthened in good, and made solid unto perseverance in good.*

A greater magnificence is added after the ruin, unto full reparation, because out of his very fall a man [1346B] is often instructed unto true humility. And then is magnificence truly enlarged, when among the great things of the virtues the virtue of humility also is unmovably kept. But from the virtue of humility the spirit's advance is both strengthened in good, and made solid unto perseverance in good. It stands, therefore, that magnificence is then truly enlarged, when unto the consummation of the good the grace of persevering is given also. The amplification of magnificence, therefore, is the virtue of perseverance. The amplification of greatness, from the virtue of humility adjoined, is divinely the grace of confirmation. This amplification of magnificence the Prophet was asking, when in psalmody he prayed: *Restore unto me the joy of thy salvation, and strengthen me with a principal spirit [n: (Psal. L)]*. An amplification of this kind we ask daily, [1346C] when we say: *Confirm, O God, this which thou hast wrought in us [n: (Psal. LXVII)]*. Thou weighest from these things, as I judge, that many fall, by God's dispensing, unto this end, that they may rise again the stronger; and they who before, prior to the fall, had only the assisting grace, after the reparation of the ruin receive at the same time the confirming grace also. Truly, according to that which is written: *The Lord killeth and maketh alive, he bringeth down unto hell and bringeth back [n: (I Reg. II)]*. Truly it is he who humbles and lifts up, he who strikes that he may heal [n: (Job V)].

## CHAPTER LI. *How, or with what profit, one ought to praise God.*

*Now I Nabuchodonosor praise and magnify and glorify the King of heaven, because all his works are true, and [1346D] his ways, judgments, and them that walk in pride he is able to humble [n: (Dan. IV)]*. [var: Vulg. *Nunc igitur ego*, "Now therefore I"] Above, as we have already heard, he blessed, praised and magnified. Here again he praises, magnifies and glorifies. Above he praised when he received his sense, and because he was not ungrateful for the divine benefits, he merited to be advanced unto greater things. For he received the lost kingdom with an amplification of magnificence. But the kingdom once received, he praises again, magnifies again. Whence also it came about that he should not again ignominiously lose what he both received when humbled and now possessed with devotion. When a benefit has been received, praise thou also, that thou mayest merit to advance unto greater things; and when promoted unto loftier things, praise none the less, that thou mayest merit to persevere in them. If after the likeness of Nabuchodonosor thou hast received thy sense, if thou hast been able to understand the things [1347A] that are to be done, praise, glorify, that what thou hast received of revealing grace, to be able to understand, may be given thee of the grace that breathes upon thee, to be able to fulfil. If after the likeness of the same Nabuchodonosor thou hast received thy kingdom, if thou hast been able to have dominion over thy passions, if thou hast received the power to exercise good affections in good, praise, magnify, glorify, that thou who hast received the grace of advancing mayest equally receive the grace of persevering also. Gladly, therefore, praise him who is supremely good, glorify him who is supremely blessed, magnify him who is immeasurable in majesty, infinite in eternity. Because all his works are true and his ways judgments. His works are his ways. Ways, I say, by which he comes unto us; ways by which he presses himself upon our understanding and makes himself known. For from his works we advance unto the knowledge [1347B] of him. All his works, therefore, because all his ways are judgments; and all his things are true, because done in truth. We often err in our judgments, whence it often comes about that we absolve the guilty and condemn the innocent. But without doubt he from whom nothing can lie hidden cannot err in his judgment. But since it is written: *All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth [n: (Psal. XXIV)]*, are those things also judgments which are done by him mercifully? But without any contradiction that divine goodness, in all the things which it mercifully bestows, forsakes not the bounds of equity. [1348A] We, when we are moved with pity, often transgress the limits of equity, and often in that very thing wherein we believe ourselves to be bestowing mercy, we act against justice. But the supernal goodness so dispenses the works of its mercy that in all these it does nothing against justice, commits nothing unjust.
