His ways therefore are judgments, because they depart not from the tenor of equity and the rectitude of justice, and them that walk in pride he is able to humble. What, I ask, does he say that this alone he is able to do, of whom it truly stands that he is able to do all things? But because one must believe him who has had the experience, perhaps he wished to express that thing more especially which he, a third, proved in his own self by his own trial. Beforehand, perhaps, he wished to impress upon our senses before all things that which it is most expedient to retain in memory? [1348B] But we know that pride is the beginning of all sin [n: (Eccle. X)]. We know that before ruin the heart shall be exalted [n: (Prov. XVI)]. [var: Vulg. *ante ruinam exaltatur spiritus*, "the spirit is exalted"] He therefore who fears the ruin of morals ought before all things to be watchful against pride. But it avails most for the crushing of pride, and for the keeping of true humility, always to retain in the spirit that he who is wont to resist the proud is able, when he will, to humble them that walk in pride. This Nabuchodonosor taught them by word, this he taught us by example: that howsoever or whensoever he will, he is able to humble them that walk in pride.

## BOOK THREE.





## CHAPTER ONE. *Of the threefold vice of mutability, and of the inconstancy of the mind.*

[1347C]

*I saw in my vision by night, and behold, the four winds of heaven strove upon the great sea. And four great beasts came up out of the sea, diverse one from another. The first was like a lioness, and had the wings of an eagle. I beheld till its wings were plucked off, and it was lifted up from the earth. And it stood upon its feet as a man, and its heart was given to it [n: (Dan. VII)]*. [var: Vulg. *cor hominis*, "a man's heart"] Let us now see what this great sea is, in which the prophet Daniel saw this battle of the winds, whatever it be. But who knows not how unstable and restless the sea is, which is ever moved at every state and impulse of the winds? Rightly therefore, if I mistake not, is the mutability and inconstancy of the heart figured in it, in that [1347D] it is truly like a wave of the sea, which is moved and carried about by the wind. But this evil is threefold. For there is a mutability of purpose, and there is a mutability of promise, and likewise a mutability of vow. A purpose is what each man determines with himself; a promise is what each man determines with his neighbour; a vow is what each man determines, but as it were with God. Of the mutability of purpose is that saying: *The sluggard willeth and willeth not [n: (Prov. XIII)]*. Hear also how the mutability of promise is reproved in that which is said: *Clouds and wind, and rains not following, a boastful man, and not fulfilling his promises [n: (Prov. XXIII)]*. He wished us to beware [1348C] of the mutability of vow who says: *If thou hast vowed anything to God, defer not to pay it; for an unfaithful and foolish promise displeaseth God [n: (Eccle. III)]*. A foolish promise is one that is made concerning that which it is not lawful to do, or which God forbids to be done. A foolish promise is concerning that which it is not expedient to do, in this, that a man either exceeds the bounds of modesty, or presumes something against obedience. Of such vows the Scripture says that the vows of fools are to be broken. Yet they who have bound themselves by such a vow ought not to break a bond of that kind at their own pleasure, but are to be absolved at the judgment of those who have received and have the power of binding and loosing. An unfaithful promise is one which repentance follows, or which duplicity of heart accompanies. It is good, therefore, to vow good things, and to vow them well, lest the promise be [1348D] foolish. It is good also fully to discharge what has been well promised, lest the promise be faithless: *Vow ye,* he says, *and pay to the Lord your God, ye that round about him bring presents [n: (Psal. CLXXV)]*. [var: Vulg. *omnes qui in circuitu ejus*, "all ye that round about him"] *Otherwise it is better not to vow, than not to pay the vows [n: (Eccle. V)]*. [var: Vulg. *Multoque melius est non vovere, quam post votum promissa non reddere*, "And much better is it not to vow, than after a vow not to perform what is promised"] In mutability of purpose is noted the vice of an inconstant spirit. In mutability of promise, the scandal of one's neighbour. In mutability of vow, the contempt and the wrong of God. Evil, therefore, is the first mutability, but worse the second, and the third the worst of all. O how bitter beyond the rest is this last evil, how fearful, how troubled it renders the human conscience! [1349A] This is that stormy water of the sea, restless through fearfulness, and salt through bitterness. This is that which we seek, the great sea, in comparison whereof none of the rest is reckoned anything. We hold the sea; it remains now to inquire concerning the winds, and the battle of the winds. But what is this battle of the winds, but the strong impulse and vehemence of temptations. For human life upon earth is a temptation. Whence also it is rightly enjoined, or admonished: *Son, when thou comest to the service of God, stand in fear, and prepare thy soul for temptation [n: (Eccle. II)]*. [var: Vulg. *sta in justitia et timore*, "stand in justice and in fear"] But the diversity of the winds of heaven is the contrary affections of the spirit. For concupiscence breathes in one way, and wrathfulness blows in another. And in one way and another, confidence, or diffidence. But who does not recognize by experience [1349B] how concupiscence breathes and pants, how vehemently it shakes the spirit, how strongly it bends it toward that which it desires? *For every man is tempted, being drawn away and allured by his own concupiscence [n: (Jac. I)]*. But often, amid the strong heats and violent impulses of concupiscence, the spirit returns unto itself, and confutes, and sharply rebukes. It is angry with itself, it is indignant with itself, and wrathfulness, blowing from the opposite quarter, strongly resists and struggles against the blasts of concupiscence. These blasts of wrathfulness, and these recoils, he wished to come about, who said? *Be ye angry, and sin not [n: (Psal. IV)]*. In this manner, therefore, the blasts of concupiscence and of wrathfulness; often clash one with the other, and rise up each against the other. A conflict of alternating blasts of this kind each one of us [1349C] is wont to experience, and must endure, so long as the flesh lusteth against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. For although concupiscence may seem at some time to rest, at least for a little, it begins again and again to rise up, and to assail more vehemently. *It was silent,* says the Scripture, *the land of Juda, for a few days [n: (I Mach. VII)]*. If the earth, and the land of Juda, can scarcely keep silence for a few days, how much more the sea? For what by the sea, but an unstable heart. and what by the earth (a solid element, that is to say, and an immovable body) do we more rightly understand than a heart firm and stable. If therefore a stable heart rarely rests, and that for a few days, what wonder if a heart restless and slippery, and such in short as is designated [1349D] by the great sea, what wonder, I say, if it is rarely silent, and scarcely for a few moments? That wind, therefore, vehemently burning (concupiscence, that is to say, breathing and boiling), after a momentary quiet often rises the more violent, and drives more strongly than is its wont, and well-nigh overturns the state of the mind, so far that the spirit now begins to grow weary and almost to fail, and to despair of perseverance, and to fall into diffidence. When therefore the wind of diffidence blows, it often befalls that the spirit is more miserably endangered than it could be by any impulses of concupiscence. For it is greatly to be feared lest that vehement wind rush suddenly from the region of the desert, and, shaking the house of conscience, overturn the whole state of the mind. For who shall stand before the face of its cold? Unless perhaps, as is wont to happen, by God's breathing [1350A] contrary blasts rise up from the opposite quarter. For it often comes about that, after much trembling of diffidence and exceeding weariness, the spirit at length at some time returns unto conscience, runs back unto the divine mercy, casts its care upon the Lord, repairs its constancy, and scarcely and late resumes its confidence. From thenceforth confidence and diffidence begin mutually to rebel, and strongly to assail, and to drive with adverse blasts, and by alternate turns, now this, now that, to have the upper hand. This is that battle of the winds, if I mistake not, which the prophet Daniel saw and described in mystical speech, and of what sort it is, experience itself has perhaps taught some of you. And would that I knew and were able to describe it as profitably as it truly stands that I have proved by [1350B] experience of what kind it is. But let us see what is sometimes wont to follow this battle of the winds. Let us see what monsters that great sea, of which we spoke above, chances to bring forth.

## CHAPTER II. *What sort, or how great, a conflict of temptation arises out of the inconstancy of the mind.*

Four great beasts, he says, came up out of the sea, diverse one from another. What, I ask, is it for beasts to come up out of the sea after the battle of the winds, but for bestial motions and irrational impulses, after the violence of temptations, to rise up out of the instability of the heart and to break forth into the open? For he puts on as it were a bestial form who lives bestially. For without doubt, he who passes his life irrationally and bestially, [1350C] in so far as irrationally, so far bestially. What are any vices whatsoever, but certain beasts? What are any depraved desires whatsoever, but beasts? Beasts of this kind tear morals, cut the throat of virtues, choke souls. The onslaughts of such beasts the Psalmist feared, when in psalmody he prayed and in praying sang: *Deliver not up unto the beasts the souls that confess to thee [n: (Psal. LXXIII)]*. There are beasts which kill the body, but have nothing that they can do to the soul. Yet to holy men such as these are not greatly to be feared, and least of all to those who by a spontaneous nod are mortified all the day long, lest they seem to incur that prophetic reproach: *There they trembled for fear, where there was no fear. Do not deliver,* he says, *unto the beast the souls that confess [1350D] to thee [n: (Psal. XIII)]*. [var: Vulg. *trepidaverunt*, "they feared"; and at Psal. LXXIII, printed a few lines above, *Ne tradas bestiis*, "deliver not up unto the beasts", plural] He says not the body of them that confess to thee, he says not the flesh of them that confess to thee, but deliver not up unto the beasts the souls that confess to thee. Those, those beasts assuredly are truly to be feared, which are able to kill souls. The onslaughts of such beasts we quickly run into, when, our deserts requiring it, we lose the light of divine illumination: *Thou hast appointed,* he says, *darkness, and it was night: in it shall all the beasts of the wood go about [n: (Psal. CIII)]*. The onslaughts of such beasts the Lord threatens against them that presume upon themselves and glory in their own merits, when in the canticle of Deuteronomy he speaks by the Prophet: *I will send the teeth of beasts upon them [n: (Deut. XXXVIII)]*. But it now remains to inquire why these beasts are said to be four only, or how they are diverse one from another.



## CHAPTER III. *That the manner of living bestially is fourfold.*

[1351A]

That I may briefly say what I think, every manner of living bestially seems to me to be fourfold. Some seem to practise good things, but without mode and measure and apart from all discretion. And although in them there be perhaps a good intention, this in them is bestial, that they live without measure, and are carried headlong, without the judgment of reason and apart from counsel. And although they may perchance have a zeal of rectitude, yet they have it not according to learning. Others, however, practise evil things, but timidly indeed, and therefore secretly; and for that reason, according to the voice of the Psalmist, they will dwell, and will hide themselves [n: (Psal. LV)], because they fear to be reproved, or blush to be caught. Others again practise good things in work, [1351B] but by hypocrisy indeed, and without any good intention, as loving the first couches at feasts, and the first chairs in the synagogues, and salutations in the market place, and to be called Rabbi by men. Others again practise evil things everywhere, openly, and freely, and without any fear and shame, so that they seem to be without a forehead, because a harlot's forehead has been made theirs, and they know not how to blush. Thou seest therefore how diverse among themselves are workmen of this kind. The first and the third exercise themselves in good things, the second and the fourth in evil. The first and the third do good things, but not well: for the first indiscreetly, the third in simulation, and by that very thing they are diverse one from the other. In evil things both the second and the fourth exercise themselves. But those secretly, these as openly as shamelessly, and therefore are they themselves diverse among themselves. The first are they who walk [1351C] in great things and in wonderful things beneath themselves [n: (Psal. CXXX)]. [var: Vulg. *neque ambulavi in magnis, neque in mirabilibus super me*, "nor have I walked in great matters, nor in wonderful things above me"] The second are they who sit in ambush with the rich in secret places, that they may kill the innocent [n: (Psal. X)]. The third are they who do all their works that they may be seen of men [n: (Matth. XXIII)]. But the fourth, they who neither fear God nor reverence men [n: (Luc. XVIII)]. In the first, therefore, there is an indiscreet religion; in the second, a hidden transgression; in the third, a feigned religion; in the fourth, a manifest transgression. These are the four states of them who live irrationally and bestially (if indeed they are to be called states, and not rather falls), which ever drive a man from evil to worse.

And it is to be noted that in these four steps of corruptions the second is worse than the first, the third than the second, and the fourth is the worst of all. [1351D] And perhaps some may doubt of the third, how it is worse than the second. But in the third state, what else is there than a dissembled equity? But, on Augustine's testimony, we have learned that a dissembled equity is not equity, but a double iniquity.

## CHAPTER IV. *By what steps of corruption the human spirit is often wont to fall.*

In the first state, therefore, there is a foolish justice; in the second, an uncurbed malice; in the third, a feigned justice; in the fourth, an unbridled malice. In the first reigns singularity, in the second impiety, in the third craftiness, in the fourth cruelty. In the first, I say, reigns singularity, and of it is said: *Woe to him that is alone, for when he shall fall he hath none [1352A] to lift him up [n: (Eccle. IV)]*. Woe, I say, to him that is alone, that is, to him who presumes upon himself alone and upon his own counsel, and lives by a certain solitary presumption. In the second reigns impiety, and of it is said: *Woe to the wicked unto evil [n: (Isa. III)]*. In the third reigns craftiness. And the crafty provoke the wrath of God, and of them is said: *Woe to the double heart, and to him that goeth on the earth two ways [n: (Eccle. II)]*. In the fourth reigns cruelty, and to the cruel it is said: *Woe to thee that spoilest, shalt not thou thyself also be spoiled [n: (Isai. XXXIII)]*. Cruelty is rapine; rapine is when a man takes away another's goods. What seems to thee of him who sows discord among brethren? Impiously indeed he deals with thee who takes away thy money; what of him who takes away thy peace? Does he act cruelly who takes away thy garment, [1352B] and not much more he who takes away thy charity? But if it is cruel to take from a man outward goods, goods that shall perish, much more cruel will it be to take from a man inward goods, goods that shall abide unto eternity: *For it is charity that never falleth away [n: (II Cor. XIII)]*. Without doubt, he who takes charity from a man takes God also away: *Because God is charity [n: (I Joan. IV)]*. Woe to thee that spoilest, shalt not thou be spoiled? As much as thou takest, so much dost thou lose; thou takest God away, and thou losest God. Thou takest heaven away, thou forfeitest heaven. What is crueller than this impiety? What is madder than this cruelty? Behold from whence and whither one comes; behold none the less also by what way one goes down: from whence, sayest thou, and whither? From the height of singularity, unto the height of cruelty. But by what way, sayest thou, and how? Through impiety and duplicity. For from the first [1352C] step one goes down to the second, from the second to the third, from the third to the fourth. For without doubt presumption cast down is wont to bring in emulation; emulation despised, simulation; simulation cast down, the unbridling of the mind. For to the first state belongs presumption, to the second emulation, to the third simulation, to the fourth the unbridling of the mind. To the first, insolence; to the second, enviousness; to the third, fraudulence; to the fourth, shamelessness; and perhaps these are those beasts which we had to seek.

## CHAPTER V. *Of the vice of insolence.*

In the description, therefore, of the first beast we understand [1352D] the vice of insolence. We say *insolitum*, as it were *non solitum*, "not customary", or "contrary to the customary", and thence we suppose *insolentia*, insolence, to be so named. Rightly therefore is it called insolence, when at random and rashly something is presumed beyond the customary. Insolence, therefore, is a headlong vice, and a rash presumption, or a headlong and presumptuous rashness, beyond the customary. But this evil is manifold. For insolence now raises itself above the customary, now restrains itself below the customary, now sets itself against the customary. But let us now see concerning the first beast, of what sort Holy Scripture describes it, or how fittingly it expresses the property of insolence. The first, he says, was like a lioness, and had the wings of an eagle. The lion is said to be of such fierceness that, when provoked, he fears not even death, so far that not even for the peril of death [1353A] does he restrain himself from the impulse of his own fury. *The lion,* he says, *the strongest of beasts, will be afraid at the meeting of none [n: (Prov. XXX)]*. Thou seest in the lion how foolish a boldness, and how bold a folly. Does it not seem a matter of lion-like boldness, and done to make oneself a name, to walk in great things and in wonderful things above oneself, to presume all things beyond one's strength, the counsel of teachers being spurned and the precept of elders contemned, to stretch fasts, vigils and observances of this kind beyond measure, and neither to spare the health of the body, nor to shudder at the death of the soul in the contempt of due obedience?

Note that it is likened not to a lion, but to a lioness, because this sex is found more forward and more obstinate in the vehemence of its impulse. See therefore how irrational and bestial and truly lion-like a thing it is to rest in no man's counsel, [1353B] in no man's precept, but obstinately to persist in the boldness of one's own rashness. Do ye wish to hear this also briefly, what I think of the wings of a beast of this kind? It seems to me that the one is of precipitancy, the other of presumption. Behold, two wings, and both of the eagle. Who knows not this of the eagle, that it is wont to fly more swiftly, or more loftily, than almost all other birds. In precipitancy mark the swiftness of the flight. In presumption weigh the loftiness of the flight. It has been said already above that insolence is a headlong and presumptuous rashness, beyond the customary. That I may therefore gird up into a compendious brevity the things said more diffusely, recognize the lion-like likeness in the rashness of singularity. Note in the eagle's wings the vice of presumption [1353C] and the vice of precipitancy. The eagle is called the king of birds, and the lion the king of beasts. Does not he therefore seem to have something of the lioness and something of the eagle, who presumes, in the active life as in the contemplative, to go before all men, and in both lives to hold a singular and highest place? On earth he is a lioness, in heaven he is an eagle, who presumes to walk more strongly than all others, to fly more loftily; to walk by action, to fly by contemplation.



## CHAPTER VI. *By what steps of insolence the human spirit is little by little corrupted.*

But let us now see what Solomon thinks of a man of this kind, who does all things precipitately and presumptuously, who in his endeavours keeps neither measure [1353D] nor modesty: *He that is hasty,* he says, *stumbleth with his feet [n: (Prov. XIX)]*. Hence it is that elsewhere he says: *The inheritance which is hastened to in the beginning, in the end shall want a blessing [n: (Prov. XX)]*. To the same sentence there seems to accord that which is added concerning the aforesaid beast: I beheld till its wings were plucked off, and it was lifted up from the earth and stood upon its feet as a man, and its heart was given to it. [var: Vulg. *cor hominis*, "a man's heart"] Behold how they who presume upon themselves beyond measure lose by degrees that whereby they swell and despise the rest. First the wings are plucked off, afterwards the body itself of the beast is lifted up from the earth; first the grace of the contemplative life, afterwards that of the active life also is lost. For what is it to lose one's wings, but to lose those lofty [1354A] flights of contemplating? For when, after many excesses of fastings and vigils, the body has begun to waste away and the head to ache, willy-nilly one must lay down the wings, return to the earth, and take care of the flesh; and it is better that they be laid down willingly than plucked off from one unwilling. What is it for the wings to be plucked off, but to lose them with huge grief, and without any hope of recovering them? The wings are plucked off when the boldness of precipitancy and of presumption is cut short, infirmity urging, necessity compelling. Does not the Lord threaten a plucking off of wings of this kind, when he speaks by the prophet: *If thou be exalted as an eagle, and set thy nest among the stars of heaven, thence will I draw thee, saith the Lord [n: (Abd. I)]*. [var: Vulg. *et si inter sidera posueris … inde detraham te*, "and if thou set thy nest among the stars, thence will I draw thee down"] After the plucking off of the wings it is lifted up from the earth; through the mind's elevation, therefore, and because of the mind's elation, [1354B] it is shaken off from the earth. And deservedly, as I believe, in that by pride, swelling, bursting, wasting, rotting, they yet at some time become as the dust which the wind driveth from the face of the earth. And so, after the loss of the wings, the habitation of the earth also is lost, because after the grace of contemplation has been withdrawn, as has been said, the grace of working well also is withdrawn from the proud soul. And he who before presumed to go strongly before all, let him now begin to follow after all, and at last to be left behind. And he who before through insolence stretched himself beyond the customary, afterwards remains short of the customary; and thus he now falls from the first step of insolence into the second, with this at last to come, which I fear, that from the second he fall back into the third. But where, I ask, will the beast already spoken of be henceforth, cast down from heaven, the others [1354C] having been lost, and lifted up from the earth? Will it perhaps return thither whence it came, and go down again into the sea, it that came up out of the sea? So indeed, so often what is presumed out of the levity of the heart, afterwards into a great fluctuation of the mind in bitterness. And this perhaps is to lose the earth: to lose all the stability of one's purpose, and, by bearing one's dejection unworthily, to run into an exceeding bitterness of heart. Thus from the earth one passes into the sea; thus are the mountains carried into the heart of the sea. For what is it for mountains to pass into the heart of the sea, but to fall from the summit of a great endeavour into the inmost malice of the heart? For according to the testimony of the Truth, iniquity abounding, the charity of many shall grow cold [n: (Matth. XXIV)]. No one therefore, in however great a [1354D] loftiness of virtues, ought to presume anything of his own powers, but all of the Lord, and to sing with the Psalmist: *Therefore we will not fear when the earth shall be troubled, and the mountains shall be carried into the heart of the sea [n: (Psal. XXV)]*. Then indeed are the mountains carried away, when that saying of John is fulfilled: *They went out from us, but they were not of us [n: (I Joan. II)]*.

## CHAPTER VII. *How from the vice of insolence a man falls into the vice of enviousness.*

But if no place now remains to this beast except the sea (for it seems to have lost both heaven and earth), it is a wonder how it is said to have stood upon its feet. Or is it perhaps believed to have stood upon some crag or rock, where it might be girt about on every side by the sea, and unceasingly [1355A] beaten by the waves of the sea? O how hard a punishment, but worthy of presumptuous singularity! Behold, it which before presumed to outrun all, and out of its own presumption wearied them, now has not whither to go, nor finds how it may rest. And upon its feet, he says, it stood as a man. And would that even late it might cease to believe itself an angel, and at length at some time leave off presuming above man. Behold, now putting off the angel, it no longer flies in the highest, but walks in the lowest; nay, now it walks not, but stands, having lost the love and the hope of advancing. Yet it lies not down, but stands, so that it never rests. Continually therefore it stands, because without intermission it labours. It wearies its feet without going forward, it labours without fruit. It stands therefore, but how? Upon its feet, as a man. A grand spectacle, but a foul [1355B] wonder, to see a four-footed beast, a lion-like shape at that, raise itself upon two feet against heaven, and stand upright against nature. What is this monstrous uprearing, but a certain enormous and exceedingly detestable pride? He rears himself against God who swells against the supercelestial majesty. Does he not swell against God who reproves his judgments? But who knows not how presumptuous minds are wont to murmur against the divine scourges, to envy the advances of others, and impatiently to bear the declines of their own glory? But they murmur not only against the justice of God, but even against the goodness of God. Against the justice of God in their own evils, against the goodness of God in the goods of others. For an insolent spirit, and one greedy of its own excellence, when [1355C] through excessive pride it falls into envy, bears almost more grievously the advance of others than its own defect. O monstrous presumption, which murmurs against the divine majesty for this, that God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace to the humble [n: (Luc. IV)]. *Is thy eye,* he says, *evil, because I am good? [n: (Matth. XX.)]* But they who are of this kind are wont to weave certain complaints as though reasonable, and to display the causes of their murmuring (though in truth they are irrational) as though just; and this perhaps is for the brutish shape to raise itself unto the likeness of a man, to be willing to put forward as it were certain reasons in an irrational murmuring against God. To this sentence there seems to accord what is further said of [1355D] this beast. For when it had been premised, it stood upon its feet as a man, straightway there is added, and its heart was given to it. Whose, its? Either the heart of a man, or the heart of the lioness. But why should the lioness be said to have received its heart, which it is not said to have lost? It received the heart of a man, and of one savouring carnally, when, God permitting, it fell into the prudence of the flesh; or else it then truly receives the heart of a man when through much experience it understands its own error, and more fully recognizes both its own defect and the advance of others. But what is divinely granted to a man for his own good, the man himself often abuses to his own evil. And when his own merits and those of others are known to be unequal, from that whereby he ought to be pricked unto penitence, thence he grows unto a greater envy. For behold, after the lioness described [1356A] received the heart of a man, there succeeds it not a lamb, but a bear [sic: *ut sus*]. For often a heart greedy of glory and livid, when the glory of others and its own ignominy have been looked upon, falls into enviousness. Thus vice succeeds vice: insolence goes before, and enviousness follows; and what is yet worse, insolence does not withdraw.



## CHAPTER VIII. *Of the vice of enviousness.*

Enviousness seems to sound something more than envy. As a man is not rightly called a reader save at that time when he is occupied in reading, so too a man is then rightly called envying when he is employing his spite. And from that which is *invidens*, envying, is *invidentia*, enviousness, named. Envy, therefore, then truly grows out into enviousness, when it so agitates the spirit that it [1356B] now scarcely at any time lets it rest. Enviousness, therefore, is a frequent envy, and one that does not let the spirit rest. But in the second beast, if I mistake not, enviousness is rightly understood. But, that this may grow clearer, let us hear how the prophetic word describes it: *And behold,* he says, *another beast, like a bear, stood on one side, and there were three rows in its mouth and in its teeth, and thus they said to it: Arise, eat much flesh [n: (Dan. VII)]*. Now the bear, as we all know, is an ugly animal, and one that is wont to dwell in remote and hidden places; and in this very thing it bears the form of envy. For envy herself too (as blushing at her own foulness) ever strives to lie hidden. But the bear is a malicious and savage animal, and perhaps such is the vice of envy. Envy is the hatred [1356C] of another's happiness; and what is more malicious? What else, therefore, is envy but a light-shunning and lurking malice? But enviousness is a boiling malice, and one that rages in secret. And the bear is a very restless animal, so that when tied to a stake it scarcely ever ceases either to go round about, or, with its feet fixed, to toss its head now to this side, now to that; and in this it has the form not only of envy, but of enviousness, which scarcely for a moment lets the spirit rest. But it is said of this beast that it stood on one side. Not yet, therefore, in this state does a man utterly forsake good things, nor yet, as in the former state, does he extend himself unto all things. It stands therefore on one side, because in certain good things it still seems to persist. For no one [1356D] becomes suddenly most base, just as, on the opposite side, no one becomes suddenly highest. As it were, therefore, it still stands on one side, since old custom still draws the man to do some good things. Behold that in this state the spirit is not yet unbridled even to open malice, in so far as it is either restrained by fear or checked by shame.

## CHAPTER IX. *Of the evil of enviousness, by what steps it is wont to increase.*

And three rows, he says, were in its mouth, and in its teeth. The Scripture itself determines how there were three rows in its mouth, that is, in its teeth. But what do we more rightly understand by the teeth than the bites of malice, of enviousness? But who knows not how familiar, and homely, and as it were [1357A] properly proper it is to envy to gnaw another's life, and to tear it with the bites of disparagement? But this evil is wont to increase by certain steps. For there are in men some things manifestly evil, and some doubtful, so that it may come into ambiguity whether they are good or evil. But a livid mind is wont always to exaggerate manifest evils the more manifoldly, to turn whatever is doubtful to the worse part, and open goods (since it cannot deny them) to darken by what art it can, and to diminish at least something of them. The first is of speaking-against, the second of derogation, the third of detraction. Speaking-against is when a biting and reproving speech is occupied about that, or is made on account of that evil, which is truly in a man. He who knows what it is *rogare*, to entreat, can from the opposite recognize what [1357B] it is *derogare*, to derogate, since they answer to one another by contraries just as to persuade and to dissuade do. Does it not seem to thee derogation when to one who holds a good estimation of some other man it is said, do not so believe, do not so esteem, thou art mistaken, thou art deceived, it is far otherwise than thou thinkest, thou believest darkness to be light and puttest bitter for sweet. This assuredly has no place in open goods, because it cannot bend the things that are manifest to the other side. But to detract is to be willing to diminish at least something of open goods, when thou canst not utterly empty them out. For he detracts who by barking against draws back something from that whereby he believes a man's reputation to be the more glorious. Speaking-against, therefore, is the disseminating of an evil opinion. Derogation, the emptying out of a good opinion. Detraction, the thinning of a good opinion. The tongue [1357C] that speaks against the Psalmist feared, when he said: *All the day long my shame is before me, and the confusion of my face hath covered me, at the face of him that reproacheth and speaketh against me [n: (Psal. XLIII)]*. [var: Vulg. *a voce exprobrantis*, "at the voice of him that reproacheth"] He touches the derogators in what he says elsewhere: *They were catching at the soul of the just, and were condemning innocent blood [n: (Psal. XCIII)]*. [var: Vulg. *Captabunt … condemnabunt*, "they shall catch … they shall condemn"] He expresses the detractors when he says: *They that render evil for good detracted from me, because I followed goodness [n: (Psal. XXXVII)]*. Behold, thou hast the three rows of teeth in the manifoldness of detractions, derogations, speakings-against.

## CHAPTER X. *How from the vice of enviousness the mind falls into the vice of fraudulence.*

Now it is easy to see how rightly there befits this [1357D] beast that which is set in the last place when it is said: Arise, eat much flesh. For what is it to eat flesh, but to tear another's weak things with a slanderous tooth? For they who gladly gnaw another's life, who zealously serve derogations, who delightedly pluck at the infirmities of their neighbours, what else do they but eat flesh? Such gnawers of flesh the Prophet had already known by experience, when he said: *They that harm me draw near upon me, to eat my flesh [n: (Psal. XXVI)]*. But that which is said, Arise, eat, what, I ask, will it be, a command or a permission, a suggestion or an instigation? But if we think it was said by good angels, let us consequently understand that in their words also only a permission was made. Such is that which is said to Judas [1358A]: *That which thou dost, do quickly [n: (Joan. XIII)]*. But if it stands that it was said by evil angels, we can understand in words of this kind both a suggestion and an instigation. For evil spirits are ever wont to suggest malignant things to malignant minds, and to instigate them unto every malice. How malicious a thing it is, and how pernicious, to serve detractions, and in this for each man to satisfy his own vice, thou canst note from that sentence of Solomon: *If a serpent bite in silence, he that detracteth secretly hath nothing the less [n: (Eccli. X)]*. Does not that accord with this sentence which the Psalmist says of such men: *Their throat is an open sepulchre, with their tongues they acted deceitfully, the venom of asps is under their lips [n: (Psal. V)]*. O evil execrable, and deadly as much to him that speaks as to him that hears: [1358B] Arise, he says, eat much flesh. And what else does the bear, what else does this wild brute know, but either to suck its own paws, or to tear the flesh of others? What other office, I say, does the monster of enviousness discharge, but either to bewail its own troubles, or to pluck at the weak things of others? But would that they tore the flesh only, would that they spared at least the bones! But now they mangle all things, they tear all things, whence it comes about that at length at some time they become hateful to all. For he who speaks, I say, cannot lie hidden. But when they begin to be recognized, they begin likewise to be despised and to be held in hatred. But an envious and proud mind, with how great a grief thinkest thou it is burned, with how great a spite is it tormented, when it sees others advance from day to day unto better things, and itself daily decrease in every opinion, and grow more and more [1358C] worthless? Whence it often comes about that it turns itself to crafty devices, while with the utmost zeal and solicitude it seeks how it may either spread wide its own glory, or becloud the glory of others. It begins therefore from thenceforth to dissemble sanctity, and through hypocrisy little by little to give itself over to every fraudulence. Thus the leopard succeeds the bear, while a slippery mind flows down from vice to vice, and through the evil of enviousness falls into fraudulence.



## CHAPTER XI. *On the vice of fraudulence.*

Then without doubt fraud grows into fraudulence, when out of much malice it now befalls the mind that it is altogether willing to deceive when it can, and after [1358D] much use and practice there is nonetheless at hand to it, through much cunning now, that it can easily deceive when it wills. For what else is fraudulence than a cunning malice, as prone to every fraud as it is prompt? Rightly is the fraudulence of hypocrites figured in the leopard, which is sprinkled over its whole body with certain spots. For hypocrites indeed make a show of holiness in their work, but what they love is perverse; and what lives within in the affection must needs at some time break forth and appear in the work. And so they that are of this sort do good things openly and evil things in secret. They therefore who break forth stealthily into works of dissoluteness, or as often as they can do it excusably, what else do they do than sprinkle the body of their own action with certain spots? Let us see, then, [1359A] of what sort this beast is said to be, which is described in the third place. *After these things,* he says, *I was beholding, and lo, another as it were a leopard, and it had wings as of a bird, four upon itself, and four heads were upon the beast, and power was given to it [n: (Dan. VII)]*. [var: Vulg. Dan. 7:6 reads *et ecce alia quasi pardus* and *quatuor capita erant in bestia*, "in the beast"; Migne prints *altera* for *alia*, and *super bestiam*, "upon the beast"] Give heed how rightly those that are designated in this beast are said to have wings. Certainly when birds fly, they lift themselves above themselves. Certainly when they will to fly, they suspend themselves through the void. Do not minds of this sort lift themselves above themselves, and suspend themselves through the void, when for the sake of ambition and empty glory they stretch out the observances of a hard strictness almost beyond the measure of human possibility? For to exercise the zeals of virtue, and not to care for or to seek the merits or the rewards of the virtues, what else is it than to suspend oneself on high through [1359B] the void? And what else is it to have many heads, than to do nothing simply? For as in the wings we understand occupation and exercise, so in the head we understand intention. For the head rules the whole body, and all our action is subservient to the intention.

## CHAPTER XII. *On the evil of fraudulence, how multiform it is in work.*

Do you wish to know yet more fully what kind of wings fraudulence is wont to have? That I may therefore briefly express what I think: let one be called the wing of simulation, another of dissimulation, the third of ostentation, the fourth of excuse. For simulating minds, and those that are slaves to hypocrisy, are wont; they are wont, I say, not only to boast of the goods they have, but even to simulate that they have [1359C] goods which they have not at all. On the contrary they are wont craftily to excuse manifest evils, but hidden evils (as if they had them not at all) cunningly to dissimulate. Simulation and dissimulation are concerning hidden things. But simulation concerning hidden goods, dissimulation concerning hidden evils. On the other side, however, ostentation and excuse are wont to be concerning manifest things; but the former concerning manifest goods, the latter concerning manifest evils. For in those goods which are manifest and cannot be denied, ostentation has its place, just as in manifest evils alone excuse is sought. Our left hand is brought forth into the midst more rarely than the right, and by that very fact is more rarely seen. Rightly therefore by the left we understand the more hidden things, and rightly by the right the more manifest. And so the wings [1359D] of simulation and of dissimulation seem to belong to the left, even as the wings of ostentation and of excuse to the right. Thou hast therefore in ostentation and simulation the first pair of wings. And thou hast likewise in excuse and dissimulation the second pair of wings. For ostentation and simulation are concerning goods alone. But the former concerning true and manifest ones, as it were a wing on the right; the latter concerning feigned ones, as it were a wing on the left. On these two wings they fly, and commending themselves to their neighbours and publishing abroad their own reputation, they spread their glory round about. But excuse and dissimulation are concerning evils alone: the former concerning manifest ones, as it were one wing on the right; the latter concerning hidden ones, as it were the other wing on the left. As on the two former, as has been said, they fly, so on these latter they veil their own [1360A] body. For beyond doubt simulators and hypocrites are wont, on this side and on that, under the covering of excuse and of dissimulation, to veil their hinder and more shameful parts.

## CHAPTER XIII. *On the evil of fraudulence, how manifold it is in intention.*

Behold, let us see concerning the number of the wings and concerning the plurality of the heads. Now we know that the fraudulence of hypocrites, in all that it keeps doing, pants after the advancement of its own honour. For all that it does, or intends in doing, is a slave to ambition. But ambition is nothing else than the coveting of honour. Now the first species of this evil is the coveting of liberty, the second the coveting of dignity, the third the coveting of authority, the fourth the coveting of power. Behold how ambition [1360B] divides itself into four heads, to which, as has been said, the whole action of hypocrites is subservient. The coveting of liberty is when one now shrinks from being under others. The coveting of dignity is, by courting higher things, always to pant from step to step. The coveting of authority is when one now courts to appear to all a man of great counsel and of holiness, and that whatever is to be established or defined should hang upon his counsel or his judgment. The coveting of power is when one now courts to be set over others. We often see even those who have professed a voluntary obedience, how gladly, how eagerly they take upon themselves occupations troublesome enough and burdensome, that from the occasion of their own administration they may obtain a somewhat greater liberty of going out, of speaking, of acting. What does this, I ask, unless the ambition of liberty? [1360C] We see others striving always from step to step, and those who are of a lower grade aspiring from the subdiaconate, subdeacons to the diaconate, deacons to the presbyterate; and though from it they have perhaps acquired nothing of greater liberty or of power, yet they judge it no small thing to hold at least a higher place than the rest. But whence is this in them, unless from the ambition of dignity? That man of that Achitopel, speaking, teaches us what the ambition of authority can do in certain men; the traitor and parricide Absalon teaches us what the ambition of power avails.

## CHAPTER XIV. *How from the vice of fraudulence the mind falls into the vice of shamelessness.*

[1360D] But it is to be noted what is said of this beast: That power was given to it; and beyond doubt, by the wonderful and hidden judgment of God, the things which hypocrites can do are almost greater, and they do them and keep the observances of a stricter life, than they who afflict themselves for God's sake; and although it is established that all flesh is hay, and all the glory thereof as the flower of hay [var: Vulg. Isa. 40:6 *flos agri*, "the flower of the field"], yet the followers of vanity often labour more for a vain and transitory glory than true emulators for the true and eternal glory. But it is very difficult, nay almost impossible, that men of this sort should be able long to lie hid. Hear what Solomon thinks here, when he says: *He that walketh simply, walketh confidently, but he that perverteth his ways shall be made manifest [n: (Prov. X)]*. It behoves therefore that those who walk doubly and fraudulently, and the perverters of their own ways, [1361A] be made manifest, and that that prophetic word be fulfilled in them: *Uncover thy shame, lay bare thy shoulder, make bare thy legs, pass over the rivers, thy ignominy shall be revealed, and thy reproach shall be seen. [n: (Isa. XLVII)]*. Men of this sort, when they have been caught in this state of fraudulence, often rush yet into worse things: for when they despair of being able any longer to lie hid in their own depravities, when they lose that one joy of their boasting without any hope of recovering it, straightway they break forth into open shamelessness. Behold how through fraudulence a man is cast headlong into shamelessness.



## CHAPTER XV. *On the vice of shamelessness.*

Give heed, I beseech thee, how bestial, and more [1361B] than bestial, a life it is, when human shame has been cast off, to give oneself headlong to all things, and the divine gaze or the countenances of men, not to blush even at things to be blushed at, and at length at some time to unbridle oneself unto every malice. For what else is shamelessness than a headlong and unbridled malice? Let us therefore now hear what is said of this last beast: *After these things I was beholding,* he says, *in the vision of the night, and lo, a fourth beast, terrible and wonderful, and exceeding strong. It had great iron teeth, eating and breaking in pieces, and treading down the rest with its feet. But it was unlike to the other beasts which I had seen before it, and it had ten horns [n: (Dan. VII)]*. Behold, he says a beast, and yet what beast it is, or to what [1361C] beast it is like, he does not say, as in the foregoing. See therefore what kind of monster among the vices this is, which is now mystically described, to which none among so many monsters of beasts is found comparable. Now we know that the mind which has been corrupted by envy and by shamelessness spares thenceforth no one at all, since it spares neither itself nor others. For envy indeed takes away from a man love and compassion for his neighbour; but shamelessness, moderation and circumspection of himself. And often they that are of this sort bear many labours, many griefs, patiently, nay even gladly, that they may afflict others; and they had rather themselves endure misery than not inflict it upon others. See therefore how wonderful, or rather how horrible a thing it is, that a man, forgetful of humanity, should put off the man, and put on a beastly heart, nay one more than beastly. [1361D] And lo, he says, a fourth beast, terrible and wonderful, and exceeding strong. Is it not strong, and exceeding strong, which, for the sake of inflicting evils upon its neighbours, is so patient in bearing evils? But he is said to have iron teeth and nails who is unbridled unto every cruelty. For iron, which tames all the other metals, rightly enough designates cruelty. He therefore receives iron teeth and nails who rages in words and in works against his neighbours, Of another beast it was said that it devoured very much flesh. But of this one it is said that it breaks all things in pieces. It therefore which breaks all things in pieces seizes, condemns, annihilates not only the weak things of others, but the strong as well. And so it tears all things by defamation, and what it cannot defame it treads down by contempt. But that I may be silent about the rest, [1362A] in this chiefly does this beast seem to be unlike the others, that in this last state the wicked mind knows not how to blush. It was unlike, he says, to the other beasts which I had seen before it, and it had ten horns.

## CHAPTER XVI. *How the mind is hardened through the vice of shamelessness, and first against God.*

O bloody beast, which both by contempt treads down all its inferiors, and with the horns of rebellion assails its superiors! Would that of horns of this kind might be fulfilled that which he who speaks in the psalm profitably threatens: *And I will break all the horns of sinners, and I will exalt the horns of the just [n: (Psal. LXXIV)]*. [var: Vulg. Ps. 74:11 *exaltabuntur cornua justi*, "the horns of the just shall be exalted"; the received text is passive, not a first-person promise] Let us therefore ask more diligently what sort of horns shamelessness has, [1362B] with which it is wont to fight back or to assail. But this we know, that horns grow out of the flesh, and harden above the sensibility of the flesh. Now in ten ways, as it seems to me, the shameless soul grows hard, and loses that sensibility of heart which it is fitting to have. For in three ways the mind grows hard toward God, in three toward itself, and in four ways against its neighbour. Toward God, through arrogance, through self-exaltation, through contumacy. Arrogance is when it ascribes to itself that which it has received from God. Self-exaltation is when it lifts itself above that which it has received: through arrogance it glories in itself over what it has, through self-exaltation even over what it has not. Through arrogance and self-exaltation [1362C] it comes about that the divine grace is deservedly withdrawn, and that it is hardened unto contumacy; and being deserted, it is made a transgressor. But there is never a willing transgression of a precept without contempt of God. Contumacy therefore is when it despises God commanding and contemns him threatening. Through arrogance the goodness of God is assailed, through self-exaltation the truth of God, through contumacy the power of God. For certain we know, and without any hesitation, that it is God who worketh all things according to good will [n: (Ephes. I)]. [var: Vulg. Eph. 1:11 reads *qui operatur omnia secundum consilium voluntatis suae*, "who worketh all things according to the counsel of his will"; *pro bona voluntate* is the phrase of Phil. 2:13] And so from the goodness of God alone is whatever of good is, or can be, in us. He therefore who arrogates to himself that whereby he ought to have glorified God, what else does he do than despoil the goodness of God of its glory? He who lifts himself above that which he is wills that to be believed false which is true, and [1362D] true which is false. But he who leans upon falsehood is convicted of striving against the truth of God. But whatever the wicked mind presumes through contumacy looks chiefly to the contumely of the divine power.

## CHAPTER XVII. *How through the vice of shamelessness, the mind grows hard in regard to itself.*

By three steps of headlong fall, nonetheless, the human spirit is wont to grow stiff in regard to itself: by the binding of the mind, by the hardening of the mind, by the unbridling of the mind. The binding of the mind is when a habitual delight so insolubly entangles it that it cannot, even when it wills, entangle itself from the custom of sin; when it now does not at all cease from sinning, so far as impunity permits it. See how him whom arrogance [1363A] despoils, self-exaltation enervates; and him whom self-exaltation enervates, contumacy casts headlong; and him whom contumacy casts headlong into sinning, the custom of sinning afterwards little by little binds. To such a soul, and so bound, that voice of the prophet cries: *Loose the bonds of thy neck, O captive daughter of Sion [n: (Isa. LII)]*. Loosed from such bonds and free, it can sing with the Psalmist: *Thou hast broken my bonds, to thee will I sacrifice the sacrifice of praise [n: (Psal. CXV)]*. But the hardening of the heart is when he that is of this sort can now be restrained from his own excesses by fear of no punishment, by no severity of vengeance. And, that we may use open examples, the shameful know what condemnation they undergo, or ought to undergo, when caught in their shameful deeds, and yet neither are they able to restrain themselves from the perpetration of shameful deeds. It is one thing not to be able to restrain one's own desire [1363B] when impunity allures, and another not to be able to beware even of that which is not committed without the utmost peril. In the former step, therefore, the spirit is insolubly bound to fault; in this one it is hardened, as it were insensibly, against punishment. In that one shame, in this one fear also, is trodden underfoot. Hear what is said of those who in this step are hardened against punishment: *I have struck,* he says, *them, and they grieved not [n: (Jer. V)]*. [var: Vulg. Jer. 5:3 *Percussisti eos*, "Thou hast struck them"; the received text addresses God in the second person, and the same verse is printed at 1276C of this work as *Percussi filios vestros*] The unbridling of the mind is when without any hesitation or drawing back the spirit exposes itself to every transgression, and, the bit of shame and the bridle of fear being shaken off, rushes headlong into all things, and becomes thenceforth as the horse and the mule which have no intellect [n: (Psal. XXXI)]. In the two former the spirit, by its own desires, even when it resists, [1363C] is overcome. But in this step it does not resist at all, but, whatever wind of temptation blows, is snatched in every direction, according to that which the prophet imprecates: *My God, set them as a wheel, and as stubble before the face of the wind [n: (Psal. LXXXII)]*. But as in the three first horns it assails God, so in the three following it fights back against God. For by the binding, the hardening, the unbridling of itself, the ill-fortified mind strongly resists, lest any impulse of divine fear should be able easily to humble it.

## CHAPTER XVIII. *How through the vice of shamelessness, the mind grows hard toward its neighbour.*

Four still remain of the aforesaid horns: the horn [1363D] of abjection, the horn of objection, the horn of dejection, the horn of subjection. By these four steps the wicked mind is hardened against its neighbour, and, what is worse, against those to whom it owes a humble service. For as with iron nails it treads down its inferiors, so with these four horns of rebellion it is armed against its superiors. For the shameless soul, which has once shaken off the yoke of fear, rises up now with wicked rashness against its own mastery. And so it rebels with the horn of abjection, when it now disdains to obey; with the horn of objection, when it strives always and everywhere strongly to resist the endeavours of its own prelates; with the horn of dejection, when it strives to cast down its own prelates; with the horn of subjection, when it now strives even to subject them to itself. Behold how the evil [1364A] rages abroad; behold by what steps the depraved soul is hardened unto the utmost shamelessness; behold in what manner a man is brought even to this, that *he neither fears God nor reverences man [n: (Luc. XVIII)]*. [var: Vulg. Luc. 18:2 *qui Deum non timebat, et hominem non reverebatur*, "who feared not God, nor regarded man"]



## CHAPTER XIX. *How the mind, when it has come into the depth of evils, often falls even into despair.*

But the depraved soul often, when it has come into the depth of evils, after all evils loses even the hope of coming to itself again, and falls into despair. This is that last horn, namely the evil of despair; a horn, I say, both little through diffidence, and, beyond the rest, hard through the obstinacy of diffidence. *I was considering,* he says, *the horns, and lo, another little horn sprang out of the midst of them, and three of [1364B] the first horns were plucked up before its face. And behold, eyes as it were the eyes of a man were in this horn, and a mouth speaking great things [n: (Dan. VII)]*. This horn arises out of the midst of the others, because by the binding of the heart, the hardening of the heart, and unbridling, the mind is chiefly cast headlong into despair. For when out of these three a man has begun to lose power over himself, he begins likewise little by little to despair of salvation. But the evil of despair renders the spirit not so much swollen as timid, and in that very thing casts down the horn of contumacy. The evil of despair is wont not so much to lift the spirit up as to cast it down, and therefore the horn of self-exaltation cannot stand before its face. The evil of despair makes the spirit the more disparaging of its own powers, because it always [1364C] compels it to fear more than is fitting: whence it is that the horn of arrogance is not able to stand before its presence. The soul that has once despaired of its own salvation, and is utterly forsaken by divine grace, when it feels that it cannot resist an inveterate custom, and cannot restrain itself from its own depravity, is often wont to show itself excusable, and to pour back its own fault upon the Creator. And this is for the horn of despair to have eyes as it were of a man, and a mouth speaking great things. Man alone among the other living things is strong in reason and shrewd in prudence. When therefore, after the evil of despair, anyone has begun cunningly to weave, and shrewdly to put forward, for the proof of his own excuse, causes as it were reasonable, he seems to have eyes as it were of a man. It must be, they say, as it has been predestined; [1364D] who can resist the will of God, who his ordinance? And such as he willed us, such he made us. For whatsoever he would he hath done, in heaven and in earth, in the sea and in all the deeps [n: (Psal. CXXXIV)]. [var: Vulg. Ps. 134:6 *Omnia quaecumque voluit Dominus fecit in caelo, in terra, in mari, et in omnibus abyssis*: the received text names the Lord as the subject, and does not join the members with *et*] What then can we do, what are we? Can we create our own merits for ourselves? It is not, assuredly, of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that showeth mercy [n: (Rom. IX)]. Why then does he not show mercy? Why does he not work in us that which pleases him, who worketh all things in all as he wills? [n: (Ephes. I.)] [var: Vulg. Eph. 1:11 reads *qui operatur omnia secundum consilium voluntatis suae*; the words printed here are those of I Cor. 12:6 and 12:11, *qui operatur omnia in omnibus … dividens singulis prout vult*] A mouth speaking great things, and things as mad as they are empty. That thou mayest excuse thyself, thou accusest God; that thou mayest justify thyself, thou blasphemest God? Is not this seen to be that which is read in what follows, and he shall speak words against the Most High. [var: Vulg. Dan. 7:25 *sermones contra Excelsum loquetur*; Migne prints *Altissimum* for *Excelsum*] Behold by what steps one descends to the lowest things. Behold whence, [1365A] whither, and in what manner one comes from an excessive levity of spirit to a shameless unbridling of spirit, from much presumption of heart to the last despair.

We have heard how the mind, falling ever from evil into worse, is at last led down into the depth of evils. Let us hear how, or whence, that same mind is sometimes, after many and last evils, reformed to the integrity of rightness. For if we rightly judge the things that go before and that follow after in this vision, I think that in this mystical description we recognize what we read in the Apostle: Since where [1366A] iniquity abounded, grace also did more abound. [var: Vulg. Rom. 5:20 *Ubi autem abundavit delictum, superabundavit gratia*, "where the offence abounded"; the noun printed here is *iniquitas*, that of Matt. 24:12] From this place of Scripture it is easy to observe that no malice of ours can conquer the divine mercy. For what is it that, after the beasts succeeding one another, a throne being set, the Ancient of days sat, unless that after many and frequent declines of the vices, he who is eternal before all times, through visiting grace, fixes the slippery heart in a firm stability of purpose, and establishes for himself a dwelling? And what is it that the power of the beasts is taken away, unless that through visiting grace, the tyranny of the vices being lulled to sleep, the kingdom of sin is destroyed?
